nodes.label: TSC
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md
nodes.description: Everolimus, a rapamycin analog (rapalog), is FDA approved for anti-seizure therapy in tuberous sclerosis complex after many years of off-label use. The EXIST-3 multicenter phase III study evaluated adjunctive everolimus in patients with treatment-resistant epilepsy due to TSC and showed significant reduction in seizure frequency, with approximately 40% of patients in the high-dose group achieving at least a 50% reduction in seizures compared to only 15% in placebo. The success reflects TSC's clearly defined molecular etiology, with highly penetrant mutations driving mTOR hyperactivation making the pathway an actionable target.

nodes.label: Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption
nodes.description: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), also known as the afterburn effect, is the elevated oxygen consumption that persists after an exercise session and represents the energy expended in excess of resting values during recovery. EPOC accounts for a portion of the total energy cost of exercise beyond the exercise itself, typically contributing an additional 7-15 percent of the exercise energy cost depending on intensity and duration. Because EPOC elevates the metabolic rate for hours after training, it is often cited to justify high-intensity training for weight management, although Speakman's analysis argues that the quantitative contribution to total daily expenditure is smaller than commonly claimed.

nodes.label: Post-exercise Energy Expenditure
nodes.description: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), also known as the afterburn effect, is the elevated oxygen consumption that persists after an exercise session and represents the energy expended in excess of resting values during recovery. EPOC accounts for a portion of the total energy cost of exercise beyond the exercise itself, typically contributing an additional 7-15 percent of the exercise energy cost depending on intensity and duration. Because EPOC elevates the metabolic rate for hours after training, it is often cited to justify high-intensity training for weight management, although Speakman's analysis argues that the quantitative contribution to total daily expenditure is smaller than commonly claimed.

nodes.label: Resting Metabolic Rate
nodes.description: Exercise causes a transient but significant elevation of resting metabolic rate that outlasts the exercise bout itself. A number of studies show RMR is increased for at least 24-48 hours following vigorous exercise, and residual increases are detectable even up to 3 days after a single session in some protocols. The elevation appears largely independent of the intensity of the exercise, with high-intensity interval exercise providing comparable post-exercise energy expenditure to continuous moderate exercise when matched for work. This post-exercise elevation is one mechanism by which physical activity raises daily energy expenditure beyond the direct cost of the exercise itself.

nodes.label: Total Daily Energy Expenditure
nodes.description: Exercise raises total daily energy expenditure (TEE) through several mechanisms acting together: the direct metabolic cost of the exercise bout itself, the elevated resting metabolic rate and excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) that persist after the session, and increases in nonexercise activity thermogenesis and appetite in some individuals. Speakman uses doubly labelled water studies to show that while athletes have high TEE, the contribution of exercise to TEE in moderately active people is modest in magnitude, and that an exercise-induced rise in TEE of 10-15 percent is not necessarily compensated by reduced activity in other parts of the day.

nodes.label: Physical Activity
nodes.description: Exercise is defined as planned, structured, and repetitive physical activity performed specifically to improve or maintain physical fitness, and it constitutes a subset of total physical activity, which also includes occupational activity, domestic activity, and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). In the energy balance framework of the Speakman review, exercise is the most flexible and controllable component of total daily energy expenditure, and its contribution to daily energy use is quantified through doubly labelled water studies. Because exercise is a voluntary component, it is the primary target of public-health interventions aimed at raising daily energy expenditure.

nodes.label: Appetite
nodes.description: An important conclusion of the Speakman review is that exercise does not reliably increase appetite, and that in many individuals appetite is suppressed both during and for a period after exercise, an effect that can persist for up to 24 hours in some protocols. This is counter to the common belief that increased exercise necessarily drives increased food intake. When exercise does raise energy intake, the increase is generally smaller than the energy cost of the exercise, so a net negative energy balance is usually achieved. These findings support the view that exercise contributes to weight control by raising expenditure without a fully compensatory increase in intake.

nodes.label: Mitohormesis
nodes.description: Physical exercise is proposed as a low-cost, non-pharmacological means to stimulate mitohormesis. Rodent models show that exercise stimulates a UPRmt response in muscle and other tissues, and mitokines including GDF15 and MOTS-c are markedly stimulated by exercise, suggesting the potential to exploit these factors as exercise mimetics. However, too much exercise in humans actually impairs mitochondrial function, reduces ROS production, and worsens metabolic health, underscoring that the hormetic benefit of exercise depends on an appropriate dose and adequate recovery.

nodes.label: Fasting
nodes.description: Intermittent fasting and time-restricted feeding compress the eating window to 8-10 hours to allow a 14-16 hour daily fasting period, described as the simplest and most effective way to activate AMPK and mitophagy. Constant snacking and chronic overeating abolish the fasting-induced AMPK signal necessary for mitophagy. Fasting-induced mitochondrial recycling is a core mitohormetic mechanism, and stopping food intake at least 3-4 hours before sleep is highlighted as a key variable that instantly improves overnight HRV by allowing the body to focus entirely on cellular repair during sleep.

nodes.label: Fat Free Mass
nodes.description: Fat free mass (FFM) is the single best predictor of resting metabolic rate (RMR), explaining the majority of inter-individual variation in energy expenditure at rest. In the doubly labelled water and metabolic chamber studies reviewed by Speakman, FFM correlates with RMR with correlations typically above 0.7, with lean tissue contributing proportionally more than fat mass. The relationship reflects the high metabolic activity of lean tissues, especially the brain, liver, and skeletal muscle at rest. Consequently, any intervention that changes FFM, such as resistance training, is expected to alter RMR in proportion, though adaptive changes in metabolic efficiency can partially blunt this effect.

nodes.label: Regulated Cell Death
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
nodes.description: Ferroptosis is a regulated, iron-dependent cell death pathway in which cells lose their ability to regulate fats and eventually die, as distinct from unregulated necrotic death or other programmed death programs like apoptosis. It was discovered and named (originally 'oxytosis') by Pam Maher in 2001. The hallmark mechanism is accumulation of lipid peroxides to toxic levels, normally kept in check by glutathione, and the pathway is increasingly linked to neurodegeneration and age-related diseases. Because ferroptosis is druggable and genetically regulatable, it has become a promising therapeutic target alongside cellular senescence for supporting healthy aging and clearing dysfunctional cells.

nodes.label: FGF21
nodes.description: FGF21 induces thermogenesis and promotes energy expenditure through UCP1-dependent mechanisms. FGF21 promotes thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue, with protein restriction stimulating WAT beiging via FGF21 action in the brain through sympathetic signaling, and PR similarly increases thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue via an FGF21-dependent mechanism. These effects drive the increased energy expenditure observed with protein restriction and contribute to its metabolic benefits including reduced body weight and adiposity despite increased food intake. FGF21 also regulates lipid homeostasis, reducing circulating triglycerides, and mediates PR effects on senescence and inflammation in white adipose tissue.

nodes.label: Thermogenesis
nodes.description: FGF21 induces thermogenesis and promotes energy expenditure through UCP1-dependent mechanisms. FGF21 promotes thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue, with protein restriction stimulating WAT beiging via FGF21 action in the brain through sympathetic signaling, and PR similarly increases thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue via an FGF21-dependent mechanism. These effects drive the increased energy expenditure observed with protein restriction and contribute to its metabolic benefits including reduced body weight and adiposity despite increased food intake. FGF21 also regulates lipid homeostasis, reducing circulating triglycerides, and mediates PR effects on senescence and inflammation in white adipose tissue.

nodes.label: Protein Restriction
nodes.description: FGF21 is essential for the longevity and many of the metabolic benefits of protein restriction. Fgf21-null mice do not live longer on PR, while mice overexpressing Fgf21 show ~30-40% lifespan extension, identifying FGF21 as the critical downstream mediator. FGF21 promotes energy expenditure in part through UCP1-dependent thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue, acting in the brain through sympathetic signaling, and increases thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue. It also regulates lipid homeostasis, reduces circulating triglycerides, mediates PR effects on cellular senescence and inflammation in white adipose tissue, and reduces hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis in obese models.

nodes.label: FIS1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Fusion and Fission The fine-tune balance for cellular homeostasis.md
nodes.description: FIS1 is a tail-anchored outer mitochondrial membrane protein that functions as a receptor for DRP1, helping to recruit the fission machinery to mitochondria. In yeast, the FIS1 ortholog Fis1p is the main membrane anchor for the Dnm1p fission GTPase, whereas in mammalian cells FIS1 plays a more accessory role alongside MFF, MID49, and MID51, and may also mediate non-DRP1 functions such as recruiting proteasomal and autophagic machinery to mitochondria. Overexpression of FIS1 fragments mitochondria, whereas FIS1 knockdown produces elongated networks, confirming its pro-fission role, although its relative importance varies between cell types and conditions.

nodes.label: Fisetin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin is a potent antioxidant that scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species and stimulates endogenous antioxidant defenses including Nrf2-dependent expression of heme oxygenase-1, catalase, and superoxide dismutase. Its multiple hydroxyl groups allow it to donate electrons to quench free radicals and chelate metal ions that catalyze oxidative damage. The anti-oxidative action of fisetin underpins its protective effects in neuronal, cardiac, hepatic, and renal models of oxidative stress, and is considered a core mechanism shared with other polyphenols in its protective pharmacology.

nodes.label: Anti-oxidative Activity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin is a potent antioxidant that scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species and stimulates endogenous antioxidant defenses including Nrf2-dependent expression of heme oxygenase-1, catalase, and superoxide dismutase. Its multiple hydroxyl groups allow it to donate electrons to quench free radicals and chelate metal ions that catalyze oxidative damage. The anti-oxidative action of fisetin underpins its protective effects in neuronal, cardiac, hepatic, and renal models of oxidative stress, and is considered a core mechanism shared with other polyphenols in its protective pharmacology.

nodes.label: Senolytic Activity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin is among the most extensively studied naturally occurring senolytics. It selectively eliminates senescent cells by inhibiting key pro-survival pathways, including the PI3K/Akt and Bcl-xL pathways that senescent cells depend on to resist apoptosis. In aged mice, a short course of oral fisetin reduced senescent cell burden in multiple tissues, extended healthspan and median lifespan, and alleviated age-related dysfunction. This senolytic activity distinguishes fisetin from many flavonoids and has driven its evaluation in human clinical trials for osteoarthritis, frailty, and other age-related conditions, though pharmacokinetic limitations remain a central obstacle.

nodes.label: Anti-cancer Activity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin shows broad anti-cancer activity against cell lines derived from lung, colon, breast, prostate, liver, melanoma, bladder, and leukemia. It inhibits cancer cell proliferation by arresting the cell cycle at G1 or G2/M phase, induces apoptosis through the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway with activation of caspases and modulation of Bcl-2 family proteins, and suppresses invasion and metastasis by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Fisetin also sensitizes tumor cells to conventional chemotherapeutics. Its anti-cancer efficacy in animal models, however, has been limited by the low concentrations achieved after oral dosing.

nodes.label: Anti-diabetic Activity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin improves glucose homeostasis in experimental diabetes by enhancing insulin sensitivity and reducing hepatic glucose output. In diabetic rodents it lowers fasting blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin, reduces insulin resistance, and protects pancreatic beta cells, in part through its antioxidant activity and activation of AMPK signaling in liver and muscle. The review notes these metabolic benefits depend on adequate systemic exposure, which the oral delivery of unformulated fisetin may not achieve, further emphasizing the need for bioavailability-improving formulations to realize its therapeutic potential in humans.

nodes.label: Limited Oral Absorption
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin is incompletely and variably absorbed after oral administration due to its low water solubility and rapid first-pass metabolism by intestinal and hepatic conjugating enzymes. Bioavailability studies report low and highly variable plasma fisetin concentrations after oral dosing, with most of the absorbed compound present as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates rather than the parent aglycone. The review identifies this limited oral absorption as the principal barrier to clinical translation of fisetin's broad preclinical pharmacology, and the majority of the formulation strategies it discusses are specifically aimed at increasing the fraction of the orally administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.

nodes.label: Low Water Solubility
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin has extremely low water solubility, reported in the range of a few micrograms per milliliter, which classifies it as a Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) class II or IV drug. The low solubility, combined with poor permeability in some assessments and extensive intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, results in low and erratic oral bioavailability. Because dissolution is the rate-limiting step for oral absorption, much of the formulation research described in the review aims to increase the dissolution rate and apparent solubility of fisetin, using approaches such as solid dispersions, cyclodextrin inclusion complexes, and nanocrystals.

nodes.label: Neuroprotective Activity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin exerts neuroprotective effects that are attributed to its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and direct signaling actions in neurons. It protects cultured neurons from oxidative and excitotoxic insults, and in animal models of ischemia and Parkinson's disease it reduces neuronal loss and improves motor function. Fisetin also acts as a cognitive enhancer, improving learning and memory in healthy rodents through modulation of ERK-CREB signaling and by promoting synaptic plasticity, and it has been proposed as a candidate for Alzheimer's disease based on its ability to reduce beta-amyloid aggregation and tau pathology. These effects motivate delivery strategies aimed at improving brain exposure.

nodes.label: Bcl-xL
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin targets the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-xL, which is overexpressed in many cancer cells and in senescent cells as a survival mechanism. By inhibiting Bcl-xL and the related pro-survival pathways PI3K/Akt, fisetin lowers the threshold for apoptosis, promoting the death of senescent cells and chemoresistant cancer cells. The reliance of senescent cells on Bcl-xL is precisely the vulnerability that senolytics exploit, and fisetin's capacity to inhibit Bcl-xL is a key mechanistic basis for its senolytic activity and for its ability to sensitize tumors to existing therapies.

nodes.label: Inflammation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin suppresses inflammation through multiple converging mechanisms. It inhibits the NF-kB pathway, reducing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6, and it inhibits cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) and inducible nitric oxide synthase, decreasing prostaglandin and nitric oxide levels. It also blocks the STAT1 and STAT3 signaling cascades that amplify inflammatory gene expression. These anti-inflammatory actions contribute to fisetin's protective effects in arthritis, colitis, acute lung injury, and neuroinflammation models, and the anti-inflammatory activity is preserved in some nanoformulations of the compound.

nodes.label: Senolytic Agent
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin belongs to the pharmacological class of senolytics, agents that selectively kill senescent cells. Senolytics, exemplified by fisetin and dasatinib plus quercetin, exploit the reliance of senescent cells on anti-apoptotic survival networks. Fisetin's senolytic profile was identified in screening studies and validated in mouse models where it cleared senescent cells in adipose tissue, bone marrow, and other organs and extended healthspan. Because senescent cell accumulation drives tissue dysfunction and age-related disease, fisetin is now being evaluated in human trials, and its classification as a senolytic frames the therapeutic rationale for improving its bioavailability.

nodes.label: Flavonoids
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin (3,3',4',7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a natural flavonoid of the flavonol subclass found in strawberries, apples, persimmons, onions, and cucumbers, with strawberries being the richest dietary source. It has the molecular formula C15H10O6 and a molecular weight of 286.24 g/mol. Fisetin is widely studied as a senolytic agent, and its anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, anti-diabetic, and neuroprotective activities are reported in numerous in vitro and in vivo studies. Despite its broad pharmacological potential, fisetin has extremely poor aqueous solubility, which severely limits its oral bioavailability.

nodes.label: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Once absorbed, fisetin is extensively conjugated by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs) and sulfotransferases in the intestinal epithelium and liver, producing fisetin glucuronide and fisetin sulfate metabolites that circulate in the plasma. Because these conjugates have reduced biological activity and are rapidly excreted via bile and urine, the parent aglycone fisetin reaches only low concentrations in tissues. The extent of this phase II metabolism is a primary cause of fisetin's poor oral bioavailability and short plasma half-life, and it is one reason most preclinical efficacy studies have used intraperitoneal injection rather than oral dosing.

nodes.label: PI3K/Akt
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review.md
nodes.description: Fisetin regulates the PI3K/Akt pathway, which is central to both its anti-cancer and senolytic activities. In cancer cells, fisetin suppresses Akt phosphorylation and downstream mTOR signaling, reducing proliferation and survival, whereas in the context of senescence, fisetin's inhibition of PI3K/Akt removes a survival signal that senescent cells rely on, triggering their elimination. Fisetin's modulation of this pathway is dose-dependent and context-dependent, and it also crosstalks with MAPK/ERK signaling. Nanoformulations designed to raise fisetin exposure are expected to amplify these pathway-level effects by delivering higher intracellular concentrations.

nodes.label: FUNDC1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
nodes.description: FUNDC1 (FUN14 domain containing 1) is an outer mitochondrial membrane protein that serves as a mitophagy receptor for hypoxia-induced mitophagy, interacting directly with LC3 after dephosphorylation by phosphoglycerate mutase 5. ULK1 interacts with FUNDC1 and phosphorylates it at serine 17, enhancing FUNDC1 binding to LC3, and FUNDC1 interacts with OPA1 and DRP1 in a manner regulated by serine 13 phosphorylation during hypoxia or membrane potential loss. DRP1 can interact with overexpressed FUNDC1 to facilitate mitochondrial fragmentation and Parkin-mediated mitophagy.

nodes.label: GCN2
nodes.description: GCN2 is an evolutionarily conserved stress-responsive serine/threonine kinase activated by amino acid restriction through uncharged tRNAs, as well as by ribosome stalling and collision. Activated GCN2 phosphorylates eIF2alpha, which suppresses global protein synthesis while selectively promoting translation of ATF4, a key transcription factor that activates stress response and autophagy genes. This selective translation of ATF4 is a central feature of the integrated stress response engaged during protein restriction. Genetic evidence confirms GCN2's importance: Drosophila lacking Gcn2 die when amino acids are restricted, deletion of Gcn2 in yeast blocks dietary restriction lifespan extension, and GCN2 overexpression extends lifespan in both organisms.

nodes.label: ATF4
nodes.description: GCN2 is an evolutionarily conserved stress-responsive serine/threonine kinase activated by amino acid restriction through uncharged tRNAs, as well as by ribosome stalling and collision. Activated GCN2 phosphorylates eIF2alpha, which suppresses global protein synthesis while selectively promoting translation of ATF4, a key transcription factor that activates stress response and autophagy genes. This selective translation of ATF4 is a central feature of the integrated stress response engaged during protein restriction. Genetic evidence confirms GCN2's importance: Drosophila lacking Gcn2 die when amino acids are restricted, deletion of Gcn2 in yeast blocks dietary restriction lifespan extension, and GCN2 overexpression extends lifespan in both organisms.

nodes.label: Tryptophan
nodes.description: Tryptophan depletion caused by IDO1 activity activates the GCN2 stress kinase, which leads to cell cycle arrest, anergy, or apoptosis in effector T cells, since tryptophan is essential for T cell proliferation. This amino-acid starvation response is one of the two main mechanisms of IDO1-mediated immunosuppression, the other being kynurenine/aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling that promotes regulatory T cells. Together these pathways create an immunosuppressive microenvironment exploited by tumors, and this biology is the rationale for IDO1 inhibitors in immuno-oncology: blocking tryptophan catabolism is intended to relieve GCN2-driven T cell suppression and restore antitumor immunity.

nodes.label: Ghrelin
nodes.description: The metabolic hormone ghrelin, a major regulator of food intake, also exerts immunomodulatory and thymopoietic effects. Ghrelin binds immune cell subsets via ghrelin-specific receptors and localizes to lipid rafts of activated T cells. Dixit et al. reported that ghrelin reduces age-associated inflammatory responses in mice, and in aged thymus both ghrelin and growth hormone levels decrease in correlation with functional thymic involution and elevated inflammation.

nodes.label: Thymopoiesis
nodes.description: The metabolic hormone ghrelin, a major regulator of food intake, also exerts immunomodulatory and thymopoietic effects. Ghrelin binds immune cell subsets via ghrelin-specific receptors and localizes to lipid rafts of activated T cells. Dixit et al. reported that ghrelin reduces age-associated inflammatory responses in mice, and in aged thymus both ghrelin and growth hormone levels decrease in correlation with functional thymic involution and elevated inflammation.

nodes.label: Glutathione
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
nodes.description: Glutathione, an antioxidant, keeps lipid peroxides at steady levels and thereby staves off ferroptosis in healthy cells. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent cell death pathway in which the accumulation of lipid peroxides becomes toxic, and glutathione's antioxidant capacity is the canonical defense against this form of death. The Salk study's discovery is notable because the acid ceramidase axis sensitizes cells to ferroptosis without involving changes in glutathione levels, operating instead through lipid metabolism - an entirely novel, GPX4/GSH-independent pathway. This contrasts with the classical view that ferroptosis sensitivity is controlled chiefly by glutathione/GPX4-dependent peroxide neutralization.

nodes.label: Glycation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Aminoguanidine An AGE Product Inhibitor  Antiaging Systems Articles.md
nodes.description: Glycation is the product of the reaction between a sugar and the free amino group of proteins, referred to as cross-linking, and the accumulation of these glycation byproducts results in large, cross-linked molecules that inhibit the ability of the cell to function normally. Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) accumulate with age in tissues, contributing to arterial stiffening and cardiac enlargement. Levels of cross-linking products in diabetics are two to three times those of non-diabetics, and AGEs are believed to play an important role in the development of diabetic complications.

nodes.label: HAF-1
nodes.description: HAF-1 is an inner mitochondrial membrane ABC-transporter family protein in C. elegans that exports matrix-derived peptides into the cytosol to signal mitochondrial stress. Proteins degraded by matrix proteases generate peptides that exit the mitochondria through HAF-1 (analogous to the yeast Mdl1 transporter), and this peptide release triggers a nuclear transcriptional response involving the ubiquitin-like protein UBL-5, the homeobox transcription factor DVE-1, and ATFS-1. The mechanism is reminiscent of peptide-based quorum sensing in gram-positive bacteria, where peptides exported via ABC transporters activate two-component histidine kinase sensors.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Peptides
nodes.description: HAF-1 is an inner mitochondrial membrane ABC-transporter family protein in C. elegans that exports matrix-derived peptides into the cytosol to signal mitochondrial stress. Proteins degraded by matrix proteases generate peptides that exit the mitochondria through HAF-1 (analogous to the yeast Mdl1 transporter), and this peptide release triggers a nuclear transcriptional response involving the ubiquitin-like protein UBL-5, the homeobox transcription factor DVE-1, and ATFS-1. The mechanism is reminiscent of peptide-based quorum sensing in gram-positive bacteria, where peptides exported via ABC transporters activate two-component histidine kinase sensors.

nodes.label: Heart Rate Variability
nodes.description: HRV is highly individual and a universal normal range does not exist; factors such as age, sex, health conditions, and activity levels all shape an individual's baseline. General adult ranges only serve as rough guidelines, and HRV declines with age. More important than any single raw number is an individual's personal baseline trend: a sustained drop of 20 percent or more in average HRV is a far more insightful signal than a specific value on a standardized chart, making trends over 3 to 7 days the practical unit of analysis.

nodes.label: Autonomic Nervous System
nodes.description: HRV is directly controlled by the autonomic nervous system, which has two main branches with opposing effects. The sympathetic nervous system, the fight-flight-freeze system, releases adrenaline and cortisol that force the heart to beat faster and more rhythmically, lowering HRV. The parasympathetic nervous system, the rest-digest-and-repair system controlled heavily by the vagus nerve, allows more fluctuation between heartbeats, raising HRV. A high HRV therefore reflects strong vagal tone and a cardiovascular system that is highly responsive and flexible, while low HRV signals chronic stress, fatigue, or illness.

nodes.label: Honokiol
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol enhances the phosphorylation and activity of Akt, a central pro-survival kinase. In senescence-accelerated mice, oral honokiol (1 mg/kg) prevented age-related memory and learning deficits by preserving cholinergic neurons and enhancing Akt phosphorylation, part of the pro-survival PI3K/Akt pathway. Akt activation contributes to honokiol's neuroprotective effects against ischemia, beta-amyloid toxicity, and other insults, complementing its GABA-A modulation, Na+/K+-ATPase preservation, and anti-inflammatory actions.

nodes.label: Akt
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol enhances the phosphorylation and activity of Akt, a central pro-survival kinase. In senescence-accelerated mice, oral honokiol (1 mg/kg) prevented age-related memory and learning deficits by preserving cholinergic neurons and enhancing Akt phosphorylation, part of the pro-survival PI3K/Akt pathway. Akt activation contributes to honokiol's neuroprotective effects against ischemia, beta-amyloid toxicity, and other insults, complementing its GABA-A modulation, Na+/K+-ATPase preservation, and anti-inflammatory actions.

nodes.label: Inflammatory Pain
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol attenuates inflammatory pain, reducing formalin-induced paw-licking behavior in the inflammatory phase and thermal hyperalgesia in mice. It blocks nociceptive signaling evoked by NMDA, glutamate, substance P, and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), and decreases formalin-induced c-Fos protein expression in superficial laminae (I-II) of the L4-L5 lumbar dorsal horn. Compared with magnolol, honokiol is more selective for NMDA-induced behavioral responses and hyperalgesia. Its analgesic effects are multifactorial, involving both the inflammatory cascade and glutamatergic/NMDA receptor pathways.

nodes.label: Neuronal Death
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: While honokiol is neuroprotective at low doses, it increases neuronal death in vitro at higher concentrations: 100 uM applied directly to fetal cortical neurons is toxic. This dose-dependent biphasic behavior underscores the need to define human pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters before clinical administration. The potential neurotoxicity at supraphysiological concentrations, combined with honokiol's antithrombotic activity, highlights the importance of careful dosing and patient selection for any therapeutic use.

nodes.label: Blood-Brain Barrier
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol, a lipid-soluble lignan extracted from Magnolia species, readily crosses the blood-brain barrier to exert its effects in the central nervous system, including anti-tumorigenic and neuroprotective actions. Its lipid solubility allows it to pass lipid bilayers and act at multiple intracellular and membrane sites, a property shared with the structurally related anesthetic propofol and the analog magnolol. BBB penetration is a prerequisite for honokiol's anxiolytic, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-seizure activities in the brain.

nodes.label: Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol increases the activity of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), the enzyme responsible for GABA synthesis, in the cortex and hippocampus of mice. By enhancing GAD(65) and GAD(67) activity, honokiol can augment the brain's synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, which may complement its direct positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors. This combined effect on GABAergic tone is consistent with honokiol's central depressant, anticonvulsant, anxiolytic, and sleep-promoting pharmacological profile.

nodes.label: Arterial Thrombosis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol is a potent inhibitor of arterial thrombosis, acting through endothelial cell protection and stimulation of prostacyclin production. This antithrombotic effect is a safety consideration: caution is advised in coagulopathic patients, those with hemorrhagic stroke or hemorrhagic transformation after ischemic stroke, patients on warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin, and individuals with clotting disorders such as hemophilia or von Willebrand's deficiency. The bleeding risk must be weighed against honokiol's neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory benefits before clinical use.

nodes.label: Caspase-3
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol inhibits caspase-3 activity as part of its protection against beta-amyloid-induced neuronal death. In PC12 neuronal cultures challenged with Abeta, honokiol's neuroprotection was associated with decreased reactive oxygen species production, suppressed intracellular calcium elevation, and inhibition of the executioner caspase-3, thereby limiting apoptotic cell death. This anti-apoptotic action complements honokiol's mitochondrial preservation and pro-survival Akt signaling, contributing to its broad neuroprotective profile against amyloid toxicity and other neurodegenerative insults.

nodes.label: Neutrophils
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol inhibits neutrophil infiltration and reactive oxygen species production after cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, as measured by luminol-amplified chemiluminescence in neutrophils. By reducing the accumulation and oxidative burst of neutrophils at the site of ischemic injury, honokiol limits secondary tissue damage following stroke. This anti-inflammatory action is complemented by inhibition of glial NF-kappaB activation and cytokine production, together contributing to honokiol's ability to reduce infarct volume in focal cerebral ischemia-reperfusion models.

nodes.label: NMDA receptor
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol inhibits NMDA-evoked cationic influx, blocking excessive calcium entry that would otherwise drive excitotoxic neuronal injury and seizures. In rat cerebellar granule cells, honokiol inhibited repetitive firing by blocking glutamate-, NMDA-, and K+-evoked cation influx, and intraperitoneal honokiol (1 and 5 mg/kg) increased seizure thresholds in NMDA-infusion models, being more potent than magnolol. In ischemic conditions honokiol also disrupts PSD95-nNOS coupling at the NMDA receptor postsynaptic complex, preventing neurotoxic nitric oxide production downstream of NMDA receptor activation.

nodes.label: Diazepam
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: In animal behavioral models, honokiol produces anxiolysis at doses as low as 0.2 mg/kg with fewer motor and cognitive side effects than the benzodiazepine diazepam. The anxiolytic effect of honokiol is blocked by flumazenil, bicuculline, CCK-4, and caffeine, whereas these agents differentially affect diazepam's anxiolysis (e.g., caffeine enhances diazepam's effect), suggesting honokiol may act through partly alternative pathways in addition to GABA-A potentiation. This favorable side-effect profile is a key rationale for developing honokiol as an anxiolytic.

nodes.label: GABA_A receptor
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol is a positive allosteric modulator of both synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors, a known target of benzodiazepines and other anxiolytics. It shows markedly higher efficacy at receptors containing the delta subunit (900-1100% response) compared with alpha-beta-gamma-only receptors (300-500%), and it allosterically increases the affinity of low-affinity sites, increasing [3H]muscimol binding about three-fold. This GABA-A modulation underpins honokiol's anxiolytic, hypnotic, and anticonvulsant properties and is the basis of its sleep-promoting effects via the benzodiazepine site.

nodes.label: Mitochondria
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol preserves mitochondrial function as part of its neuroprotective mechanism. In preclinical ischemia models, honokiol maintained enzymatic mitochondrial function alongside Na+/K+-ATPase activity, and it protects neurons by preventing glucose- and ROS-mediated damage while preserving mitochondrial integrity. Honokiol also reduces beta-amyloid-induced neuronal death through decreased ROS production, suppressed intracellular calcium elevation, and inhibition of caspase-3 activity. These effects collectively position mitochondrial preservation and reduced oxidative stress as core components of honokiol's cytoprotective profile.

nodes.label: Sodium Potassium ATPase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol exerts neuroprotection in part by preserving the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase, the membrane pump critical for maintaining neuronal resting potential and ion homeostasis. In mouse models of cerebral ischemia, honokiol treatment preserved Na+/K+-ATPase activity and enzymatic mitochondrial function, correlating with reduced neuronal damage. Together with phosphorylation of pro-survival factors, preservation of mitochondrial function, and GABA-A modulation, Na+/K+-ATPase preservation is one of at least five distinct parallel mechanisms through which honokiol protects neurons from ischemic and oxidative injury.

nodes.label: Non-REM Sleep
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol promotes non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and shortens sleep latency. In mouse studies, honokiol at 10 and 20 mg/kg significantly decreased sleep latency and increased the amount of NREM sleep without affecting REM sleep or EEG power density, and it excited sleep-promoting neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area. These effects occur through the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor. The combined sleep-promoting and anxiolytic actions suggest a potential role for honokiol as an anesthetic adjunct.

nodes.label: Amyloid Beta
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol significantly decreased beta-amyloid (Abeta)-induced neuronal death in neuronal culture models of Alzheimer's disease. In screening nine compounds from Chinese herbs for anti-Alzheimer's activity, only honokiol and magnolol markedly reduced Abeta-induced cell death. The protective mechanism involves decreased ROS production, suppressed intracellular calcium elevation, and inhibition of caspase-3 activity. A honokiol-containing extract of Magnolia officinalis also prevented lipopolysaccharide-induced memory deficiency via antineuroinflammatory and antiamyloidogenic effects, supporting honokiol's therapeutic potential in Alzheimer's disease.

nodes.label: Stroke
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol reduces cerebral infarction in rodent stroke models, including both pre-ischemic and post-ischemic administration paradigms. In MCA occlusion models, intravenous honokiol significantly reduced total infarct volume without creating significant hemodynamic changes. The neuroprotection is multifactorial, involving inhibition of neutrophil infiltration and reactive oxygen species production, suppression of post-ischemic glucose intolerance, disruption of PSD95-nNOS coupling to prevent neurotoxic nitric oxide generation, and inhibition of glial NF-kappaB activation and inflammatory cytokine production during ischemia-reperfusion.

nodes.label: Epilepsy
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol and its structural analog magnolol have been evaluated as potential therapies for epilepsy and related seizure disorders. Intraperitoneal injections of honokiol or magnolol (1 and 5 mg/kg) increased seizure threshold in mice challenged with intravenous NMDA, with honokiol appearing more potent than magnolol. Honokiol also ameliorated the behavioral and neurotoxic impairments induced by NMDA injection into the cerebral ventricular system, showing augmented neuroprotection compared with tea polyphenol or memantine alone, supporting a role for honokiol in seizure prevention.

nodes.label: c-Fos
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol decreases formalin-induced c-Fos protein expression in the superficial (I-II) laminae of the L4-L5 lumbar dorsal horn in mice, a marker of spinal nociceptive neuron activation. Along with reducing formalin-induced paw-licking, this shows honokiol acts at the spinal level to dampen pain transmission during the inflammatory phase of the formalin model. Honokiol's ability to suppress dorsal-horn c-Fos parallels its blockade of NMDA-, glutamate-, substance P-, and PGE2-evoked nociception, supporting a spinal component to its analgesic activity.

nodes.label: TNF-alpha
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Honokiol reduces TNF-alpha secretion from LPS-stimulated mouse macrophages. Using lipopolysaccharide to induce inflammation, honokiol decreased tumor necrosis factor-alpha secretion, inhibited nitric oxide expression, blocked protein kinase C-alpha membrane translocation, and suppressed NF-kappaB activation in macrophages, with similar anti-inflammatory effects translated to human monocyte-derived dendritic cells. By dampening this central pro-inflammatory cytokine, honokiol mitigates the inflammatory cascade that drives neuroinflammation and inflammatory pain, making it a candidate adjunct for inflammatory conditions.

nodes.label: Hormesis
nodes.description: Atypical dose-response curves where a drug's effect does not follow a monotonic shape are referred to as hormetic or biphasic. This computational study shows that all hormetic networks share a similar core structure: an incoherent bivalent network motif centered on the target of the drug, in which the two interactions emanating from the target have net opposite (direct or indirect) effects over the downstream output. Around 18% of all three-node network topologies contain this motif, and topologies with an incoherent bivalent motif show a roughly five-fold increased probability of exhibiting hormesis compared with all topologies.

nodes.label: Incoherent Bivalent Motif
nodes.description: Atypical dose-response curves where a drug's effect does not follow a monotonic shape are referred to as hormetic or biphasic. This computational study shows that all hormetic networks share a similar core structure: an incoherent bivalent network motif centered on the target of the drug, in which the two interactions emanating from the target have net opposite (direct or indirect) effects over the downstream output. Around 18% of all three-node network topologies contain this motif, and topologies with an incoherent bivalent motif show a roughly five-fold increased probability of exhibiting hormesis compared with all topologies.

nodes.label: Network Motif
nodes.description: The study screened 5346 possible three-node network topologies of a coarse-grained signaling cascade model using a high-throughput computational approach, with 5000 parameter sets and 30 inhibitor concentrations per topology. More than 500 topologies show clear non-monotonic dose-response curves, and hormesis is favored in networks with a high number of repressing interactions on average, with the highest fraction of hormetic parameter sets in a topology composed of four repressing interactions. The probability of hormesis increases as the network becomes more complex, indicating it depends on the density and complexity of the network.

nodes.label: ATM
nodes.description: HSPA8 (HSC70), a member of the heat shock protein 70 family, directly binds phosphorylated ATM, as shown by p-ATM-mediated co-immunoprecipitation, and this interaction is specifically attenuated by apigenin treatment. ATM is the central modulator of the DNA damage response whose activation drives a persistent SASP; the HSPA8-ATM crosstalk represents an upstream transduction step in the transition from the acute stress-associated phenotype to the full SASP.

nodes.label: p38 MAPK
nodes.description: HSPA8 (HSC70) also directly binds p38 MAPK, a stress kinase downstream of TAK1 that, together with PI3K/Akt/mTOR engagement, supports formation of the chronic secretory phenotype (SASP). Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed that HSPA8 interacts with p38 MAPK, and this interaction is markedly weakened when senescent cells are treated with apigenin, whereas NPM1-p38 MAPK binding is unchanged. Because apigenin's target PRDX6 co-immunoprecipitates with HSPA8, the model is that apigenin restrains PRDX6 PLA2 activity, affecting HSPA8 activation and thereby abrogating its downstream interactions with both ATM and p38 MAPK, blocking multiple signaling sections that mediate SASP progression.

nodes.label: Human Growth Hormone
nodes.description: Human growth hormone (HGH) is widely used for rejuvenation and longevity, yet it actually accelerates aging and shortens lifespan. Growth hormone is a pro-aging hormone because it indirectly activates mTOR, and the hype around growth hormone is based on a single publication that misinterpreted its acute effects. Unlike HGH, the anti-aging effects of rapamycin are not based on a single paper or a wild guess but on the work of thousands of scientists studying mTOR and its inhibitors in diverse organisms from yeast to humans.

nodes.label: IGF1
nodes.description: Growth hormone (GH) is a peptide hormone that impacts the immune system via its stimulatory effects on insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). Hematopoietic cells can produce GH that indirectly promotes immune reconstitution via IGF-1 production, and IGF-1 provides anti-apoptotic signals and promotes immune cell survival. IGF-1 may also act directly on thymic stromal cells as a component of the thymus microenvironment cross-talk network and stimulate IL-7 production, and intrathymic IL-7 in turn promotes and regulates T cell survival and function.

nodes.label: Humanin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: FPRL1, a seven-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor, was the first humanin receptor to be described. Humanin acts as an agonist for FPRL1 by inducing Ca2+ mobilization and rapid activation of ERK1/2 signaling, a commonly induced downstream pathway of G-protein-coupled receptors. In neuroblasts, both the 42-aa form of beta-amyloid peptide and humanin activate FPRL1, but only Abeta42 is cytotoxic, and this cytotoxicity is reversed by humanin, suggesting that the neuroprotective effects of humanin might be accomplished by competitively binding to FPRL1, which may contribute to its cytoprotective aspects.

nodes.label: FPRL1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: FPRL1, a seven-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor, was the first humanin receptor to be described. Humanin acts as an agonist for FPRL1 by inducing Ca2+ mobilization and rapid activation of ERK1/2 signaling, a commonly induced downstream pathway of G-protein-coupled receptors. In neuroblasts, both the 42-aa form of beta-amyloid peptide and humanin activate FPRL1, but only Abeta42 is cytotoxic, and this cytotoxicity is reversed by humanin, suggesting that the neuroprotective effects of humanin might be accomplished by competitively binding to FPRL1, which may contribute to its cytoprotective aspects.

nodes.label: BAX
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: Humanin was cloned by a third group as a binding partner of Bax, a central pro-apoptotic protein that translocates to the mitochondria to initiate a cell death signal. The humanin-Bax complex is retained in the cytoplasm and this interaction protects cells from apoptosis. Humanin also prevents Bax translocation and activation in response to staurosporine, preventing the subsequent release of cytochrome c into the cytoplasm, and binds to Bax-like BH3 proteins Bid and BimEL, inhibiting their pro-apoptotic activity. Endogenous humanin suppresses tBID- and BimEL-induced apoptosis in vitro.

nodes.label: IGFBP3
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: A second group cloned humanin using a yeast two-hybrid screen as a partner of IGFBP3, and demonstrated that humanin binds to IGFBP3 with high affinity and specificity. IGFBP3 regulates IGF bioactivity and also induces apoptosis and inhibits cell growth independently of IGFs, and humanin protects against IGFBP3-induced apoptosis. Humanin does not interfere with IGF-I/IGFBP-3 binding but appears to bind to the heparin-binding domain of IGFBP-3, and a single amino acid substitution of alanine for phenylalanine at position 6 (F6AHN) abrogates IGFBP-3 binding.

nodes.label: Insulin Sensitivity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: Peripheral intravenous and central intra-cerebro-ventricular infusion of humanin and its derivatives F6AHN, HNG, and HNGF6A significantly improve overall insulin sensitivity, mediated in part by hypothalamic STAT3 activation in rats. The enhanced insulin sensitivity was coupled with a significant reduction of hepatic glucose production together with increased peripheral glucose uptake, raising the rate of glucose infusion in euglycemic clamp studies. A single treatment with the highly-potent analog HNGF6A normalizes blood glucose levels in Zucker diabetic fatty rats, a model of type 2 diabetes.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial-Derived Peptide
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: Humanin is the first small peptide of a putative set of mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs), a novel concept that challenges the traditional view of mitochondria as passive end-function organelles. It was discovered in 2001 by screening a cDNA library from the surviving fraction of an Alzheimer's disease patient brain for clones protecting neuronal cells from cell death induced by APP mutants, and identified as a 75bp open reading frame yielding a 24 amino acid peptide encoded within the mitochondrial 16S rRNA. Humanin is a harbinger of additional MDPs, as numerous putative ORFs are dispersed throughout the mitochondrial genome.

nodes.label: Retrograde Signaling
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: Mitochondria communicate back to the cell through processes collectively referred to as retrograde signaling, and traditionally described means include Ca2+, cytochrome c, and ROS. Mitochondrial-derived peptides such as humanin are recently identified retrograde signals that are unique in that they are encoded within the mitochondrial genome sequences, unlike other retrograde molecules which are nuclear-encoded. Humanin functions as both an endocrine factor and an intracellular survival factor with several biological roles regulating cell survival and metabolism, and retrograde signaling is a biological process well conserved from simple yeast to humans.

nodes.label: Mitokines
nodes.description: Humanin is a peptide of approximately 24 amino acids believed to derive from a short, cryptic open reading frame within the mitochondrial 16S rRNA gene, and it was the first identified mammalian mitokine. Originally isolated as a protective factor against familial Alzheimer's disease, humanin circulates in plasma and exerts cytoprotective and metabolic effects in various experimental paradigms. It is considered the founding member of a class of mitochondrially-derived peptides (MDPs) causing systemic effects in mammals.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial DNA
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: The mitochondrial origin of humanin is supported by strong circumstantial evidence, though still debated. Northern blot analysis using the humanin ORF as a probe showed hybridization to total RNA from HeLa cells identical in size to mitochondrial 16S rRNA, whereas RNA from rho0 HeLa cells lacking mtDNA showed no significant hybridization. Formylated humanin has enhanced activity by increasing affinity to FPRL1, and N-terminal formylation is a hallmark of mitochondrially encoded proteins. However, NUMTs reflecting humanin sequences are found in chromosomes 1-13 with varying homology, so a NUMT-derived humanin has not been ruled out.

nodes.label: Cells
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: The humanin peptide sequence has been proposed to contain a pseudo-signal peptide, and when transfected into neuronal cells humanin is detected in the culture medium, indicating a secretory capacity that is blocked by inhibition of ER-golgi transport processes. Humanin is secreted from cells and found in circulation (plasma) as well as bound to cellular membranes, and its actions are thought to be mediated by specific receptors. This endocrine mode of action distinguishes humanin from other stress-induced mitochondrial retrograde signals, which are cell-autonomous, and supports its role as a non-autonomous signaling factor.

nodes.label: Neuron
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: Humanin's cytoprotective effects were first tested and confirmed in vitro against mutant forms of APP and presenilin 1 and 2 which cause familial AD. F11 neuronal cells were challenged by transfecting APP or PS1/2 cDNA or treating with Abeta1-43, and humanin effectively protected neuronal cells from these FAD-related toxicities as shown by trypan blue exclusion and WST-8 assays. Humanin also protects against Abeta25-35 cell death and behavioral deficits, scopolamine-induced memory loss, H2O2-induced cell death in cortical neurons, serum starvation-induced apoptosis, and CoCl2-induced apoptosis in retinal ganglion cells.

nodes.label: Pancreatic Beta Cells
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
nodes.description: Humanin improves glucose tolerance and delays the onset of diabetes in NOD mice, a model of type 1 diabetes involving progressive accumulation of lymphocytes within the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. In NOD mouse pancreata, humanin treatment dramatically suppressed inflammation and lymphocyte infiltration. Furthermore, humanin decreases serum starvation- and cytokine-induced apoptosis in the pancreatic beta-cell line NIT-1, protecting against the IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma released by T cells and activated macrophages, in an ERK- and STAT3-dependent manner, suggesting it may be a therapeutic target for type 1 diabetes.

nodes.label: Immune Evasion
nodes.description: IDO1 is a major target in immuno-oncology due to its role in tumor evasion: it is often upregulated in cancers and the tumor microenvironment, where its tryptophan depletion and kynurenine accumulation create an immunosuppressive niche that suppresses effector T cells and promotes regulatory T cells. Inhibitors such as epacadostat, navoximod and linrodostat (BMS-986205) have been tested in clinical trials, often in combination with checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1/PD-L1), though results have been mixed.

nodes.label: Dioxygenase
nodes.description: IDO1 belongs to the family of heme-dependent dioxygenases (EC 1.13.11.52), distinct from but functionally related to tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO, mainly hepatic) and IDO2 (a less active paralog). It is a monomeric cytosolic protein of about 45 kDa encoded by the IDO1 gene on human chromosome 8p11.21. Crystal structures (e.g., PDB 2D0T, 5EK2) reveal a large domain with a deep heme-binding pocket and a smaller domain, and the active site shows plasticity that allows inhibitor and substrate binding. This structural information underpins the design of IDO1 inhibitors for immuno-oncology.

nodes.label: Dendritic cells
nodes.description: IDO1 is highly expressed in the placenta, lymph nodes, lungs, small intestine, and certain immune cells including dendritic cells, macrophages and monocytes, and it is inducible in many tissues during inflammation. In antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells, IDO1 modulates T cell responses peripherally through local tryptophan depletion and kynurenine production, creating an immunosuppressive environment. This expression pattern underlies IDO1's roles in maternal-fetal tolerance (high placental expression), antimicrobial defense, regulation of inflammation and autoimmunity, and tumor immune escape.

nodes.label: Interferon-gamma
nodes.description: IDO1 is strongly induced by inflammatory cytokines, especially interferon-gamma (IFNγ) via JAK/STAT signaling, but also by IFNα/β, TNF-α, IL-1, LPS, and other signals in immune and other cells; glucocorticoids can synergize in some contexts. Expression is high in placenta, lymph nodes, lungs, small intestine, and certain immune cells including dendritic cells, macrophages and monocytes, and is inducible in many tissues during inflammation. Post-translational control involves phosphorylation of ITIM motifs that recruit SOCS3, leading to ubiquitination and degradation as a negative feedback mechanism, and IDO1 can also mediate non-enzymatic signaling such as PI3K activation.

nodes.label: IDO2
nodes.description: IDO2, a less active paralog of IDO1, may compete for heme and act as a negative regulator in some settings. Both are heme-dependent dioxygenases functionally related to TDO (tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase, mainly hepatic). The existence of these compensatory pathways is a major challenge for IDO1-targeted therapy, as IDO2 and TDO can partially substitute for IDO1 in maintaining tryptophan catabolism and immunosuppression. This isospecificity issue, along with context-specific effects, has contributed to the mixed results of IDO1 inhibitor trials in immuno-oncology, where single-target blockade may be insufficient to relieve metabolic immunosuppression.

nodes.label: IL-22
nodes.description: Interleukin 22, an IL-10 gene family member produced by T helper 17 cells and innate lymphoid cell subsets, signals through the IL-22 receptor on the surface of thymic epithelial cells and promotes the proliferation and survival of thymocytes. Dudakov et al. showed that IL-22 administration to wild-type mice after total body irradiation significantly increases thymic cellularity, including both developing thymocytes and TEC subsets, and that immune recovery in irradiated IL-22-deficient mice is impaired.

nodes.label: Thymic Epithelial Cells
nodes.description: Interleukin 22, an IL-10 gene family member produced by T helper 17 cells and innate lymphoid cell subsets, signals through the IL-22 receptor on the surface of thymic epithelial cells and promotes the proliferation and survival of thymocytes. Dudakov et al. showed that IL-22 administration to wild-type mice after total body irradiation significantly increases thymic cellularity, including both developing thymocytes and TEC subsets, and that immune recovery in irradiated IL-22-deficient mice is impaired.

nodes.label: IL-7
nodes.description: Interleukin 7 is a 25 kDa glycoprotein produced by stromal cells in the thymus and bone marrow that promotes both survival and differentiation of immature triple-negative and mature single-positive thymocytes. IL-7 binds the IL-7 receptor expressed on lymphoid precursors (CD3-CD4-CD8-), double-positive CD4+CD8+ thymocytes, and single-positive CD4 or CD8 T cells. Schluns et al. demonstrated that IL-7 administration to non-lymphopenic mice expands naive and memory peripheral CD4 and CD8 T cells, and treatment with IL-7 restores thymopoiesis in IL-7-deficient mice. Recombinant human IL-7 (CYT 99 007) showed low toxicity and dose-dependent expansion of naive and memory T cells in patients.

nodes.label: T Lymphocyte
nodes.description: In the periphery, IL-7 regulates T cell survival and function. IL-7 binds the IL-7 receptor expressed on many immune cells, including lymphoid precursors, double-positive thymocytes, and single-positive CD4 or CD8 T cells, promoting survival and differentiation of immature triple-negative and mature single-positive thymocytes. The IL-7 receptor is a target for therapeutic intervention, particularly for restoring T cells in subjects undergoing T cell-depleting regimens.

nodes.label: mTORC1
nodes.description: The hormesis exhibited by rapamycin is proposed to arise from a network topology that resembles an incoherent bivalent motif centered in its target mTORC1. In this architecture mTORC1 has a dual role: it is the target of rapamycin inhibition and simultaneously feeds an indirect activating path (via IRS1/S6K negative feedback and PI3K) toward the output mTORC2, yielding two net-opposite influences over the output. This topology induces biphasic dose-responses with high probability, and the backward reaction of the motif has a low Michaelis-Menten constant, consistent with the general rules identified in the coarse-grained screening.

nodes.label: IRS1
nodes.description: IRS1 is the upstream insulin receptor substrate in the mTOR-PI3K signaling cascade: the IRS receptor upstream of the pathway is activated by binding reversibly to insulin, and active IRS1 promotes the activation of PI3K by phosphorylation. PI3K in turn activates mTORC2 by phosphorylation and activates IRS1 indirectly via AKT, forming a positive feedback loop. Active IRS1 is inactivated by phosphorylation by S6K1/2, closing a negative feedback arm. IRS1 therefore sits at the hub of the incoherent bivalent motif, and the backward reaction from the target toward IRS1 is central to the hormetic response.

nodes.label: Isoleucine
nodes.description: Dietary isoleucine correlates with body mass index in humans, and increased circulating isoleucine is associated with increased mortality risk. In Western diet-fed mice, increasing dietary isoleucine promotes weight gain, fat accretion, glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance. In contrast, isoleucine restriction consistently improves metabolic health across dietary contexts and age groups, extends lifespan of both Drosophila and mice, reduces frailty and increases healthspan, rejuvenates aged mice at the molecular level, induces substantial epigenetic changes, and improves Alzheimer's disease outcomes in male mice. Isoleucine is described as an exceptionally powerful modifier of the hallmarks of protein restriction.

nodes.label: Body Mass Index
nodes.description: Dietary isoleucine correlates with body mass index in humans, and increased circulating isoleucine is associated with increased mortality risk. In Western diet-fed mice, increasing dietary isoleucine promotes weight gain, fat accretion, glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance. In contrast, isoleucine restriction consistently improves metabolic health across dietary contexts and age groups, extends lifespan of both Drosophila and mice, reduces frailty and increases healthspan, rejuvenates aged mice at the molecular level, induces substantial epigenetic changes, and improves Alzheimer's disease outcomes in male mice. Isoleucine is described as an exceptionally powerful modifier of the hallmarks of protein restriction.

nodes.label: Keratinocyte Growth Factor
nodes.description: Keratinocyte growth factor (KGF, FGF7) signaling through FGFR2IIIb is critical for fetal thymus organogenesis and linked to proliferation and differentiation of fetal and postnatal thymic epithelial cells. KGF administration is well-documented to increase thymus size, TEC differentiation, and thymocyte production in aged animals. Min and colleagues showed that a single course of KGF treatment increases thymic cellularity in aged mice, maintained for two months, with restoration of cortical and medullary compartments, increased naive CD4 T cell output, and increased humoral responses to a T-dependent antigen.

nodes.label: Thymus
nodes.description: Keratinocyte growth factor (KGF, FGF7) signaling through FGFR2IIIb is critical for fetal thymus organogenesis and linked to proliferation and differentiation of fetal and postnatal thymic epithelial cells. KGF administration is well-documented to increase thymus size, TEC differentiation, and thymocyte production in aged animals. Min and colleagues showed that a single course of KGF treatment increases thymic cellularity in aged mice, maintained for two months, with restoration of cortical and medullary compartments, increased naive CD4 T cell output, and increased humoral responses to a T-dependent antigen.

nodes.label: Kynurenine
nodes.description: Kynurenine and its derivatives activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), promoting regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation and suppressing effector T/NK cells. This metabolite-driven AhR signaling is the second major mechanism of IDO1-mediated immunosuppression alongside local tryptophan depletion, and together they create an immunosuppressive microenvironment in tissues such as tumors, placenta and inflamed sites. The context-dependent nature of this pathway is notable: it is protective via tolerance induction in autoimmunity but potentially detrimental when overactive in metabolic inflammation, where elevated KP activity links to insulin resistance and chronic low-grade inflammation.

nodes.label: Kynurenine Pathway
nodes.description: Downstream of IDO1, the kynurenine pathway (KP) leads to metabolites including kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine, quinolinic acid (a neurotoxin and NAD+ precursor), and ultimately NAD+. The KP accounts for about 95% of tryptophan degradation outside protein synthesis and serotonin production, making it the dominant route of tryptophan-to-NAD+ flux. Both type 1 and type 2 diabetes show disrupted NAD+ homeostasis, with the KP (via IDO1/TDO) being a major Trp-to-NAD+ route. This positions IDO1 at the intersection of metabolism, immunity and inflammation, integrating tryptophan availability with immune modulation and NAD+ biosynthesis.

nodes.label: Quinolinic Acid
nodes.description: The kynurenine pathway leads to metabolites including kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine, quinolinic acid (a neurotoxin and NAD+ precursor), and ultimately NAD+. Because the pathway accounts for approximately 95% of tryptophan degradation outside protein synthesis and serotonin production, its flux through IDO1 and TDO substantially shapes systemic NAD+ levels and neuroactive metabolite balance. KP dysregulation is implicated in neurodegeneration, depression, chronic inflammation, and infections (e.g., HIV modulates IDO1), in part because of the neuroactive and excitotoxic properties of kynurenine and quinolinic acid. This links IDO1 activity to both metabolic and neurological outcomes.

nodes.label: Leucine
nodes.description: Leucine is a potent activator of the master nutrient sensor mTORC1 and stimulates skeletal muscle anabolism. Leucine signals to mTORC1 in specific neurons by binding to and activating a voltage-gated calcium channel (Cav3.1). In humans, leucine supplementation increases muscle protein synthesis but does not improve muscle function, and its effects on fat mass are mixed. Leucine's cardiovascular effects are divergent: some studies show supplementation accelerates atherosclerotic plaque progression in an mTORC1-dependent manner and its metabolite isovaleric acid accelerates atrial fibrillation, while others report improved vascular function. Notably, leucine supplementation does not extend mouse lifespan, suggesting changes in leucine are unlikely to be responsible for protein restriction benefits.

nodes.label: LHRH
nodes.description: Luteinizing hormone releasing hormone (LHRH) analogues achieve pharmacological sex steroid ablation and are a clinically tolerable alternative to surgical castration. Agents such as Lupron (leuprolide) act on the pituitary gland, desensitizing LHRH receptors and thereby decreasing luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, leading to reduced estrogen and testosterone production. Human studies with LHRH analogues have resulted in increased thymic weight and reversal of age-related thymic structural defects.

nodes.label: Sex Steroid Ablation
nodes.description: Luteinizing hormone releasing hormone (LHRH) analogues achieve pharmacological sex steroid ablation and are a clinically tolerable alternative to surgical castration. Agents such as Lupron (leuprolide) act on the pituitary gland, desensitizing LHRH receptors and thereby decreasing luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, leading to reduced estrogen and testosterone production. Human studies with LHRH analogues have resulted in increased thymic weight and reversal of age-related thymic structural defects.

nodes.label: Magnolol
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
nodes.description: Magnolol is the structural analog of honokiol, both being lipid-soluble polyphenolic lignans from Magnolia species. The two compounds show broadly overlapping pharmacology - both are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors, inhibit NMDA receptor signaling and NF-kappaB activation, protect neurons against beta-amyloid toxicity, and reduce inflammatory pain - but magnolol is generally slightly less potent or less selective, particularly for NMDA-driven responses where honokiol shows greater selectivity. The structural homology with the anesthetic propofol likely explains some shared pharmacologic actions.

nodes.label: Mdivi-1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
nodes.description: Mdivi-1 (mitochondrial division inhibitor 1), a quinazolinone derivative that specifically inhibits DRP1, attenuates cardiac dysfunction in diverse mouse cardiomyopathy models, likely by promoting mitochondrial elongation or reducing autophagy. It also attenuates neuronal cell death through mitochondrial elongation and inhibition of complex I activity and ROS generation in neurodegenerative disease models including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. However, treatment of myocardial infarction in pigs with Mdivi-1 did not reduce infarct size or preserve cardiac function, and Mdivi-1 has off-target effects such as cleaving L-OPA1 and altering OXPHOS complex protein expression.

nodes.label: Melatonin
nodes.description: Melatonin is described as a critical, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant whose endogenous production is maximized by ensuring complete darkness during sleep. Circadian alignment and sleep hygiene are presented as high-impact behaviors supporting the mitohormesis protocol, since deep sleep is when cellular repair and neural recovery occur. The document ties melatonin production to sleep quality, which in turn determines overnight HRV and recovery capacity, completing the loop between circadian biology, antioxidant defenses, and mitochondrial adaptation.

nodes.label: Antioxidant
