These uptake mechanisms complement each other and explain how orally administered NMN is rapidly absorbed from the intestine into the bloodstream and converted to NAD+ in tissues.

nodes.label: NAAD
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: NAAD (nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide) is a product of NR utilization in humans and a biomarker of increased NAD+ metabolism. NR supplementation raised NAAD by 4.5-fold in blood, and healthy middle-aged adults taking 1 g/day NR for 6 weeks showed around a fivefold increase in blood NAAD. In another study, NAAD was undetectable before NR supplementation but increased by approximately 2,900% after single doses of up to 1 g NR. These findings corroborate studies in mice showing that the deamidated Preiss-Handler pathway predominates after NR intake, making NAAD a sensitive readout of the deamidated route of NAD+ precursor metabolism.

nodes.label: Biomarker
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: NAAD (nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide) is a product of NR utilization in humans and a biomarker of increased NAD+ metabolism. NR supplementation raised NAAD by 4.5-fold in blood, and healthy middle-aged adults taking 1 g/day NR for 6 weeks showed around a fivefold increase in blood NAAD. In another study, NAAD was undetectable before NR supplementation but increased by approximately 2,900% after single doses of up to 1 g NR. These findings corroborate studies in mice showing that the deamidated Preiss-Handler pathway predominates after NR intake, making NAAD a sensitive readout of the deamidated route of NAD+ precursor metabolism.

nodes.label: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: In an oncogenic mouse model, supplementation with NMN (500 mg/kg body weight daily for 13 days) significantly increased the secretory phenotype associated with pro-inflammatory senescence, promoting pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma progression. This raises the hypothesis that dietary supplements that increase NAD+ may be tumorigenic in vivo under stress conditions such as premalignant senescent lesions induced by activated oncogenes. The finding highlights the complex, context-dependent interplay between NAD+ metabolism and cancer biology, cautioning that NAD+ precursor supplementation could accelerate tumorigenesis in certain premalignant settings even as it confers health benefits in normal aging and metabolic disease.

nodes.label: Combined Metabolic Activators
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Combined metabolic activators (CMAs), consisting of NR (1 g), l-carnitine tartrate (3.73 g), N-acetylcysteine (2.55 g), and serine (12.35 g), improved COVID-19 outcomes in clinical trials. Patients taking the mixture orally for 14 days had significantly faster complete recovery times than placebo (6.6 vs 9.3 days in a phase 2 study and 5.7 vs 9.2 days in a phase 3 study). CMAs were found to reinforce the immune response and regulate amino acid and lipid metabolism, and patients showed improvements in plasma levels of inflammation and antioxidant metabolism-related biomarkers including alanine aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, glucose, and proteins. NR within the mixture contributes NAD+ restoration supporting antiviral PARP function.

nodes.label: COVID-19
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Combined metabolic activators (CMAs), consisting of NR (1 g), l-carnitine tartrate (3.73 g), N-acetylcysteine (2.55 g), and serine (12.35 g), improved COVID-19 outcomes in clinical trials. Patients taking the mixture orally for 14 days had significantly faster complete recovery times than placebo (6.6 vs 9.3 days in a phase 2 study and 5.7 vs 9.2 days in a phase 3 study). CMAs were found to reinforce the immune response and regulate amino acid and lipid metabolism, and patients showed improvements in plasma levels of inflammation and antioxidant metabolism-related biomarkers including alanine aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase, creatinine, glucose, and proteins. NR within the mixture contributes NAD+ restoration supporting antiviral PARP function.

nodes.label: Viral Translation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: PARPs play a critical antiviral role by inhibiting the translation of viral transcripts through ADP-ribosylation of the viral genome, a process requiring NAD+. However, several viral families including SARS-CoV encode a macrodomain protein that hydrolyses the ADPR units from proteins and nucleic acids, inhibiting this PARP protective effect and facilitating replication and virulence. Excessive PARP activation then occurs to compensate for ADPR hydrolysis, accompanied by NAD+ consumption. This suggests that increasing NAD+ levels may restore the antiviral functions of PARPs to support immunity against SARS-CoV-2, providing a rationale for NAD+ precursor supplementation in COVID-19.

nodes.label: SARS-CoV-2 macrodomain
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: The SARS-CoV-2 macrodomain is a viral protein that hydrolyses the ADP-ribose (ADPR) units added by PARPs to proteins and nucleic acids, thereby inhibiting the protective antiviral effect of PARPs and facilitating viral replication and virulence. Because PARPs require NAD+ to ADP-ribosylate viral transcripts, this counteraction leads to excessive PARP activation and NAD+ consumption during infection, dysregulating the NAD+ metabolome. Restoring NAD+ levels with precursors may therefore restore PARP antiviral function and support innate immunity to SARS-CoV-2, connecting NAD+ metabolism directly to COVID-19 severity and immune defense.

nodes.label: SIRT6
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 attenuates NF-kB signaling via histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9) deacetylation at the chromatin of NF-kB target gene promoters, which are related to apoptosis and cellular senescence. Alongside SIRT1, SIRT2, and SIRT3, which suppress both NF-kB and NLRP3 inflammasome activity through multiple mechanisms, SIRT6 helps coordinate the intensity of inflammatory responses and prevent cytokine storms. Because sirtuins are NAD+-dependent, NAD+ precursor supplementation that raises NAD+ levels can reinforce this sirtuin-mediated restraint of NF-kB-driven inflammation, linking NAD+ metabolism to control of the pro-inflammatory transcription program during infection and aging.

nodes.label: Aerobic Capacity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) enhances aerobic capacity, as demonstrated in a randomized, double-blind study in amateur runners. NMN also improves mitochondrial function and energy metabolism: long-term administration in drinking water at 100 or 300 mg/kg/day for 12 months increased mitochondrial respiratory ability in skeletal muscle and reversed age-associated gene expression changes in a tissue-specific manner in aged mice. These mitochondrial and aerobic benefits are attributed to NMN raising NAD+ levels, which activates sirtuins and supports oxidative metabolism, energy expenditure, and oxygen consumption, positioning NMN as a performance- and healthspan-enhancing NAD+ precursor.

nodes.label: NAD+/NADH redox imbalance
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: The hallmark hyperglycemia of diabetes mellitus causes a redox imbalance between NAD+ and NADH that can lead to oxidative stress and a variety of metabolic syndromes. In cells whose glucose uptake is not insulin-dependent, glucose oversupply leads to NADH overproduction by both the conventional glucose combustion pathways (glycolysis and the Krebs cycle) and the polyol pathway. This NAD+/NADH imbalance, also known as pseudohypoxia, initially causes reductive stress and mitochondrial overload and dysfunction, which lead to oxidative stress and oxidative damage to DNA, lipids, and proteins. Additionally, PARP overactivation depletes NAD+, and this redox imbalance is a major factor contributing to the development of diabetic complications.

nodes.label: CD38 knockdown
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: CD38 knockdown in mice suppressed axon degeneration, demyelination, and immune cell infiltration after facial nerve axotomy compared with wild-type mice, identifying CD38 as a candidate molecule for regulating neurodegeneration. Correspondingly, intraperitoneal injection of NR at 400 mg/kg once daily for 1 week prior to facial nerve axotomy delayed axon degeneration and demyelination and significantly increased NAD+ levels in the facial nucleus and facial nerve of wild-type mice. These findings connect the age-related rise in CD38 activity to NAD+ depletion and axonal vulnerability, and show that NAD+ precursor supplementation can mimic the protection achieved by CD38 deletion.

nodes.label: Axon Degeneration
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: CD38 knockdown in mice suppressed axon degeneration, demyelination, and immune cell infiltration after facial nerve axotomy compared with wild-type mice, identifying CD38 as a candidate molecule for regulating neurodegeneration. Correspondingly, intraperitoneal injection of NR at 400 mg/kg once daily for 1 week prior to facial nerve axotomy delayed axon degeneration and demyelination and significantly increased NAD+ levels in the facial nucleus and facial nerve of wild-type mice. These findings connect the age-related rise in CD38 activity to NAD+ depletion and axonal vulnerability, and show that NAD+ precursor supplementation can mimic the protection achieved by CD38 deletion.

nodes.label: Niacin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinic acid (niacin) at pharmacological doses reduces serum cholesterol levels in humans, but its clinical use is limited by a side effect of skin flushing accompanied by an unpleasant warmth sensation and often itching. Niacin, together with tryptophan and nicotinamide, is one of the classic NAD+ biosynthesis precursors historically used to prevent and treat pellagra, a disease characterized by dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Tryptophan alone is not sufficient to sustain cellular NAD+ levels because it participates in other metabolic pathways such as serotonin, melatonin, and picolinic acid synthesis, making nicotinic acid an important dietary NAD+ precursor with distinct pharmacological actions.

nodes.label: Serum Cholesterol
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinic acid (niacin) at pharmacological doses reduces serum cholesterol levels in humans, but its clinical use is limited by a side effect of skin flushing accompanied by an unpleasant warmth sensation and often itching. Niacin, together with tryptophan and nicotinamide, is one of the classic NAD+ biosynthesis precursors historically used to prevent and treat pellagra, a disease characterized by dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Tryptophan alone is not sufficient to sustain cellular NAD+ levels because it participates in other metabolic pathways such as serotonin, melatonin, and picolinic acid synthesis, making nicotinic acid an important dietary NAD+ precursor with distinct pharmacological actions.

nodes.label: NAD+ Precursor
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is one of the most studied nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) precursors, and it is the third NAD+ precursor discovered, naturally occurring in milk and already commercially available as a nutraceutical. Alongside nicotinamide (NAM), nicotinic acid (NA), and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), NR feeds into NAD+ biosynthetic salvage pathways and is regarded as a favorable precursor because it lacks the serious side effects and flushing attributed to other NAD+ precursors, and because its chloride salt has been granted GRAS (generally regarded as safe) status.

nodes.label: NMRK1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: NMRK1 (nicotinamide ribose kinase 1), together with its isoform NMRK2, directly phosphorylates nicotinamide riboside (NR) to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), bypassing the rate-limiting enzyme NAMPT. This route also circumvents the requirement for energetically costly PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate) and the feedback inhibition by NAD+. NMRK1 is expressed ubiquitously across tissues, whereas NMRK2 expression is concentrated in cardiac and skeletal muscle, which helps explain why these tissues respond well to NR supplementation. NR is an orally available NAD+ precursor that increases NAD+ levels and sirtuin activity in multiple tissues.

nodes.label: NMNAT
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: NMNAT (NMN/NaMN adenylyltransferases) catalyzes the final biosynthetic step in which nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is converted to the essential coenzyme NAD+. This step is shared by the salvage pathways from both nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide (NAM): NR is first phosphorylated to NMN by NMRK1/NMRK2, while NAM is converted to NMN by NAMPT. NAD+ is required for glycolysis, fatty acid oxidation, and the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and it serves as the substrate for NAD+-consuming enzymes such as sirtuins and PARPs. Elevating NAD+ through precursor supplementation underlies the beneficial metabolic, cardiovascular, and neuroprotective effects attributed to NR.

nodes.label: Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (NP) converts nicotinamide riboside (NR) into nicotinamide (NAM), which can then be converted back to NAD+ via NMN through the NAMPT and NMNAT enzymes. This NP-mediated cleavage is believed to be the variable step that degrades NR to NAM in the gut, potentially explaining the low and interindividually variable oral bioavailability of NR. NAM is the most common NAD+ precursor in mammals, and when administered at higher doses it can exert sirtuin-inhibiting effects. The balance between the direct NMRK pathway and this NP/NAMPT route determines how efficiently supplemented NR is converted to NAD+ in different tissues.

nodes.label: Coenzyme
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is an essential coenzyme that plays central roles in cellular oxidation-reduction reactions, including most catabolic and anabolic processes such as glycolysis, fatty acid beta-oxidation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and the synthesis of fatty acids, cholesterol, and steroids. Beyond its redox function, NAD+ is consumed by enzymes including sirtuins, poly-ADP-ribose polymerases (PARPs), CD38/CD157 ectoenzymes, and mono-ADP-ribose transferases, whose activity can deplete cellular NAD+ content.

nodes.label: DNA Repair
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Sirtuins, the NAD+-dependent deacetylases, are major downstream mediators of NAD+ biology and carry out numerous regulatory functions that include DNA repair, metabolism, stress response, chromatin remodeling, and circadian rhythm control. Because their deacetylase activity is absolutely dependent on NAD+, their function is sensitive to NAD+ depletion caused by aging and by consumption from PARPs and CD38. Supplementation with NAD+ precursors such as nicotinamide riboside can increase sirtuin activity, contributing to improved DNA repair, preserved mitochondrial function, and the beneficial metabolic and longevity effects documented in animal models.

nodes.label: PARP1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: PARP1, together with PARP2, is a poly-ADP-ribose polymerase that responds to DNA breaks in the nucleus and facilitates DNA repair by using NAD+ to build chains of ADP-ribose molecules. As DNA damage accumulates with age, PARP activation increases and competes with sirtuins for the shared NAD+ substrate, thereby lowering SIRT1 activity. PARP2 additionally binds the Sirt1 promoter and represses its expression. This PARP-mediated NAD+ depletion has been confirmed to play a major role in the pathogenesis of DNA repair disorders such as Cockayne syndrome, xeroderma pigmentosum, and ataxia-telangiectasia, and NAD+ precursor supplementation can improve these phenotypes in mouse models.

nodes.label: PARP2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: PARP2 represses the expression of SIRT1 by binding to the promoter of the Sirt1 gene, and it competes with SIRT1 for the shared NAD+ substrate alongside PARP1. As DNA damage accumulates with age, increased PARP activation thereby lowers SIRT1 activity both through substrate competition and through this direct transcriptional repression. SIRT1 is an NAD+-dependent deacetylase whose activity is important for prevention of type 2 diabetes, preservation of insulin sensitivity, and healthy vascular function. Restoring NAD+ through precursor supplementation such as nicotinamide riboside can support SIRT1 activity and counteract the suppressive effects of PARP activation.

nodes.label: cADP-Ribose
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: CD38 is the primary NADase in mammals, an ectoenzyme that uses NAD+ to produce and hydrolyze cADP-ribose, a Ca2+-mobilizing second messenger. Because CD38 also degrades the NAD+ intermediates nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), its activity further decreases the content of NAD+. CD38 content increases with age, contributing to the age-related decline in NAD+ and mitochondrial dysfunction. In CD38-deficient mice, NAD+ levels remain high, preserving mitochondrial respiration and metabolic function with age, and pharmacological inhibition of CD38 can increase NAD+ levels and improve glucose and lipid metabolism.

nodes.label: Axonal Degeneration
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: SARM1 (sterile alpha and Toll/interleukin-1 receptor motif-containing 1) is an additional NAD+-depleting enzyme that uses NAD+ to promote axonal degeneration after injury, thereby decreasing overall NAD+ content. Axonal degeneration is an early event in acute cerebral injury and in chronic neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, and it is caused by excitotoxicity, during which neurons undergo strong NAD+ depletion. Preserving axonal NAD+ to supply damage-induced SARM1 activation has been proposed as one of two mechanisms underlying the neuroprotective effects of nicotinamide riboside, which can protect neurons from excitotoxicity-induced axonal degeneration.

nodes.label: Glucose Tolerance
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: In mouse models, nicotinamide riboside (NR) increases NAD+ metabolism and thereby improves glucose tolerance, reduces weight gain, and exhibits neuroprotective effects against diabetic neuropathy and liver steatosis. NR also restores the significantly decreased hepatic NADP+ and NADPH levels seen in prediabetic and type 2 diabetic mice, both of which are important for resistance to oxidative stress. These benefits are mediated in part through activation of SIRT1, which promotes glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic beta-cells and protects against insulin resistance in peripheral tissues.

nodes.label: NADPH
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a precursor not only of NADH but also of hepatic NADP+ and NADPH, and supplementation with NR restores the significantly decreased hepatic NADP+ and NADPH levels observed in prediabetic and type 2 diabetic mouse models. Both NADP+ and NADPH are important for resistance to oxidative stress, while NADPH is thought to be a major contributor to insulin resistance. Since the hepatic NAD+ metabolome reflects the progression of prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, NADP+ and NADPH can be used to assess disease progression, and their restoration by NR supports improved metabolic health and protection against diabetic complications such as neuropathy and liver steatosis.

nodes.label: Hepatic Steatosis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) reduces lipid accumulation and liver steatosis in mouse models, effects that are mediated through induction of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response and through SIRT1 activation, which promotes fatty acid oxidation and inhibits lipogenesis, protecting the liver from steatosis. NR also restores hepatic NADP+ and NADPH in prediabetic and type 2 diabetic mice and reduces cholesterol levels via SIRT1 and cholesterol-homeostasis factors. Sirtuins are downregulated in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), a hepatic manifestation of metabolic syndrome associated with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and insulin resistance, so raising NAD+ with NR

nodes.label: Hepatocyte Replication
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: In the regenerating liver, nicotinamide riboside (NR) reduces lipid accumulation, promotes hepatocyte replication, and increases hepatic ATP content, leading to a faster regaining of liver weight in mice. This hepatoprotective and regenerative effect is tied to NAD+ biosynthesis, which supports the energy-producing and biosynthetic demands of liver regeneration. In addition, dietary NR supplementation restored NAD+ levels that were depressed by impaired biosynthesis in a mouse model of hepatocellular carcinoma, preventing both DNA damage and tumorigenesis.

nodes.label: NMRK2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: In several models of cardiac injuries, including heart failure (HF), the NAMPT enzyme is repressed while Nmrk2 expression is robustly upregulated, and a similar shift was observed in human failing hearts in models of cardiomyopathy. Activation of the NMRK2 pathway therefore represents a common adaptive mechanism in the failing heart, where NAD+ levels are low, and the Nmrk2 gene can be activated in response to NAMPT inhibition. This shift from NAMPT to NMRK2 for NAD+ synthesis is an energy-sparing mechanism, since NMN synthesis from NR by NMRK enzymes requires a single ATP while synthesis from NAM by NAMPT requires more than three ATP equivalents.

nodes.label: Cardiac Function
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: A strong beneficial effect of nicotinamide riboside (NR) was discovered in mouse models of heart failure, with preservation of cardiac function and limitation of cardiac remodeling, effects that were associated with maintained NAD+ levels in the heart. NR supplementation normalizes the myocardial NAD+/NADH ratio and, by improving NAD+ homeostasis and activating NMRK2, can prevent the deterioration of cardiac function and adverse remodeling in a mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure.

nodes.label: Cardiac Remodeling
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) supplementation exhibits protective effects in adverse cardiac remodeling and prevents the deterioration of cardiac function and adverse remodeling in a mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure. NR normalizes the myocardial NAD+/NADH ratio, and long-term supplementation increases nucleocytoplasmic protein acetylation by stimulating citrate and acetyl-CoA metabolism and antioxidant gene expression. NAD+ precursor supplementation also protects against adverse cardiac remodeling by activating sirtuins and maintaining Ca2+ homeostasis.

nodes.label: Systolic Blood Pressure
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) supplementation reduces systolic blood pressure (SBP) and aortic stiffness, two clinically important risk indicators of cardiovascular function and health. These effects may occur through nuclear and cytosolic SIRT1 activation, since NAD+ is an obligate substrate for the deacetylase SIRT1, which has been implicated in the maintenance of healthy vascular function, including endothelium-dependent vascular relaxation. In mouse models, NR-induced reduction of SBP and aortic stiffness was documented alongside improved NAD+ homeostasis.

nodes.label: Arterial Stiffness
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) supplementation reduces aortic stiffness and systolic blood pressure, both clinically important risk indicators of cardiovascular function and health. These NR-induced effects may occur via nuclear and cytosolic SIRT1 activation, because NAD+ is an obligate substrate for the deacetylase SIRT1, which maintains healthy vascular function and promotes endothelium-dependent vascular relaxation through endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Arterial stiffness reduction aligns with the broader cardiovascular benefits of NR, which normalizes the myocardial NAD+/NADH ratio and preserves cardiac function in models of heart failure and dilated cardiomyopathy, supporting the

nodes.label: Cardiac Hypertrophy
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: In vivo activation of SIRT1 protects against cardiac hypertrophy, metabolic dysregulation, and cardiac inflammation in a mouse model of cardiac hypertrophy, and exhibits protective effects in other models of cardiac dysfunction. SIRT1 is an NAD+-dependent deacetylase that mediates much of the cardioprotective benefit of NAD+ precursor supplementation, and NAD+ is an obligate substrate for its activity. In the failing heart, protein hyperacetylation driven by decreasing NAD+-dependent deacetylation increases both in mouse models of hypertrophy and in human patients with ischemic heart failure or dilated cardiomyopathy.

nodes.label: NAD+ Depletion
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: NAD+ depletion was observed during the aging process in multiple animals, including humans, and is considered the major risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD). Neurodegenerative disorders such as AD are associated with DNA damage and oxidative stress, which accumulate with age and lead to impaired mitochondrial function, while excitotoxicity-driven axonal degeneration causes strong NAD+ depletion in neurons. When administered in AD mouse models, nicotinamide riboside (NR) displays beneficial effects on both oxidative stress and DNA repair by increasing NAD+ levels, and it improves pTau, amyloid-beta, neurogenesis, neuroinflammation, hippocampal synaptic plasticity, and cognition.

nodes.label: PARylation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Increased PARylation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and it could be decreased in AD mice with nicotinamide riboside (NR) supplementation. Increased PARylation has also been detected in several other neurodegenerative disorders that involve DNA repair defects, including Cockayne syndrome, xeroderma pigmentosum, and ataxia-telangiectasia, where PARP-mediated NAD+ depletion plays a major role in pathogenesis. Despite the underlying DNA repair deficiencies, NR dramatically improved the phenotype of each of these conditions in mouse models, prolonging survival by more than three times in ataxic mice.

nodes.label: Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) has been shown to prevent noise-induced hearing loss and neurite retraction from hair cells in the inner ear through a SIRT3-dependent mechanism, in which the NR-induced increase in NAD+ supports the activity of the mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3. This illustrates the broader neuroprotective and therapeutic potential of NR, which also protects neurons from excitotoxicity-induced axonal degeneration and preserves axonal NAD+ content. SIRT3 activity is sensitive to the reduction of NAD+ content detected in multiple disorders with retinal degeneration, and NR may therefore have therapeutic applications for a variety of sensory and neurodegenerative conditions.

nodes.label: Retinal Photoreceptors
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 and SIRT5 are both critical for the health of retinal photoreceptors, and SIRT3 activity is sensitive to the reduction of NAD+ content detected in multiple disorders with retinal degeneration, including age-associated dysfunction, diabetic retinopathy, and light-induced degeneration in mice. SIRT3 is a mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacetylase that supports ATP homeostasis, ROS detoxification, and neuroprotection, and increasing mitochondrial NAD+ to support SIRT3 is one proposed mechanism of nicotinamide riboside's neuroprotective effects. This suggests a potential therapeutic treatment with NR for a variety of disorders that include photoreceptor degeneration.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Function
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Oral supplementation with nicotinamide riboside (NR) is associated with improved mitochondrial function, and increasing NAD+ content with NR can stimulate energy production and improve mitochondrial abundance and function in two different mitochondrial myopathies, even though supplementation could not correct the underlying genetic defects. In mice, NR also confers increased endurance and improved cold tolerance in high-fat-diet-fed mice, while a nonsignificant trend toward increased endurance was seen in regular chow-fed mice.

nodes.label: Fibrosis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) was found to improve muscular function and heart pathology in mdx mouse models of Duchenne's muscular dystrophy (DMD) and to decrease PARylation, inflammation, and fibrosis. DMD is characterized by increased PARP activity, fibrosis, and muscular degeneration, and decreased NAD+ levels and Nampt expression are also observed in this condition. By improving muscular strength, rejuvenating senescent muscle stem cells, and reducing levels of inflammation and fibrosis, NR could be effective in managing the progression of muscular dystrophy and degeneration. These findings support the use of NR for the human condition of DMD.

nodes.label: Macrophage Infiltration
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Preclinical studies have reported that nicotinamide riboside (NR) reduces macrophage infiltration in damaged muscles and attenuates plasma TNF-alpha in models of fatty liver disease. These anti-inflammatory effects contribute to the improvement of metabolism and the decrease in chronic inflammation, a hallmark of aging, that underlie the life-prolonging benefits attributed to NR supplementation. Macrophage infiltration into injured tissue promotes inflammation and fibrosis, and its reduction by NR supports the management of muscular dystrophy and age-related tissue degeneration.

nodes.label: SARS-CoV-2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: SARS-CoV-2 infected cell lines of a ferret and lungs of deceased patients showed disturbed NAD+ metabolism and gene expression with respect to synthesis and utilization of NAD+. During infection, the expression of the NMRK1 pathway was upregulated together with the concentrative nucleoside transporter CNT3, indicating a higher capacity for NR conversion to NAD+ and NADP+, while the expression of NNMT (nicotinamide N-methyltransferase) was decreased, suggesting promotion of the NAM salvage pathway.

nodes.label: NAD+ Metabolism
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: SARS-CoV-2 infected cell lines of a ferret and lungs of deceased patients showed disturbed NAD+ metabolism and gene expression with respect to synthesis and utilization of NAD+. During infection, the expression of the NMRK1 pathway was upregulated together with the concentrative nucleoside transporter CNT3, indicating a higher capacity for NR conversion to NAD+ and NADP+, while the expression of NNMT (nicotinamide N-methyltransferase) was decreased, suggesting promotion of the NAM salvage pathway.

nodes.label: Lymphopenia
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers a maladaptive immune response, notably an exaggerated proinflammatory response leading to a cytokine storm in lung tissue, and lymphopenia with a drastic decline of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Upon activation of the adaptive immune response, the overexpression of CD38 in both CD4+ and CD8+ lymphocytes further exaggerates NAD+ depletion, leading to increased production and release of proinflammatory cytokines, reactive oxygen species, and macrophage infiltration. Drastic NAD+ depletion impairs sirtuin function, and replenishment of NAD+ body content could restore energy levels and impaired sirtuin function, possibly rebalancing the maladaptive immune response to

nodes.label: PARPs
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: As the innate immune response activates to fight infection, the activation of PARPs increases due to extensive DNA damage and IFN-induced MARylation (mono-ADP-ribosylation) of target SARS-CoV-2 proteins, and this PARP response is required for inhibition of viral replication. However, this antiviral effect is reversed by the ADP-ribosylhydrolase macrodomain of the viral nonstructural protein nsp3, whose activity is required for virulence. These findings indicate that key events in the innate immune response to viral infections occur within the infected cell's NAD+ metabolome, and boosting NAD+ content through NAM and NR kinase pathways may restore antiviral PARP functions to support

nodes.label: Viral Replication
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: As the innate immune response activates to fight infection, the activation of PARPs increases due to extensive DNA damage and IFN-induced MARylation (mono-ADP-ribosylation) of target SARS-CoV-2 proteins, and this PARP response is required for inhibition of viral replication. However, this antiviral effect is reversed by the ADP-ribosylhydrolase macrodomain of the viral nonstructural protein nsp3, whose activity is required for virulence. These findings indicate that key events in the innate immune response to viral infections occur within the infected cell's NAD+ metabolome, and boosting NAD+ content through NAM and NR kinase pathways may restore antiviral PARP functions to support

nodes.label: SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: The ADP-ribosylhydrolase macrodomain of the viral nonstructural protein nsp3 reverses the antiviral effect of PARPs, which is required for inhibition of viral replication during infection, and the activity of nsp3 is itself required for SARS-CoV-2 virulence. By removing mono-ADP-ribose (MARylation) marks deposited on viral proteins by IFN-induced PARP activation, nsp3 counteracts the host's antiviral ADP-ribosylation response. These events occur within the infected cell's NAD+ metabolome, and boosting NAD+ content through nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide kinase pathways may restore antiviral PARP functions to support innate immunity to SARS-CoV-2.

nodes.label: ADP-Ribose
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: The ADP-ribosylhydrolase macrodomain of the viral nonstructural protein nsp3 reverses the antiviral effect of PARPs, which is required for inhibition of viral replication during infection, and the activity of nsp3 is itself required for SARS-CoV-2 virulence. By removing mono-ADP-ribose (MARylation) marks deposited on viral proteins by IFN-induced PARP activation, nsp3 counteracts the host's antiviral ADP-ribosylation response. These events occur within the infected cell's NAD+ metabolome, and boosting NAD+ content through nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide kinase pathways may restore antiviral PARP functions to support innate immunity to SARS-CoV-2.

nodes.label: CD4+ T Cells
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Upon activation of the adaptive immune response, the overexpression of CD38 in both CD4+ and CD8+ lymphocytes further exaggerates NAD+ depletion, leading to increased production and release of proinflammatory cytokines, reactive oxygen species, and macrophage infiltration. Drastic NAD+ depletion impairs the function of sirtuins, the regulators of cell death and viability, and loss of sirtuin function along with increased oxidative damage and an overall energy decrease culminates in cell death. Replenishment of NAD+ body content could restore energy levels and impaired sirtuin function and possibly rebalance the maladaptive immune response to SARS-CoV-2 infection, which causes

nodes.label: Vitamin B3
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: High efficiency of vitamin B3 (niacin or nicotinamide) in preventing lung tissue damage was confirmed in several animal models with bleomycin- and LPS-induced lung injury, and considering this strong lung-protective effect, vitamin B3 has been proposed as an early treatment-supporting agent against COVID-19, which otherwise causes a maladaptive hyperinflammatory response with a cytokine storm in lung tissue. Nicotinamide riboside (NR), as a vitamin B3 derivative, is therefore considered a potential therapeutic or supporting agent to reduce hyperinflammation and regenerate damaged lung tissue during SARS-CoV-2 infection, where excess leucocyte infiltration causes extensive tissue damage

nodes.label: Acute Lung Injury
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: High efficiency of vitamin B3 (niacin or nicotinamide) in preventing lung tissue damage was confirmed in several animal models with bleomycin- and LPS-induced lung injury, and considering this strong lung-protective effect, vitamin B3 has been proposed as an early treatment-supporting agent against COVID-19, which otherwise causes a maladaptive hyperinflammatory response with a cytokine storm in lung tissue. Nicotinamide riboside (NR), as a vitamin B3 derivative, is therefore considered a potential therapeutic or supporting agent to reduce hyperinflammation and regenerate damaged lung tissue during SARS-CoV-2 infection, where excess leucocyte infiltration causes extensive tissue damage

nodes.label: Adenosine Kinase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Adenosine kinase (ADK) acts as an NRH kinase in a recently discovered novel biosynthetic route of NAD+ from NRH (the reduced form of nicotinamide riboside) through the NMNH intermediate, providing a NMRK-independent pathway for the NRH-induced NAD+ increase. NRH is more stable than nicotinamide riboside (NR), which degrades to nicotinamide in the blood, and NRH increases NAD+ in both cultured cells (5-10-fold above the baseline) and mice, in a more potent and faster manner than NR. Endogenous NRH was detected in the liver of mouse models, establishing NRH as a valid natural precursor of NAD+.

nodes.label: GPR109A
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) administration can elevate NAD+ levels in mammalian cells and tissues without activating GPR109A, the receptor that mediates nicotinic acid-induced flushing, which is why NR is not associated with the painful flushing side effect seen with niacin. Although nicotinic acid (NA) and nicotinamide (NAM) can enter the NAD+ salvage pathway, several preclinical studies have confirmed that both can cause painful flushing sensations at therapeutic doses or other toxic effects. NR, in contrast, was confirmed across a number of studies as well-tolerated up to 2 g of a daily dose, with no flushing or severe side effects reported.

nodes.label: Nicotinic acid
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinic acid (NA, niacin) is implicated with flushing at doses higher than 50 mg/day, and several preclinical studies have confirmed that both NA and nicotinamide (NAM) can cause painful flushing sensations at therapeutic doses or other toxic effects. NA shows lowering effects on blood lipid levels and is used to treat dyslipidemia, but this flushing side effect limits its tolerability. In contrast, nicotinamide riboside (NR) elevates NAD+ levels without activating GPR109A, the receptor that mediates nicotinic acid-induced flushing, and was confirmed across a number of studies as well-tolerated up to 2 g of a daily dose, with no flushing or severe side effects.

nodes.label: Flushing
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinic acid (NA, niacin) is implicated with flushing at doses higher than 50 mg/day, and several preclinical studies have confirmed that both NA and nicotinamide (NAM) can cause painful flushing sensations at therapeutic doses or other toxic effects. NA shows lowering effects on blood lipid levels and is used to treat dyslipidemia, but this flushing side effect limits its tolerability. In contrast, nicotinamide riboside (NR) elevates NAD+ levels without activating GPR109A, the receptor that mediates nicotinic acid-induced flushing, and was confirmed across a number of studies as well-tolerated up to 2 g of a daily dose, with no flushing or severe side effects.

nodes.label: Dyslipidemia
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinic acid (NA, niacin) shows lowering effects on blood lipid levels, and it is used to treat dyslipidemia, although it is implicated with flushing at doses higher than 50 mg/day. In contrast, nicotinamide (NAM) does not affect lipid blood levels, yet it can exhibit sirtuin-inhibiting effects at higher doses, while nicotinamide riboside (NR) does not cause flushing because it does not activate GPR109A. The distinct physiological responses of the NAD+ precursors NA, NAM, and NR, despite all three raising NAD+ and NADP+ levels, are important for selecting the appropriate precursor for specific therapeutic indications.

nodes.label: Milk
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is the third discovered NAD+ precursor and naturally occurs in milk, and it is already available as a nutraceutical, with its chloride salt given GRAS (generally regarded as safe) status. NAD+ intermediates such as NR are found in a wide variety of foods, including meat, eggs, dairy, certain vegetables, and whole wheat, and high availability of NR has been observed in the normal human diet. Oral supplementation with NR has been shown to increase NAD+ levels in multiple tissues along with increased sirtuin activity, improved mitochondrial function, and regenerative potential of stem cells, making NR a leading candidate among NAD+ precursors.

nodes.label: Urolithins
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Urolithin A (UA) is a naturally occurring compound classified within the urolithins, a family of gut-microbiota-derived metabolites that form when dietary polyphenols are processed in the gastrointestinal tract. The review describes urolithins as compounds present in pomegranates and certain other fruits and nuts such as strawberries, walnut kernels, and peanuts, with ellagitannins serving as their precursors. As a member of this family, Urolithin A has attracted considerable research attention due to its pharmacological effects, encompassing anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-tumor, and anti-aging properties, and it is a primary focus of research into muscle health and performance.

nodes.label: Ellagitannins
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Urolithin A is a natural metabolite derived from ellagitannins, polyphenolic precursors found in pomegranate, walnut, almond, strawberry, and blueberry. During digestion, microbial enzymes in the colon convert ellagitannins through stepwise enzymatic and metabolic reactions to yield urolithin A. Because ellagitannin intake is a precondition for urolithin A formation, dietary consumption of ellagitannin-rich foods supplies an abundance of precursor molecules for intestinal microbial metabolism, facilitating the generation of urolithin A and increasing its systemic availability.

nodes.label: Pomegranate
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Pomegranate is cited as one of the primary and richest dietary sources of urolithin A. Pomegranate peel and seeds contain abundant polyphenolic compounds, including ellagitannins that are metabolized by the gut microbiota into urolithin A. Consequently, consuming pomegranate supplies an abundance of precursor molecules for intestinal microbial metabolism, facilitating the generation of urolithin A, and pomegranate consumption is a standard dietary route to increase systemic urolithin A exposure alongside other sources such as walnut, almond, strawberry, and blueberry.

nodes.label: Kidney
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Urolithin A and its metabolites can be excreted from the body through the kidneys and intestines. Renal function can influence the rate of urolithin A elimination, since a portion of the compound and its conjugated forms is cleared in the urine, while additional urolithin A is further metabolized into other compounds within the intestines before being eliminated through feces. Renal function, intestinal permeability, and individual characteristics are therefore among the physiological factors that shape the bioavailability, metabolism, and distribution of urolithin A.

nodes.label: Rifampicin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Rifampicin is a hepatic enzyme inducer that can increase the activity of certain metabolic enzymes in the liver, potentially accelerating the metabolism of urolithin A and reducing its half-life in the body. This illustrates the broader principle that drugs interacting with cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver can competitively inhibit or induce these enzymes, thereby disrupting the metabolism and clearance of urolithin A and altering its systemic exposure. Common antibiotics, antifungal drugs, and anticancer drugs have been reported to interact with CYP450 enzymes in this way.

nodes.label: Urolithin A metabolism
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Rifampicin is a hepatic enzyme inducer that can increase the activity of certain metabolic enzymes in the liver, potentially accelerating the metabolism of urolithin A and reducing its half-life in the body. This illustrates the broader principle that drugs interacting with cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver can competitively inhibit or induce these enzymes, thereby disrupting the metabolism and clearance of urolithin A and altering its systemic exposure. Common antibiotics, antifungal drugs, and anticancer drugs have been reported to interact with CYP450 enzymes in this way.

nodes.label: Glutathione S-Transferase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: NRF2, acting through the Antioxidant Response Element, upregulates the expression of glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), which are pivotal detoxifying enzymes intricately related to antioxidant capacity. This transcriptional program, stimulated in the setting of urolithin A treatment, enhances cellular autophagy and mitochondrial quality control. GSTs are therefore downstream effectors of NRF2 signaling that help protect cells against oxidative and electrophilic stress and that support the removal and turnover of damaged mitochondria.

nodes.label: CDK
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Urolithin A can regulate the cell cycle by inhibiting the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and reducing the expression of cell cycle proteins such as cyclin D1, leading to cell cycle arrest in the G1 phase. It also increases the levels of cell cycle inhibitory proteins such as p21 and p27. This cell-cycle control, achieved through modulation of CDK activity and cyclin expression, contributes to urolithin A's reported antiproliferative activity and to its effects on cell cycle-related protein kinase complexes.

nodes.label: Bax/Bcl-2 ratio
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Urolithin A induces apoptosis by increasing the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, which results in the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, release of cytochrome c, and activation of the cascade of caspases, ultimately leading to cell apoptosis. Modulation of the pro-apoptotic to anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family ratio is a classical intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis trigger. It represents one of the several mechanisms through which urolithin A promotes programmed cell death, in addition to its activation of JNK and p38 MAPK signaling.

nodes.label: Caspases
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Upon loss of mitochondrial membrane potential induced by an increased Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, cytochrome c is released from mitochondria and activates the cascade of caspases, ultimately leading to cell apoptosis. This mitochondrial intrinsic pathway of apoptosis is engaged by urolithin A as part of its pro-apoptotic actions. Cytochrome c release and subsequent activation of executioner caspases are central to intrinsic cell death signaling downstream of mitochondrial permeabilization and contribute to the anti-tumor activity reported for urolithin A.

nodes.label: Fatty acid oxidation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Activation of AMPK promotes fatty acid oxidation and insulin sensitivity while reducing fatty acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis, and it can also increase mitochondrial biogenesis and glycogen synthesis. Through AMPK-dependent signaling, urolithin A improves muscle energy supply and metabolism. AMPK is therefore a central node connecting cellular energy status to muscle metabolic adaptation, endurance, and overall muscle performance, and its activation is a key mechanism underlying the metabolic effects attributed to urolithin A.

nodes.label: PPARγ
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Urolithin A modulates the activity of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ), a crucial transcription factor involved in adipocyte differentiation, glucose metabolism, and cholesterol metabolism. Studies indicate that urolithin A can increase the expression of PPARγ and the transcription of its downstream target genes, thereby promoting fatty acid oxidation, improving insulin sensitivity, and reducing cholesterol synthesis and absorption. These metabolic regulatory effects position PPARγ signaling as a mediator of urolithin A's influence on energy metabolism.

nodes.label: LKB1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: The literature demonstrates that urolithin A activates AMPK through a cascade involving the activation of SIRT3 and, subsequently, LKB1. In this cascade, the mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3 promotes the activation of LKB1, which in turn activates AMPK. This SIRT3-LKB1-AMPK axis links urolithin A treatment to enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and improved muscle energy metabolism and performance, and it illustrates how mitochondrial deacetylase activity connects to cellular energy-sensing signaling.

nodes.label: muscle protein synthesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: The mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) pathway plays a key role in regulating muscle protein synthesis and cell growth. Research has found that urolithin A can regulate protein synthesis and growth of muscle cells by inhibiting specific regulatory factors within the mTOR signaling pathway, such as PI3K and AKT. Balanced mTOR signaling supports muscle growth and maintains muscle quality, while urolithin A's inhibitory effects on this pathway favor autophagy induction and anti-inflammatory responses in addition to metabolic regulation.

nodes.label: TLR3/TRIF signaling
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: The literature indicates that urolithin A blocks the NF-κB/STAT1 axis through the inactivation of TLR3/TRIF signaling, reducing inflammation and enhancing antioxidant defense. TLR3/TRIF is an upstream innate immune signaling route whose inactivation dampens downstream NF-κB activation and the production of inflammatory mediators. This mechanism contributes to urolithin A's anti-inflammatory activity in settings such as poly(I:C)-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages and supports its role in muscle recovery and protection from inflammation-induced damage.

nodes.label: FOXO
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: The FoxO (forkhead box O) family is a group of transcription factors involved in regulating the synthesis and degradation of muscle proteins. Studies have found that urolithin A can inhibit the degradation of muscle proteins by suppressing the activation of FoxO, primarily by inhibiting the nuclear activity of FoxO and reducing its regulation of specific protein degradation pathways. This suppression of FoxO signaling preserves muscle mass under catabolic conditions and complements urolithin A's anabolic effects on protein synthesis.

nodes.label: muscle protein degradation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: The FoxO (forkhead box O) family is a group of transcription factors involved in regulating the synthesis and degradation of muscle proteins. Under catabolic conditions, nuclear FoxO drives expression of atrophy-related genes and activates specific protein degradation pathways that break down muscle proteins. Urolithin A suppresses FoxO activation, primarily by inhibiting its nuclear activity and reducing its regulation of these degradation pathways, thereby attenuating muscle protein degradation and helping to preserve muscle mass.

nodes.label: Ubiquitin-Proteasome System
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: The ubiquitin-proteasome system stands as one of the main pathways responsible for the degradation of intracellular proteins, including muscle proteins. Studies have found that urolithin A can attenuate the degradation of muscle proteins by inhibiting the activity of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, possibly by influencing the activity of specific ubiquitin ligases or proteasomes. This inhibition contributes to urolithin A's muscle-sparing and anti-atrophic effects, helping to preserve muscle mass during catabolic states.

nodes.label: Atrogin-1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 (muscle-specific RING finger protein 1 and 2) are pivotal molecules involved in muscle protein synthesis and degradation, functioning as muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases that drive protein breakdown during atrophy. Studies have shown that urolithin A can regulate muscle protein synthesis and degradation by inhibiting the activity of mTORC1 and the expression of Atrogin-1/MuRF1, thereby reducing atrophy signaling, attenuating protein degradation, and preserving muscle mass.

nodes.label: MuRF1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: MuRF1 (muscle-specific RING finger protein 1) is a muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligase that, together with Atrogin-1, marks muscle proteins for ubiquitin-proteasome degradation during atrophy. Studies have shown that urolithin A can regulate muscle protein synthesis and degradation by inhibiting the activity of mTORC1 and the expression of Atrogin-1/MuRF1, thereby reducing muscle protein degradation and supporting the maintenance of muscle mass under catabolic conditions. Suppressing this E3 ligase reduces ubiquitination of muscle proteins and complements urolithin A's anabolic effects on protein synthesis.

nodes.label: Muscle Hypertrophy
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Urolithin A may have a positive impact on muscle hypertrophy and maintenance of muscle mass through multiple pathways, including promotion of muscle cell repair and growth, enhancement of mitochondrial function and energy metabolism, and regulation of protein synthesis and degradation processes. It can increase the cross-sectional area of muscle fibers, muscle protein content, and muscle strength, thus promoting muscle hypertrophy. Current research is still limited and mostly conducted in vitro or in animal experiments, so human studies are needed.

nodes.label: Muscle Atrophy
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: In pathological conditions characterized by muscle atrophy, such as certain neuromuscular diseases or extended periods of immobility, urolithin A may offer potential benefits. It can stimulate muscle protein synthesis while inhibiting protein degradation pathways, including FoxO signaling, the ubiquitin-proteasome system, and the expression of Atrogin-1/MuRF1, helping to preserve muscle mass and mitigate muscle wasting. Human clinical validation of these anti-atrophic effects remains limited, but the mechanistic evidence is supportive.

nodes.label: ATP synthesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Urolithin A can promote the formation and enhanced function of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes, thereby improving the synthesis rate of ATP in muscle cells. ATP is the primary energy molecule for muscle cells and is crucial for muscle contraction and exercise performance. By promoting mitochondrial function and muscle energy metabolism, urolithin A increases the energy supply to muscle cells, improving endurance, strength, and recovery, and providing sustained energy support during prolonged or high-intensity exercise.

nodes.label: muscle fatigue
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
nodes.description: Existing evidence suggests that urolithin A may have a positive role in improving endurance and delaying muscle fatigue, both of which are intricately linked to mitochondrial function. By enhancing mitochondrial activity and ATP synthesis, urolithin A provides sustained energy support during prolonged or high-intensity exercise, and its anti-inflammatory properties alleviate tissue damage and muscle soreness caused by inflammation. Most studies have been conducted in vitro or on animals, so more human studies are needed to validate these effects.

nodes.label: Persulfates
nodes.description: Persulfates are employed as the oxidizing agent to convert adrenaline (epinephrine) into adrenochrome. The use of persulfates is advantageous because it precludes the effluent disposal problems associated with potassium ferricyanide and is significantly cheaper, although persulfate oxidation alone is slow and requires catalysts such as water-soluble bismuth salts. Suitable persulfates include potassium persulfate, sodium persulfate, and ammonium persulfate, with the sodium and ammonium salts preferred for their good solubility in water.

nodes.label: Bismuth
nodes.description: Water-soluble salts of bismuth, such as bismuth nitrate, bismuth oxynitrate, bismuth oxycarbonate, and bismuth citrate, accelerate the persulfate oxidation of adrenaline into adrenochrome, producing high-quality adrenochrome in high yields in a short period of time (about 30 to 45 minutes). Bismuth salts are used in amounts of 0.001 to 0.01 mole per mole of adrenaline; amounts below this do not significantly increase the reaction rate, while amounts above 0.01 mole may cause excessive oxidation and decompose the adrenochrome into tar-like by-products.

nodes.label: adrenochrome synthesis
nodes.description: Water-soluble salts of bismuth, such as bismuth nitrate, bismuth oxynitrate, bismuth oxycarbonate, and bismuth citrate, accelerate the persulfate oxidation of adrenaline into adrenochrome, producing high-quality adrenochrome in high yields in a short period of time (about 30 to 45 minutes). Bismuth salts are used in amounts of 0.001 to 0.01 mole per mole of adrenaline; amounts below this do not significantly increase the reaction rate, while amounts above 0.01 mole may cause excessive oxidation and decompose the adrenochrome into tar-like by-products.

nodes.label: Potassium ferricyanide
nodes.description: Adrenochrome has been commercially prepared by oxidizing adrenaline or its salts with potassium ferricyanide in an aqueous medium. This process is uneconomical because of the large quantities of potassium ferricyanide needed, the ensuing effluent disposal problems, and variability in product quality. The patent presents a bismuth-catalyzed persulfate process as a superior alternative that precludes these problems and yields less-colored carbazochrome and adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine products.

nodes.label: Hydrazines
nodes.description: Adrenochrome is very unstable due to its ortho-quinoid structure and is therefore usually stabilized by conventional derivatization with hydrazines, e.g., aminoguanidine, semicarbazide, phenylhydrazine, o-nitrophenylhydrazine, p-nitrophenylhydrazine, and 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine. These hydrazine derivatives serve both for the stabilization of adrenochrome and for the preparation of useful medicines such as hemostatics. The stabilization treatment is generally conducted for 30 minutes to 3 hours at a temperature of 0 to 15 degrees C.

nodes.label: Semicarbazide
nodes.description: Semicarbazide reacts with adrenochrome to form adrenochrome monosemicarbazone (carbazochrome), a hemostatic agent. In the patented process, semicarbazide hydrochloride is added to the adrenochrome solution at below 10 degrees C in the presence of a potassium acetate buffer, with the stabilization carried out at pH 5 to 7. The reaction yields about 40.0 g of crude powder that is purified by dissolving in dilute sodium hydroxide, active carbon treatment, and precipitation at pH 5.5, and the purified product shows an ultraviolet absorption maximum at 354 nm and characteristic infrared absorptions matching those of an authentic sample.

nodes.label: Sodium hydrogencarbonate
nodes.description: The aqueous reaction medium for adrenochrome synthesis is maintained at a pH from 4 to 8, preferably with a buffer such as sodium hydrogencarbonate, sodium dihydrogenphosphate, disodium hydrogenphosphate, potassium acetate, or sodium acetate, with sodium hydrogencarbonate being preferred. The buffer is generally used in an amount of 4 to 7 moles, preferably 5 to 6 moles, per mole of adrenaline. Maintaining this pH range supports the persulfate oxidation of adrenaline catalyzed by water-soluble bismuth salts.

nodes.label: Ammonium Persulfate
nodes.description: Ammonium persulfate is one of the suitable persulfate oxidizing agents for converting adrenaline into adrenochrome, together with potassium persulfate and sodium persulfate. Sodium and ammonium persulfates are preferred over potassium persulfate for their good solubility in water. In the examples, ammonium persulfate (about 0.42 mole) is used with a sodium hydrogencarbonate buffer and a bismuth salt catalyst at 0 to 5 degrees C to produce adrenochrome in maximum yield within about 30 to 45 minutes.

nodes.label: 495 nm wavelength
nodes.description: During the oxidation of adrenaline, the reaction mixture is tinged with purplish red due to the production of adrenochrome, and its color becomes deeper with increasing adrenochrome content. The reaction is continued until the absorbance at a wavelength of 495 nm, measured by sampling the reaction mixture at an appropriate time, reaches a maximum, at which point further oxidation of the product is minimized and adrenochrome is obtained in maximum yield. The reaction time required for maximum yield varies from 30 to 45 minutes depending on the temperature of the reaction mixture and the level of catalyst employed.

nodes.label: Yoshinori Ohsumi
nodes.description: Yoshinori Ohsumi was awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his pioneering work using yeast genetics to identify the core autophagy-related (ATG) genes that govern the process. Through systematic mutagenesis screens, he uncovered the molecular machinery responsible for autophagosome formation, including the ubiquitin-like conjugation systems that build the phagophore membrane. His discoveries established autophagy as a genetically tractable and evolutionarily conserved degradation pathway, providing the conceptual framework for all subsequent mammalian autophagy research. The recognition underscored the fundamental importance of autophagy in cellular homeostasis, development, and human disease.

nodes.label: Lysosomal catabolic process
nodes.description: Autophagy is a conserved lysosome-dependent catabolic process in which cytoplasmic constituents—including misfolded proteins, protein aggregates, damaged organelles, and intracellular pathogens—are sequestered into double-membrane autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes for enzymatic degradation. The resulting macromolecular building blocks such as amino acids, fatty acids, and nucleotides are recycled to sustain metabolism and biosynthetic capacity during nutrient stress. As the cell's principal quality-control and nutrient-recycling system, autophagy is essential for maintaining proteostasis and organellar integrity across nearly all eukaryotic cells. Defects in autophagic flux are causally linked to aging, neurodegeneration, cancer, and metabolic disease, making it a central node in cellular homeostasis.

nodes.label: Macroautophagy
nodes.description: Macroautophagy (commonly termed autophagy) is the best-characterized form, in which a de novo formed double-membrane structure called the phagophore expands to engulf cytoplasmic cargo and seals into an autophagosome. The autophagosome then fuses with a lysosome, forming an autolysosome where luminal contents are degraded by acidic hydrolases. This bulk and selective degradative route is orchestrated by the conserved ATG machinery, including the ULK1 initiation complex and the PI3K III/Beclin 1 nucleation complex. Macroautophagy is the dominant pathway induced by starvation, stress, and many pharmacological interventions and is the primary focus of most therapeutic autophagy modulation.

nodes.label: Microautophagy
nodes.description: Microautophagy involves the direct engulfment of cytoplasmic cargo by the lysosomal (or vacuolar) membrane through invagination, tubulation, or protrusion of the limiting membrane, without the requirement for a distinct autophagosome intermediate. The entrapped material is then internalized into the lysosomal lumen for degradation, a process that is particularly prominent in yeast vacuoles and in mammalian late endosomes/multivesicular bodies. Compared with macroautophagy, microautophagy operates with less selectivity and is regulated by distinct machineries, though it similarly contributes to organelle and protein turnover. It plays roles in lipid droplet turnover, membrane protein degradation, and quality control under both basal and stress conditions.

nodes.label: Chaperone-Mediated Autophagy
nodes.description: Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) is a selective form of lysosomal degradation in which individual soluble cytosolic proteins bearing a pentapeptide KFERQ-like targeting motif are recognized by the cytosolic chaperone HSC70. The substrate-chaperone complex is then delivered to the lysosomal membrane, where the receptor LAMP-2A monomers translocate the unfolded substrate across the membrane into the lumen for degradation. Unlike macro- and microautophagy, CMA degrades one protein at a time and does not require membrane engulfment or autophagosome formation. CMA activity declines with age and is implicated in neurodegeneration and cancer, and it is subject to regulation by mTORC2 and other signaling nodes.

nodes.label: ULK1
nodes.description: The ULK1 complex, composed of ULK1 or ULK2 kinase together with Atg13, FIP200, and Atg101, acts as the primary initiator of autophagosome formation downstream of nutrient sensing. Under starvation, AMPK directly activates ULK1 while mTORC1 is withdrawn, allowing the complex to phosphorylate targets and recruit the downstream PI3K III/Beclin 1 nucleation machinery. ULK1 kinase activity is essential for the localized recruitment of ATG proteins to the phagophore assembly site and for the earliest steps of membrane expansion. Thus the ULK1 complex serves as the integration point that converts nutrient and energy signals into the physical initiation of autophagosome biogenesis.

nodes.label: PI3K III complex
nodes.description: The class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K III) complex, centered on Vps34 and including Beclin 1, Atg14, Vps15, and Ambra-1, generates phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) at membranes to drive autophagosome nucleation. PI3P recruits effector proteins carrying PI3P-binding domains that organize the expanding phagophore and tether downstream ATG conjugation systems. Beclin 1 is a tumor suppressor whose activity is modulated by interacting partners and by anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins that restrain autophagy under fed conditions. This nucleation complex functions immediately downstream of the ULK1 initiator and is a critical control node for the magnitude of autophagic responses.

nodes.label: Intermittent Fasting
nodes.description: Intermittent fasting (IF) is a dietary intervention that periodically restricts caloric intake, producing the nutrient deprivation signals that robustly induce autophagy in many tissues. In preclinical cancer models, cycles of IF combined with chemotherapy have been shown to slow tumor growth and improve therapeutic index by exploiting the differential stress resistance of normal versus malignant cells. The protective effect of autophagy during fasting helps normal cells tolerate chemotherapy, while many tumors remain reliant on constitutive autophagy for survival. These findings position IF as a translational strategy to modulate autophagic tone for anti-cancer and pro-longevity benefits.

nodes.label: Beclin 1
nodes.description: Beclin 1 is a core autophagy protein and a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor whose monoallelic deletion is frequently observed in human ovarian, breast, and prostate cancers. Loss of one BECN1 allele reduces autophagic flux, increasing susceptibility to oxidative damage, genomic instability, and inflammation that favor tumor initiation. Mechanistically, Beclin 1 functions as the scaffold of the PI3K III nucleation complex, and its interaction with Bcl-2 family members further couples autophagy to apoptotic regulation. Its frequent deletion in epithelial cancers established autophagy as a genuine tumor-suppression pathway.

nodes.label: Tumor suppressor
nodes.description: Beclin 1 is a core autophagy protein and a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor whose monoallelic deletion is frequently observed in human ovarian, breast, and prostate cancers. Loss of one BECN1 allele reduces autophagic flux, increasing susceptibility to oxidative damage, genomic instability, and inflammation that favor tumor initiation. Mechanistically, Beclin 1 functions as the scaffold of the PI3K III nucleation complex, and its interaction with Bcl-2 family members further couples autophagy to apoptotic regulation. Its frequent deletion in epithelial cancers established autophagy as a genuine tumor-suppression pathway.

nodes.label: RAS
nodes.description: Oncogenic RAS signaling drives a metabolic reprogramming in which transformed cells upregulate basal autophagy to supply the amino acids, lipids, and nucleotides needed for sustained proliferation. Mutant RAS activates both mTOR and, via nutrient and energy stress feedback, the autophagic machinery, allowing tumor cells to survive in nutrient-poor microenvironments. Pharmacologic or genetic blockade of autophagy selectively impairs the viability of RAS-driven tumors, highlighting autophagy as a dependency in these cancers. This dependency has motivated clinical efforts to combine RAS pathway-targeted or standard therapies with autophagy inhibition.

nodes.label: Dietary Restriction
nodes.description: Dietary restriction (DR) and its variants are among the most potent physiological activators of autophagy, engaging the pathway in most cultured cells and across many organs in vivo. By lowering circulating nutrients and insulin while raising AMP/ATP ratios, DR relieves mTORC1 inhibition and activates AMPK, thereby de-repressing the ULK1 complex and TFEB-dependent lysosomal programs. In model organisms such as C. elegans, DR induces autophagy through coordinated transcriptional changes mediated by orthologs like HLH-30/TFEB. The health- and lifespan-extending effects of DR are widely attributed in substantial part to this induction of adaptive autophagy.

nodes.label: Caloric Restriction Mimetics
nodes.description: Caloric restriction mimetics are pharmacological agents that reproduce the metabolic and autophagic benefits of caloric restriction without sustained food reduction.
