nodes.description: Senescent cells characteristically show reduced expression of lamin B1 (encoded by LMNB1), a structural component of the nuclear lamina. Lamin B1 loss detaches lamina-associated domains (LADs) from the nuclear periphery, spatially reorganizing chromatin and contributing to the altered gene expression and genomic instability of senescence. This marker is relatively conserved across cell types and tissues, making it a practical histological and molecular signature of senescent cells in vivo. A caveat is that lamin B1 loss can also occur in certain differentiation and disease states, so it is best used in combination with other markers.

nodes.label: Senolytics
nodes.description: Senescence is a direct therapeutic target of senolytics, agents that selectively eliminate senescent cells. Genetic or pharmacological clearance of p16-positive senescent cells in murine models delays age-related dysfunction, extends healthspan, and alleviates multiple pathologies. The strategy exploits the pro-survival SCAP network that senescent cells depend on, pushing them into apoptosis while sparing healthy cells. Clinical translation is ongoing, with the key caveat that intermittent, tissue-specific clearance is preferable to chronic ablation, which could impair beneficial acute-senescence functions.

nodes.label: Senomorphics
nodes.description: Senescence is modulated by senomorphics, compounds that suppress the deleterious SASP without killing the senescent cell itself. By targeting upstream SASP regulators (mTOR, NF-κB, JAK-STAT3, p38 MAPK, BRD4), senomorphics dampen the paracrine and inflammatory consequences of senescence. This is conceptually complementary to senolytics, which remove the cell rather than its output. Senomorphics preserve potentially beneficial acute-senescence functions (e.g., wound healing, tumor suppression) while mitigating chronic harm.

nodes.label: Secretory Phenotype
nodes.description: The SASP is a hypersecretory state -- a specialized secretory phenotype -- in which senescent cells upregulate and release hundreds of factors including interleukins, chemokines, growth factors, proteases, and extracellular vesicles. This secreted output contrasts with the quiescent, low-turnover secretome of non-senescent cells and is a defining non-cell-autonomous feature of the senescent state. The composition of the SASP is variable, shaped by the senescence inducer, cell type, and tissue context. Its classification as a secretory phenotype emphasizes that senescence exerts its effects largely through communication with the microenvironment.

nodes.label: JAK-STAT3
nodes.description: The JAK-STAT3 signaling axis promotes a pro-inflammatory SASP by interacting with p38 MAPK and mTOR and by transducing cues from SASP cytokines such as IL-6. STAT3 activation contributes to age-related frailty and to the immune-modulatory and tumor-promoting facets of the secretome. JAK1/2 inhibitors (e.g., ruxolitinib) reduce SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8, validating the axis as a senomorphic target. The pathway is especially important for the feed-forward, self-reinforcing inflammation characteristic of chronic senescence.

nodes.label: Nutlin 3a
nodes.description: Nutlin 3a suppresses the pro-inflammatory SASP by inhibiting MDM2, thereby stabilizing p53; p53 in turn restrains NF-κB-driven SASP factor expression. This mechanism exploits the natural tumor-suppressive rheostat of p53 rather than broadly blocking inflammation. The compound is primarily a research tool with limited clinical development, constraining its translational confidence. Mechanistically, its SASP-suppressive effect is well grounded in the p53 restraint of the secretome.

nodes.label: Paracrine Senescence
nodes.description: SASP factors such as IL-1α, TGFβ, VEGF, and CCL2 can act in an autocrine and paracrine manner to reinforce the senescent state and induce growth arrest in neighboring healthy cells -- a process termed paracrine (or bystander) senescence. This spreads the arrested phenotype through tissues, amplifying the functional impact of a small senescent fraction. The directionality is outward: the secretome of one cell converts adjacent cells into a senescent state. A caveat is that paracrine senescence requires susceptible recipients and sufficient SASP magnitude, and it can be both tumor-suppressive and pathological.

nodes.label: Natural Killer Cells
nodes.description: SASP chemokines including CCL2, CCL5, CXCL1, and CXCL10 act as find-me signals that recruit natural killer (NK) cells to sites of senescence. NK cells then directly kill senescent cells via NKG2D recognition of stress-induced ligands (MICA, MICB, ULBP2). This recruitment is a key arm of senescence surveillance, converting the SASP into an immune-clearance stimulus. The efficiency of recruitment declines with immunosenescence, allowing senescent-cell accumulation.

nodes.label: MMP-3
nodes.description: Matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3) is a SASP protease associated with extracellular matrix degradation, tissue remodeling, and, in tumor contexts, cancer cell invasion and metastasis. Its secretion reflects the matrix-remodeling arm of the secretome that supports both wound healing and pathological tissue breakdown. MMP-3 acts on ECM substrates and can activate other MMPs in a cascade. It is a representative of the protease component that distinguishes the SASP from a purely cytokine profile.

nodes.label: CCL2
nodes.description: CCL2 (MCP-1) is a SASP chemokine regulated by IL-1α/IL-1β that is a potent chemoattractant for monocytes and CCR2+ myeloid precursors, recruiting macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells. It thus links the senescent secretome to innate and suppressive immune infiltration. CCL2 also contributes to paracrine senescence and to inflammaging. Its recruitment functions make it a central communicator between senescent cells and the immune milieu.

nodes.label: TNFalpha
nodes.description: Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha) is a pro-inflammatory SASP cytokine that contributes to immune modulation, NF-κB reinforcement, and inflammaging. It can act in an autocrine loop to amplify the secretome and in a paracrine manner to affect neighboring cells. TNFalpha is less universally dominant than IL-6 in the SASP but is consistently present in many models. Its pleiotropic inflammatory actions solidify its status as a canonical SASP component.

nodes.label: GATA4
nodes.description: GATA4 is a transcriptional regulator that promotes the pro-inflammatory SASP by activating NF-κB, in part via TRAF3IP2 (Act1), and by inhibiting autophagy, which would otherwise clear damaging organelles. Its accumulation in senescence makes it an upstream driver of the secretome's inflammatory arm. GATA4 thus couples defective organelle turnover to cytokine production. The mechanism is well supported and positions GATA4 as a senescence-specific SASP regulator.

nodes.label: METTL3/METTL14
nodes.description: The METTL3-METTL14 m6A methyltransferase complex promotes SASP factor expression by installing N6-methyladenosine marks that facilitate enhancer-promoter looping and stabilize SASP transcripts. This epitranscriptomic layer adds post-transcriptional control to the secretome. The relationship is mechanistically plausible and supported by knockout studies, but the field is newer and less consolidated than the NF-κB/mTOR axes. Confidence is therefore moderate.

nodes.label: Ruxolitinib
nodes.description: Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, reduces SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8 in senescent fibroblasts by blocking JAK-STAT3 signaling downstream of SASP cytokines. As a clinically approved myelofibrosis drug, it is a translatable senomorphic agent. Its suppression is targeted to the JAK-STAT arm rather than the entire secretome. The evidence is robust in cellular models and supported by its known immunomodulatory profile.

nodes.label: Lamivudine
nodes.description: Lamivudine (3TC), a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, suppresses the SASP by inhibiting LINE-1 (L1) reverse transcription, thereby reducing cytosolic retroelement cDNA that would activate cGAS-STING-NF-κB signaling. This repurposes an antiretroviral agent as a senomorphic, targeting the retrotransposon arm of SASP induction. The mechanism is supported by studies showing reduced SASP upon L1 inhibition. Clinical relevance is still investigative, keeping confidence moderate.

nodes.label: SAMD
nodes.description: Senescent cells exhibit senescence-associated mitochondrial dysfunction (SAMD), characterized by reduced oxidative phosphorylation capacity, altered mitochondrial morphology, and elevated ROS production. SAMD is not merely a bystander but an active driver: mitochondrial stress releases mtDNA via minority MOMP, activating cGAS-STING and reinforcing the SASP. The dysfunctional mitochondria also elevate ROS that cause further DNA damage, amplifying arrest. SAMD thus couples metabolic remodeling to the inflammatory secretome.

nodes.label: Dasatinib
nodes.description: Dasatinib, a multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is a component of the foundational D+Q (dasatinib + quercetin) senolytic combination. It is proposed to act by inhibiting pro-survival kinases in senescent cells, lowering their apoptotic threshold. Dasatinib has established clinical use in chronic myeloid leukemia, aiding its repurposing. Its senolytic activity is well demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, though tissue selectivity varies.

nodes.label: Navitoclax
nodes.description: Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a potent BCL-2/BCL-XL/BCL-W inhibitor with strong senolytic activity, effectively inducing apoptosis in senescent cells. It is limited clinically by on-target thrombocytopenia due to BCL-XL dependence of platelets, spurring the development of more selective derivatives. Its senolytic efficacy is well established in multiple models. The toxicity caveat shapes its use toward intermittent or tissue-targeted regimens.

nodes.label: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
nodes.description: Senolytic therapy (D+Q) has been tested for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) in a pilot clinical trial (NCT02874989), where it improved physical function. The rationale is that senescent cell accumulation and SASP-driven fibrosis contribute to IPF pathogenesis. Results support further evaluation of senolytics in fibrotic lung disease. This is among the most advanced clinical indications for senolytic therapy.

nodes.label: Diabetic Kidney Disease
nodes.description: Senolytic therapy (D+Q) has been tested in a pilot/phase trial for diabetic kidney disease (NCT02848131), based on evidence that senescent cells and SASP drive renal fibrosis and dysfunction in diabetes. The trial assesses feasibility, safety, and biomarkers of renal senescence. Early data inform the potential of senolytics in metainflammation and nephropathy. Clinical confidence remains preliminary pending larger trials.

nodes.label: Senotherapeutic
nodes.description: The term 'senotherapeutic' is an umbrella encompassing both senolytics (which eliminate senescent cells) and senomorphics (which suppress the SASP). Senolytics act on the cellular driver, while senomorphics act on the secretory effector, together spanning the intervention space against senescence. This inclusive definition reflects the field's two-pronged therapeutic philosophy. Recognizing both under one term aids classification of anti-senescence strategies.

nodes.label: Senotherapy
nodes.description: Senotherapy encompasses senolytics, the cell-elimination arm that selectively induces apoptosis in senescent cells by disabling SCAPs. This is one of the two principal divisions of senotherapy, the other being senomorphics. The term captures the spectrum of interventions aimed at the senescent cell. Encompassing senolytics underscores the elimination-based strategy's centrality to the field.

nodes.label: Notch
nodes.description: Notch signaling is essential for establishing paracrine senescence and, paradoxically, weakens the secondary SASP in receiving cells. Notch integrates cues from the SASP to reinforce arrest in neighbors while modulating their secretory output. Its role indicates that paracrine senescence is an active, regulated program rather than passive factor exposure. The precise directionality (establish vs. dampen SASP) reflects context-dependent Notch outputs.

nodes.label: IFITM3
nodes.description: IFITM3 is enriched in exosomes released from senescent cells and mediates paracrine senescence by transmitting senescence signals to recipient cells. As an exosomal cargo, it represents a vesicle-based, rather than soluble-factor, route of spread. Its inclusion highlights that paracrine senescence is not solely cytokine-driven. The mechanism adds a non-classical communication modality to the SASP paradigm.

nodes.label: Immunosenescence
nodes.description: Senescence surveillance is impaired by immunosenescence -- the age-related decline in immune competence -- which compromises NK, macrophage, and T-cell mediated clearance of senescent cells. Elevated MDSCs and immune suppression further blunt surveillance. The result is permissive accumulation of senescent cells and increased tumor and inflammatory risk. This positions immunosenescence as both cause and consequence of senescence pathology.

nodes.label: mtDNA
nodes.description: SAMD releases mtDNA into the cytosol via minority MOMP -- sublethal, intermittent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization that leaks mtDNA without triggering full apoptosis. The escaped mtDNA acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern activating cGAS-STING. This release is a pivotal link between mitochondrial stress and innate immune activation in senescence. It exemplifies how senescent cells walk a fine line between life and death.

nodes.label: HIRA/ASF1a
nodes.description: SAHF are assembled by the HIRA-ASF1a histone chaperone complex, which deposits macroH2A and core histones to establish H3K9me3-marked heterochromatin at SAHF. This chaperone-driven deposition is required for the formation of the DAPI-dense foci. The process links histone dynamics directly to senescence-specific chromatin reorganization. HIRA/ASF1a thus provide the assembly machinery for the repressive structures.

nodes.label: SADS
nodes.description: SADS (senescence-associated distal satellite) is a form of heterochromatin decompaction in senescent cells, specifically the relaxation of constitutive pericentromeric and pericentrosomal satellite heterochromatin. Unlike SAHF (which compacts facultative heterochromatin), SADS decompacts constitutive repeats. This structural change alters the nuclear architecture and chromatin accessibility of repetitive regions. SADS represents a distinct, counterintuitive chromatin reorganization during senescence.

nodes.label: Heterochromatin Decompaction
nodes.description: SADS (senescence-associated distal satellite) is a form of heterochromatin decompaction in senescent cells, specifically the relaxation of constitutive pericentromeric and pericentrosomal satellite heterochromatin. Unlike SAHF (which compacts facultative heterochromatin), SADS decompacts constitutive repeats. This structural change alters the nuclear architecture and chromatin accessibility of repetitive regions. SADS represents a distinct, counterintuitive chromatin reorganization during senescence.

nodes.label: T Cell
nodes.description: Immunosenescence impairs T-cell immunity, featuring perturbed memory responses, thymic involution, reduced naive T-cell generation, and accumulation of differentiated, often dysfunctional memory/effector subsets (e.g., EMRA CD8+ T cells). This limits responses to infection and vaccination in the elderly. The impairment is a hallmark of adaptive immune aging. It directly weakens senescence surveillance mediated by T cells.

nodes.label: DNA-SCARS
nodes.description: Genotoxic stress in TIS generates persistent DNA damage foci termed DNA-SCARS (DNA segments with chromatin alterations reinforcing senescence), which are precursors to cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCF). These structures sustain DDR signaling and the arrested state. DNA-SCARS thereby mechanistically link damage to durable senescence. They are a defining feature distinguishing TIS from transient damage responses.

nodes.label: Glucocorticoids
nodes.description: NF-κB is inhibited by glucocorticoids, which block pro-inflammatory SASP by impairing IL-1α-mediated NF-κB activity. Glucocorticoids repress NF-κB transactivation via co-repressor recruitment, reducing SASP cytokine output. This explains their classic anti-inflammatory action in senescence contexts. The inhibition is well established pharmacologically, though chronic use carries significant side effects.

nodes.label: SB203580
nodes.description: p38 MAPK is inhibited by SB203580, a classical pyridinyl imidazole inhibitor that suppresses p38alpha/beta and thereby reduces SASP from fibroblasts of older donors. By blocking p38, SB203580 lowers NF-κB activation and SASP transcript stabilization. This provides a tool compound validating p38 as a senomorphic target. The inhibition is specific and well characterized in cellular models.

nodes.label: p21 CIP1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which transcriptionally induces the CDK inhibitor p21CIP1; p21 binds and inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes (notably CDK2), enforcing a G1/S arrest. This p53 to p21 axis is a primary, rapid enforcement mechanism of senescence and quiescence. The induction is dose-dependent and reversible in the short term but locks arrest when sustained. It exemplifies tumor-suppressive cell-cycle control.

nodes.label: CDK2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
nodes.description: p21CIP1 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) by binding the cyclin E/A-CDK2 complex, preventing phosphorylation of Rb and thereby enforcing G1/S arrest. This is a direct enzymatic inhibition central to p53-driven senescence and quiescence. By blocking S-phase entry, p21 locks cells out of the cell cycle. Its inhibitory action is a canonical CDK-inhibitor function.

nodes.label: Early SASP
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
nodes.description: p21 supports an early secretory phenotype -- including factors such as CXCL14 and IGFBP3 -- that places stressed cells under immunosurveillance prior to full senescence. This early p21-associated secretome differs from the later NF-κB-dominated SASP. It suggests p21 contributes to both arrest and the initial communicative state of stressed cells. The relationship is more nuanced than simple arrest enforcement, giving moderate confidence.

nodes.label: CDK4
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: p16INK4a inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) by binding the cyclin D-CDK4 complex, preventing Rb phosphorylation and maintaining the growth-suppressive, hypophosphorylated state of Rb. This is a primary mechanism by which p16 enforces the durable, p53-independent phase of senescence. Loss of p16 is a common event in cancer, underscoring its tumor-suppressive role. The inhibition is direct and well established.

nodes.label: CDK6
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: p16INK4a also inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 6 (CDK6), similarly preventing cyclin D-CDK6-mediated Rb phosphorylation and stabilizing the arrested state. This broad inhibition of both CDK4 and CDK6 ensures robust G1 blockade. The dual targeting makes p16 a potent, non-redundant cell-cycle inhibitor. Its action underpins the irreversibility of established senescence.

nodes.label: Senescent Cell Accumulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial dysfunction in cellular senescence a bridge to neurodegenerative disease.md
nodes.description: Aging causes senescent-cell accumulation as telomere shortening, cumulative DNA damage, and stem-cell stress increase senescent-cell formation, while declining immune clearance reduces removal. The burden rises across multiple tissues, often described as exponential with age. This accumulation is a cardinal hallmark linking cellular senescence to organismal aging. The causal direction is reinforced by experiments showing that clearing these cells alleviates age-related dysfunction.

nodes.label: SASP Enhancers
nodes.description: H3K27ac marks senescence-activated super-enhancers that drive SASP expression, identifying the enhancer landscape licensed during senescence. These acetylated, active enhancers recruit BRD4 and transcription factors such as AP-1 and NF-κB to SASP loci. The mark thus charts the chromatin basis of the secretome. Targeting these enhancers (e.g., with BET inhibitors) suppresses SASP.

nodes.label: Activin A
nodes.description: Activin A is a homodimer of inhibin beta-A (INHBA) subunits and a member of the TGFβ superfamily of cytokines. Like other family members it signals through serine/threonine kinase receptors to regulate cell fate and inflammation. Its classification within the TGFβ superfamily situates it among the SASP factors with paracrine arrest-inducing capacity. Activin A is a structurally defined ligand distinct from TGFβ1 but functionally overlapping.

nodes.label: TGFβ Superfamily
nodes.description: Activin A is a homodimer of inhibin beta-A (INHBA) subunits and a member of the TGFβ superfamily of cytokines. Like other family members it signals through serine/threonine kinase receptors to regulate cell fate and inflammation. Its classification within the TGFβ superfamily situates it among the SASP factors with paracrine arrest-inducing capacity. Activin A is a structurally defined ligand distinct from TGFβ1 but functionally overlapping.

nodes.label: ALK4
nodes.description: Activin A signals through the type I receptor ALK4 and type II receptors activin RIIA/RIIB, which phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3 to transmit signals to the nucleus. This receptor architecture is canonical for activin/nodal signaling within the TGFβ superfamily. The ALK4-SMAD2/3 axis is required for Activin A's biological effects in senescence. It links ligand binding directly to transcriptional reprogramming of recipient cells.

nodes.label: SMAD2
nodes.description: Phosphorylated SMAD2 (with SMAD3) complexes with SMAD4 and translocates to the nucleus to regulate target gene transcription downstream of Activin A-ALK4 signaling. This SMAD-dependent transduction is the principal route by which Activin A alters gene expression in receiving cells. It drives expression of cell-cycle inhibitors that reinforce arrest. The pathway is a standard TGFβ-superfamily output mechanism.

nodes.label: CDKN2B
nodes.description: Activin A-SMAD signaling induces p15INK4b (encoded by CDKN2B) and p21CIP1 in receiving cells during paracrine senescence, reinforcing growth arrest. By engaging the CDK inhibitor network, Activin A helps lock neighboring cells into a senescent state. This positions it as a effector of transmissible arrest. The induction is part of the concerted SASP-mediated paracrine program.

nodes.label: Follistatin
nodes.description: Follistatin binds and neutralizes Activin A extracellularly, acting as a soluble antagonist that can block its paracrine senescence-inducing activity. This provides a natural brake on Activin A signaling and a potential therapeutic route to limit SASP-mediated arrest spread. The follistatin-Activin A axis is a classic antagonistic ligand-binding pair. Neutralization experiments confirm its functional relevance in paracrine senescence.

nodes.label: Acute Stress-Associated Phenotype
nodes.description: The acute stress-associated phenotype (ASAP) is the early, prompt cellular response mounted upon stress before full senescence markers become evident; it can transition into the chronic SASP. ASAP represents a pre-secretome state that licenses subsequent inflammatory output. Its precedence establishes a temporal hierarchy: stress sensing first, then durable secretome. Understanding ASAP helps separate acute protective responses from chronic, deleterious senescence.

nodes.label: TRAF6
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
nodes.description: The ATM-TRAF6-TAK1 axis drives ASAP signaling: ATM activates TRAF6, which undergoes auto-ubiquitination and recruits TAK1 to propagate stress and inflammatory signals. TAK1 in turn activates p38 MAPK and NF-κB downstream, linking DNA damage sensing to SASP transcription. This axis is a conserved scaffold connecting genotoxic stress to senescence inflammation. It operates upstream of the established SASP regulatory network.

nodes.label: CCL20
nodes.description: CCL20 (MIP-3alpha) is a CC chemokine that signals exclusively through the receptor CCR6, belonging to the broader chemokine family that directs leukocyte trafficking. Its classification as a chemokine situates it among the SASP components that recruit immune cells. As a SASP factor, CCL20 extends the communicative reach of senescent cells to adaptive immunity. Its restricted receptor usage gives it a focused recruitment profile.

nodes.label: Chemokine
nodes.description: CCL20 (MIP-3alpha) is a CC chemokine that signals exclusively through the receptor CCR6, belonging to the broader chemokine family that directs leukocyte trafficking. Its classification as a chemokine situates it among the SASP components that recruit immune cells. As a SASP factor, CCL20 extends the communicative reach of senescent cells to adaptive immunity. Its restricted receptor usage gives it a focused recruitment profile.

nodes.label: CCR6
nodes.description: CCL20 is the sole ligand for CCR6, a Gai-coupled GPCR that drives chemotaxis via PI3K/Akt, p38 MAPK, and Ca2+ flux in target cells. This exclusive pairing directs recruitment of CCR6+ cells such as TH17 lymphocytes and dendritic cells. In the senescence context, CCL20-CCR6 links the SASP to adaptive immune infiltration. The signaling mechanism is well characterized in lymphocyte biology.

nodes.label: TH17
nodes.description: The CCL20-CCR6 axis links the SASP to adaptive immunity by recruiting TH17 cells, which express CCR6 and are drawn to CCL20-rich senescent foci. TH17 recruitment can amplify local inflammation and shape the immune milieu around senescent cells. This connects the secretome to a distinct T-cell subset with pro-inflammatory roles. The relationship expands the immunological consequences of the SASP.

nodes.label: p15INK4b
nodes.description: CDKN2B encodes p15INK4b, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that blocks CDK4/6 and thereby enforces G1 arrest. As a tumor-suppressor locus often co-regulated with CDKN2A, its product is a core effector of growth inhibition. In senescence, CDKN2B induction is a key event in paracrine and TGFβ-driven arrest. The encoding relationship is a fundamental gene-to-protein fact.

nodes.label: HLA-E
nodes.description: HLA-E is a non-classical (class Ib) major histocompatibility complex molecule with limited polymorphism, presenting a restricted set of peptides (often leader peptides) to innate lymphoid receptors. Its classification distinguishes it from classical MHC class Ia molecules. In senescence, HLA-E upregulation becomes a mechanism of immune evasion. The class Ib identity underpins its specialized ligand-receptor interactions.

nodes.label: MHC Class Ib
nodes.description: HLA-E is a non-classical (class Ib) major histocompatibility complex molecule with limited polymorphism, presenting a restricted set of peptides (often leader peptides) to innate lymphoid receptors. Its classification distinguishes it from classical MHC class Ia molecules. In senescence, HLA-E upregulation becomes a mechanism of immune evasion. The class Ib identity underpins its specialized ligand-receptor interactions.

nodes.label: NKG2A
nodes.description: HLA-E is the ligand for the inhibitory receptor NKG2A/CD94 heterodimer expressed on NK cells and CD8+ T cells. This binding delivers a cognate inhibitory signal upon engagement. The interaction is a canonical innate immune checkpoint. In senescence, HLA-E-NKG2A engagement becomes a route by which arrested cells dampen their own immune clearance.

nodes.label: CD8 T Cells
nodes.description: HLA-E-NKG2A/CD94 engagement on CD8+ T cells suppresses their cytotoxic killing, extending the immune-evasive effect beyond NK cells. This allows HLA-E-upregulated senescent and malignant cells to evade adaptive cytotoxic lymphocytes. The suppression contributes to failed clearance and persistence. It reinforces the dual (innate and adaptive) immune evasion by HLA-E.

nodes.label: Inflammasome
nodes.description: Inflammasomes are cytosolic supramolecular complexes of the innate immune system that assemble in response to pathogens or sterile danger signals to activate inflammatory caspases. They are not antibodies (immune complexes) but rather multiprotein scaffolds; the original classification here as an immune complex is loose, though inflammasomes are innate immune signaling platforms. They serve as a key intersection between senescence, DAMPs, and inflammation. Their activation links cellular damage to IL-1 family cytokine release.

nodes.label: Immune Complex
nodes.description: Inflammasomes are cytosolic supramolecular complexes of the innate immune system that assemble in response to pathogens or sterile danger signals to activate inflammatory caspases. They are not antibodies (immune complexes) but rather multiprotein scaffolds; the original classification here as an immune complex is loose, though inflammasomes are innate immune signaling platforms. They serve as a key intersection between senescence, DAMPs, and inflammation. Their activation links cellular damage to IL-1 family cytokine release.

nodes.label: Caspase-1
nodes.description: Canonical inflammasomes activate caspase-1, which processes pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature secreted forms and cleaves gasdermin D to execute pyroptosis. This activation is the central effector step of the inflammasome pathway. In senescence, caspase-1 activity also feeds the SASP. The relationship is a foundational inflammasome mechanism with direct relevance to senescence inflammation.

nodes.label: Noncanonical Inflammasome
nodes.description: Senescent cells activate the noncanonical inflammasome (caspase-5/11), which cleaves IL-1α and drives SASP establishment. This provides a caspase-5-dependent route to the secretome that is distinct from the canonical NLRP3/caspase-1 pathway. The noncanonical activation is increasingly recognized as a core SASP licensing mechanism. It links intracellular LPS/cytosolic sensing to senescence inflammation.

nodes.label: MyD88
nodes.description: MyD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor protein serving as the central hub of Toll-like receptor (TLR) and IL-1R signaling, linking receptor engagement to downstream kinase cascades. Its classification as an adaptor reflects its role in assembling signaling complexes rather than enzymatic catalysis. In senescence, MyD88 transduces IL-1α signals that sustain the SASP. It is a foundational innate immune signaling scaffold.

nodes.label: Adaptor Protein
nodes.description: MyD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor protein serving as the central hub of Toll-like receptor (TLR) and IL-1R signaling, linking receptor engagement to downstream kinase cascades. Its classification as an adaptor reflects its role in assembling signaling complexes rather than enzymatic catalysis. In senescence, MyD88 transduces IL-1α signals that sustain the SASP. It is a foundational innate immune signaling scaffold.

nodes.label: IL-1R
nodes.description: IL-1R recruits MyD88 via TIR-TIR interactions, and MyD88 assembles the myddosome to propagate IL-1α/IL-1β signals in senescent cells and responding macrophages. This transduction is essential for the NF-κB activation that drives SASP and paracrine arrest. The relationship positions MyD88 as the immediate downstream effector of IL-1R. It is a canonical IL-1R signaling mechanism.

nodes.label: IRAK4
nodes.description: MyD88 recruits IRAK4 via death-domain interactions, the first step in myddosome assembly after receptor engagement. IRAK4 then phosphorylates IRAK1/IRAK2, propagating the signal. This recruitment is a conserved early event in TLR/IL-1R pathways. In senescence it initiates the cascade that licenses SASP transcription. The relationship is a well-established adaptor-kinase interaction.

nodes.label: IRAK1
nodes.description: Active IRAK4 phosphorylates IRAK1, which then recruits TRAF6 through its C-terminal TRAF6-binding motifs, extending the myddosome signaling complex. This step connects the receptor-proximal kinases to E3 ubiquitin ligase activity and TAK1 activation. In senescence, IRAK1 is required for full SASP establishment. The relationship is a standard component of IL-1R/TLR signal propagation.

nodes.label: Myddosome
nodes.description: MyD88 assembles into the helical oligomeric myddosome with IRAK4 and IRAK1/2, serving as the scaffolding platform that activates downstream kinases (e.g., TAK1) and transcription factors (NF-κB). This supramolecular complex is the mechanistic core of IL-1R/TLR signaling. In senescence, myddosome formation underlies IL-1α-driven SASP. The assembly is a defining structural feature of MyD88-dependent signaling.

nodes.label: Senescent Cells to Macrophages
nodes.description: Senescent-cell surface IL-1α engages IL-1R on macrophages, recruiting MyD88 to activate NF-κB and amplify SASP both in the sender (autocrine) and in recruited immune cells (paracrine). This bridges the senescent cell and the macrophage through IL-1R/MyD88 signaling, propagating inflammation. The relationship situates MyD88 at the interface of senescence and innate immunity. It explains how local senescence ignites broader inflammatory responses.

nodes.label: Myeloid-Derived Suppressor Cells
nodes.description: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are a heterogeneous population of immature myeloid cells with potent immunosuppressive activity, expanded under pathological stress including cancer and chronic inflammation. Their classification reflects an arrested differentiation state rather than a single lineage. In senescence contexts, MDSCs are recruited by SASP factors and blunt anti-tumor and anti-senescence immunity. They represent a key immunosuppressive cell type in aging and cancer.

nodes.label: Immature Myeloid Cell
nodes.description: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are a heterogeneous population of immature myeloid cells with potent immunosuppressive activity, expanded under pathological stress including cancer and chronic inflammation. Their classification reflects an arrested differentiation state rather than a single lineage. In senescence contexts, MDSCs are recruited by SASP factors and blunt anti-tumor and anti-senescence immunity. They represent a key immunosuppressive cell type in aging and cancer.

nodes.label: GM-CSF
nodes.description: The SASP factor GM-CSF stimulates myeloid expansion and biases differentiation toward immunosuppressive MDSCs, recruiting them into senescent and tumor tissues. GM-CSF thereby shapes the myeloid compartment to be tolerogenic and arrest-promoting. The relationship links a specific SASP cytokine to myeloid suppressor accumulation. It is a recognized driver of MDSC expansion in inflammation and cancer.

nodes.label: Caspase-5
nodes.description: Caspase-5 (human) is the inducible noncanonical effector caspase that cleaves IL-1α and gasdermin D to drive SASP and pyroptosis. Its activation is essential for the noncanonical inflammasome's role in senescence. The relationship positions caspase-5 as the enzymatic executor of the pathway in human cells. It is supported by cleavage-site and loss-of-function studies.

nodes.label: Caspase-11
nodes.description: Caspase-11 (mouse) is the noncanonical effector caspase that cleaves IL-1α and gasdermin D, paralleling human caspase-4/5. It is activated by cytosolic LPS and drives SASP establishment in murine senescence models. The relationship establishes the species-specific executor of the noncanonical pathway. It is a well-supported component of senescence inflammasome biology.

nodes.label: Gasdermin D
nodes.description: Active caspase-4/5/11 cleave gasdermin D between its N-terminal pore-forming domain and C-terminal inhibitory domain, releasing the N-terminal fragment to form plasma-membrane pores. This drives inflammatory cell death (pyroptosis) and IL-1α release in senescent and responding cells. The relationship is the canonical execution step of noncanonical inflammasome signaling. It links the pathway to both death and SASP amplification.

nodes.label: LPS
nodes.description: The hexa-acylated lipid A of LPS binds directly to the CARD domain of caspase-4/5/11, inducing their dimerization and activation -- the defining trigger of the noncanonical inflammasome. While classically microbial, this mechanism can be engaged in senescence-associated inflammatory contexts. The relationship is the canonical activation mode of the pathway. It links Gram-negative sensing to caspase-11/4/5 activation.

nodes.label: Paracrine Reprogramming
nodes.description: Paracrine reprogramming is the biological process by which SASP factors alter the differentiation status and fate of neighbouring cells, pushing them toward stemness, EMT, or altered lineage commitment. Distinct from paracrine senescence (which induces arrest), it remodels recipient identity. The process is mediated by cytokines such as IL-6, TGFβ, and VEGF family members. It expands the non-cell-autonomous influence of senescent cells beyond growth arrest.

nodes.label: Biological Process
nodes.description: Paracrine reprogramming is the biological process by which SASP factors alter the differentiation status and fate of neighbouring cells, pushing them toward stemness, EMT, or altered lineage commitment. Distinct from paracrine senescence (which induces arrest), it remodels recipient identity. The process is mediated by cytokines such as IL-6, TGFβ, and VEGF family members. It expands the non-cell-autonomous influence of senescent cells beyond growth arrest.

nodes.label: Stemness
nodes.description: IL-6 is a central driver of in vivo reprogramming toward pluripotency and stemness via JAK/STAT3 signaling, promoting a dedifferentiated, stem-like state in recipient cells. This underlies both wound-healing plasticity and, pathologically, cancer stemness. The relationship links a core SASP cytokine to cell-fate reprogramming. It is supported by reprogramming and cancer-stemness studies.

nodes.label: Chronic SASP
nodes.description: Chronic SASP (IL-6, IL-8 via JAK/STAT3) promotes cancer stem-cell traits and expands the CSC pool in neighbouring epithelial and tumour cells, enhancing tumour initiation and relapse potential. By driving stemness and survival, the persistent secretome fosters malignant progression. The relationship is a key mechanism by which senescence can become tumor-promoting. It is supported by cancer-stemness and senescence co-culture studies.

nodes.label: Myeloid Differentiation
nodes.description: GM-CSF and CCL2 skew myeloid differentiation toward immunosuppressive MDSCs and specific macrophage phenotypes, reshaping the myeloid compartment in senescence and cancer. This biases haematopoiesis away from inflammatory resolution toward tolerance and suppression. The relationship links SASP factors to myeloid lineage outcomes. It is supported by myeloid-differentiation and tumor-immunology studies.

nodes.label: VEGFc
nodes.description: VEGF-C is a member of the VEGF family of cysteine-knot growth factors, structurally related to VEGF-A but with distinct receptor usage and lymphatic specificity. Its classification situates it among the growth-factor arm of the SASP. In senescence, VEGF-C is an early-induced angiogenic/lymphangiogenic factor. The family membership underpins its receptor interactions.

nodes.label: VEGF Family
nodes.description: VEGF-C is a member of the VEGF family of cysteine-knot growth factors, structurally related to VEGF-A but with distinct receptor usage and lymphatic specificity. Its classification situates it among the growth-factor arm of the SASP. In senescence, VEGF-C is an early-induced angiogenic/lymphangiogenic factor. The family membership underpins its receptor interactions.

nodes.label: VEGFR3
nodes.description: VEGF-C signals primarily through VEGFR-3 on lymphatic endothelium, promoting lymphangiogenesis and lymphatic vessel sprouting. This receptor usage distinguishes VEGF-C from VEGF-A's preferential VEGFR2 engagement. In the SASP, VEGF-C-VEGFR3 signaling contributes to lymphatic remodeling around senescent tissue. The relationship is a canonical VEGF-C function.

nodes.label: VEGFR2
nodes.description: At higher concentrations or after proteolytic processing, VEGF-C also engages VEGFR2 on blood vascular endothelium, supporting angiogenesis in addition to its lymphatic actions. This dual receptor usage broadens its angiogenic potential within the SASP. The relationship explains how VEGF-C can drive both blood- and lymphatic-vessel formation. It is supported by receptor-binding and processing studies.

nodes.label: Lymphangiogenesis
nodes.description: Full-length VEGF-C preferentially activates VEGFR-3 and promotes lymphatic vessel sprouting, driving lymphangiogenesis. In senescence, this contributes to lymphatic remodeling and potentially to immune cell trafficking routes. The relationship is the canonical lymphangiogenic function of VEGF-C. It expands the vascular consequences of the SASP beyond blood vessels.

nodes.label: DNA Replication Stress
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: Constitutive oncogenic RAS signaling pushes cells into hyper-replication, where DNA replication forks are initiated at excessive frequency and become stalled or collapsed. This generates single-stranded DNA gaps and replication stress that activate checkpoint kinases. The relationship is a central mechanism linking oncogene activation to senescence-inducing damage. It is well established in OIS biology.

nodes.label: ATR
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: Stalled or collapsed replication forks generate single-stranded DNA gaps that engage the ATR-CHK1 cascade, activating a checkpoint that senses replication stress. In OIS, ATR signaling contributes to arrest and senescence establishment. The relationship is a canonical DNA-damage-checkpoint response. It links oncogene-driven hyper-replication to cell-cycle enforcement.

nodes.label: CDKN2A
nodes.description: The CDKN2A locus encoding p16INK4a is derepressed in OIS via loss of PRC1/2-mediated H3K27me3 repression, allowing p16 accumulation that enforces durable arrest. This epigenetic switch is a hallmark of the p53-independent senescence phase. The relationship couples oncogene signaling to stable CDK-inhibitor expression. It is a well-characterized epigenetic event in OIS.

nodes.label: Sir2 (yeast)
nodes.description: Sir2 (silent information regulator 2) is the founding member of the sirtuin family, first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a regulator of mating-type locus silencing and replicative lifespan. The seven mammalian paralogues SIRT1–SIRT7 evolved from this ancestral NAD+-dependent deacetylase, retaining the conserved catalytic core while diversifying in subcellular localization and substrate repertoire. This phylogenetic continuity means insights from yeast Sir2 historically informed mammalian sirtuin biology, although the mammalian enzymes acquired lineage-specific regulatory domains. The relationship is directional: yeast Sir2 is the evolutionary precursor, not a downstream effector, of the SIRT1–7 family.

nodes.label: Sirtuins (SIRT1–7)
nodes.description: Sir2 (silent information regulator 2) is the founding member of the sirtuin family, first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a regulator of mating-type locus silencing and replicative lifespan. The seven mammalian paralogues SIRT1–SIRT7 evolved from this ancestral NAD+-dependent deacetylase, retaining the conserved catalytic core while diversifying in subcellular localization and substrate repertoire. This phylogenetic continuity means insights from yeast Sir2 historically informed mammalian sirtuin biology, although the mammalian enzymes acquired lineage-specific regulatory domains. The relationship is directional: yeast Sir2 is the evolutionary precursor, not a downstream effector, of the SIRT1–7 family.

nodes.label: Mono-ADP-ribosyl transferases
nodes.description: Beyond deacetylation, several sirtuins catalyze mono-ADP-ribosylation, transferring the ADP-ribose moiety of NAD+ onto target proteins without removing an acetyl group. SIRT4 and SIRT6 prominently display this mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase activity, with SIRT6 using it to recruit heterochromatin proteins such as KAP1/HP1α. The directionality is that NAD+ is the donor and the target lysine (or other residue) is the acceptor, producing a mono-ADP-ribosylated product rather than free OAADPr. Biologically, ADP-ribosylation allows sirtuins to regulate processes—such as DNA repair and LINE-1 repression—distinct from their deacetylase functions.

nodes.label: Sirtuin deacetylation reaction
nodes.description: During the sirtuin-catalyzed deacetylation of a lysine, NAD+ is cleaved between its nicotinamide and ADP-ribose moieties, and the acetyl group is transferred to the ADP-ribose to generate 2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose (OAADPr) plus free nicotinamide. OAADPr is a stoichiometric by-product, released in equimolar amounts with the deacetylated substrate on every catalytic cycle. This molecule is not merely waste: it binds and activates the TRPM2 cation channel, linking sirtuin activity to calcium signaling and cellular stress responses. A caveat is that OAADPr accumulation can itself feed back on cellular metabolism, and its levels reflect the integrated deacetylase flux of the cell.

nodes.label: OAADPr (2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose)
nodes.description: During the sirtuin-catalyzed deacetylation of a lysine, NAD+ is cleaved between its nicotinamide and ADP-ribose moieties, and the acetyl group is transferred to the ADP-ribose to generate 2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose (OAADPr) plus free nicotinamide. OAADPr is a stoichiometric by-product, released in equimolar amounts with the deacetylated substrate on every catalytic cycle. This molecule is not merely waste: it binds and activates the TRPM2 cation channel, linking sirtuin activity to calcium signaling and cellular stress responses. A caveat is that OAADPr accumulation can itself feed back on cellular metabolism, and its levels reflect the integrated deacetylase flux of the cell.

nodes.label: OAADPr
nodes.description: OAADPr (2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose) binds to the cytoplasmic N-terminal domain of the TRPM2 non-selective cation channel, promoting its opening and calcium influx into the cytosol. Because OAADPr is generated directly by sirtuin deacetylase activity, TRPM2 activation acts as a sensor of cellular sirtuin flux and NAD+ utilization. The directionality is unidirectional under basal conditions: sirtuin activity produces OAADPr, which then gates TRPM2, rather than TRPM2 regulating sirtuins. This coupling provides a mechanistic link between metabolic state, redox stress, and calcium-dependent processes such as insulin secretion and apoptotic signaling.

nodes.label: TRPM2
nodes.description: OAADPr (2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose) binds to the cytoplasmic N-terminal domain of the TRPM2 non-selective cation channel, promoting its opening and calcium influx into the cytosol. Because OAADPr is generated directly by sirtuin deacetylase activity, TRPM2 activation acts as a sensor of cellular sirtuin flux and NAD+ utilization. The directionality is unidirectional under basal conditions: sirtuin activity produces OAADPr, which then gates TRPM2, rather than TRPM2 regulating sirtuins. This coupling provides a mechanistic link between metabolic state, redox stress, and calcium-dependent processes such as insulin secretion and apoptotic signaling.

nodes.label: Nucleus (euchromatin)
nodes.description: SIRT1 is the predominant nuclear sirtuin and is enriched at euchromatic regions, where it deacetylates both histones and many transcriptional regulators to shape gene expression. Its nuclear residence allows it to directly access chromatin and nuclear factors such as p53, FOXO, NF-κB, and PGC-1α. Subcellular localization is dynamic and can shift toward DNA double-strand break foci during genotoxic stress, reflecting its role in DNA repair. A caveat is that a fraction of SIRT1 is also cytosolic, so 'nuclear' describes its dominant but not exclusive compartment.

nodes.label: Cytoplasm
nodes.description: SIRT2 is the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin and is most abundant in the cytosol, where it deacetylates α-tubulin and a range of metabolic and regulatory proteins. Its localization is cell-cycle regulated, with SIRT2 accumulating and being hyperphosphorylated as cells transit the G2/M boundary. The cytoplasmic residence underpins its roles in microtubule dynamics, mitosis, and cytoplasmic autophagy regulation rather than direct chromatin modification. Note that SIRT2 can also shuttle to the nucleus under certain stress conditions, so localization is not absolute.

nodes.label: SIRT4
nodes.description: SIRT4 resides in the mitochondrial matrix and acts mainly as a mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase on metabolic enzymes such as GDH and MTPα. Its mitochondrial localization enables direct control of amino-acid and fatty-acid fueling of the TCA cycle. The directionality is SIRT4 positioned to brake mitochondrial anabolism. Its activity often opposes the protective actions of SIRT3.

nodes.label: SIRT5
nodes.description: SIRT5 localizes to the mitochondrial matrix and is specialized for removing lysine succinyl, malonyl, and glutaryl groups from metabolic enzymes including CPS1, HMGCS2, and β-oxidation/TCA enzymes. Its mitochondrial residence makes it a key regulator of catabolic flux during fasting. The directionality is SIRT5 sensing mitochondrial acylation state to optimize energy production. It is the sole mammalian member of an ancient prokaryotic sirtuin class.

nodes.label: Nucleus (heterochromatin)
nodes.description: SIRT6 is a nuclear sirtuin enriched at heterochromatic and telomeric regions, where it deacetylates H3K9 and H3K56 and performs mono-ADP-ribosylation of KAP1. Its heterochromatin association is critical for genome stability, telomere maintenance, and suppression of repetitive elements such as LINE-1. SIRT6 thus integrates chromatin regulation with metabolic control of glycolysis, DNA repair, and inflammation. Loss of SIRT6 produces a pronounced premature-aging phenotype, highlighting its non-redundant role in the nucleus.

nodes.label: SIRT7
nodes.description: SIRT7 is concentrated in the nucleolus, the site of ribosomal DNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis, where it deacetylates histone H3K18 and regulates RNA polymerase I. Its nucleolar residence positions it to control rRNA synthesis and, consequently, protein synthetic capacity and growth. SIRT7 also deacetylates extra-nucleolar targets such as GATA4 and SMAD3, linking it to cardiac and fibrotic pathways. Deficiency of SIRT7 yields extensive myocardial fibrosis and cardiomyopathy, revealing its importance in stress responses of the heart.

nodes.label: Nucleolus
nodes.description: SIRT7 is concentrated in the nucleolus, the site of ribosomal DNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis, where it deacetylates histone H3K18 and regulates RNA polymerase I. Its nucleolar residence positions it to control rRNA synthesis and, consequently, protein synthetic capacity and growth. SIRT7 also deacetylates extra-nucleolar targets such as GATA4 and SMAD3, linking it to cardiac and fibrotic pathways. Deficiency of SIRT7 yields extensive myocardial fibrosis and cardiomyopathy, revealing its importance in stress responses of the heart.

nodes.label: ADP-ribosylation
nodes.description: SIRT4 functions principally as a mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase, using NAD+ to attach a single ADP-ribose group to target lysines rather than removing acetyl marks. Its best-characterized ADP-ribosylation target is glutamate dehydrogenase, whose activity it inhibits to dampen amino-acid-stimulated insulin secretion. This enzymatic orientation means SIRT4 generally acts as a metabolic suppressor within mitochondria, opposing anabolic and growth signals. A caveat is that SIRT4's deacetylase activity is weak in vitro, so ADP-ribosylation is its physiologically dominant modality.

nodes.label: Drosophila melanogaster
nodes.description: Dietary restriction in Drosophila extends lifespan and, as in yeast, this benefit requires the dSir2 (Sir2) gene, indicating evolutionary conservation of the sirtuin-mediated CR pathway. The effect is thought to operate through improved protein homeostasis, stress resistance, and metabolic efficiency rather than simple calorie shortage. Directionally, reduced nutrient signaling upstream engages dSir2 to produce the longevity phenotype. Caveats include that the magnitude and requirement vary with sex, genetic background, and the precise restriction paradigm used.

nodes.label: SIRT1 expression
nodes.description: In rodents, caloric restriction raises SIRT1 levels in multiple tissues, and this elevation is linked to reduced inflammatory and oxidative responses. Higher SIRT1 expression translates into enhanced deacetylation of targets such as NF-κB, FOXO, and PGC-1α, promoting stress resistance and metabolic health. The directionality is that CR is the upstream stimulus and increased SIRT1 abundance/activity the downstream mediator. This adaptation is considered a key explanation for the anti-aging and disease-protective effects of CR in mammals.

nodes.label: NAD+/nicotinamide ratio (brain)
nodes.description: Caloric restriction elevates the brain NAD+/nicotinamide ratio, which both supplies more co-substrate for sirtuins and relieves nicotinamide-mediated feedback inhibition of SIRT1. The resulting gain in sirtuin activity supports neuronal stress resistance, mitochondrial function, and suppression of neuroinflammatory signaling. The relationship is directional: CR shifts the ratio upward, which then potentiates sirtuin-dependent protective programs. This mechanism is frequently invoked to explain CR's protective effects against age-related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative pathology.

nodes.label: SIR2 overexpression (yeast)
nodes.description: Integration of an extra SIR2 copy in yeast increases replicative lifespan by up to about 30%, implicating Sir2 dosage directly in longevity. The mechanism involves reinforced silencing at rDNA repeats, which reduces spurious recombination and the accumulation of extrachromosomal rDNA circles that drive aging. This is a gain-of-function, directional relationship: more Sir2 yields longer lifespan, though the effect saturates and very high doses can be detrimental. The finding established the foundational idea that boosting sirtuin activity can extend lifespan in a simple eukaryote.

nodes.label: sir-2.1 overexpression (C. elegans)
nodes.description: A chromosomal duplication that increases sir-2.1 dosage in C. elegans extends lifespan by up to approximately 50%, paralleling the yeast finding in a multicellular organism. The longevity effect depends on intact insulin/IGF-1-like signaling, because sir-2.1 acts downstream of the DAF-2 pathway to promote stress resistance. The relationship is directional: elevated sir-2.1 produces the lifespan gain. A key caveat is that the requirement for DAF-16 (FOXO) ties sirtuin longevity to the conserved FOXO transcription-factor network.

nodes.label: sir-2.1 lifespan extension
nodes.description: The lifespan extension produced by sir-2.1 overexpression in C. elegans is strictly dependent on the forkhead transcription factor DAF-16, the worm FOXO ortholog. DAF-16 is the downstream effector that induces stress-resistance and xenobiotic-detoxification genes once sir-2.1 releases it from repression. Mechanistically, sir-2.1 deacetylates and cooperates with DAF-16 to drive the longevity transcriptional program. Thus the directionality is sir-2.1 → DAF-16 → lifespan, and removing DAF-16 abolishes the benefit.

nodes.label: DAF-16 (FOXO)
nodes.description: The lifespan extension produced by sir-2.1 overexpression in C. elegans is strictly dependent on the forkhead transcription factor DAF-16, the worm FOXO ortholog. DAF-16 is the downstream effector that induces stress-resistance and xenobiotic-detoxification genes once sir-2.1 releases it from repression. Mechanistically, sir-2.1 deacetylates and cooperates with DAF-16 to drive the longevity transcriptional program. Thus the directionality is sir-2.1 → DAF-16 → lifespan, and removing DAF-16 abolishes the benefit.

nodes.label: dSir2 overexpression (Drosophila)
nodes.description: Ubiquitous overexpression of the Drosophila Sir2 ortholog extends female lifespan by about 29%, with a more modest or absent effect in males. The sexually dimorphic response reflects differences in nutrient sensing and reproductive physiology between the sexes. Directionally, increased dSir2 acts upstream to produce the longevity phenotype, consistent with the conserved sirtuin-CR axis. As in worms, the effect is intertwined with insulin/FOXO signaling and dietary restriction pathways.

nodes.label: Histone H1 (Lys9, Lys26)
nodes.description: SIRT1 removes acetyl groups from Lys9 and Lys26 of linker histone H1, a modification that influences higher-order chromatin compaction and gene accessibility. Deacetylated H1 is generally associated with a more condensed, transcriptionally repressed chromatin state at SIRT1-target loci. The relationship is directional: SIRT1 acts enzymatically on H1 to remodel chromatin and silence specific programs. Because H1 links nucleosomes, this action helps SIRT1 enforce long-range repression independently of core histone modifications.

nodes.label: Histone H3 (Lys14)
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates Lys14 of histone H3, a mark associated with active transcription, thereby contributing to gene silencing at targeted promoters. Loss of H3K14ac reduces promoter accessibility and cooperates with other repressive modifications to restrain transcription. The directionality is strictly enzymatic: SIRT1 removes the acetyl mark, shifting chromatin toward repression. This activity underlies many of SIRT1's roles in repressing inflammatory and metabolic gene programs.

nodes.label: Histone H4
nodes.description: SIRT1 removes the acetyl group from Lys16 of histone H4, a site whose acetylation is linked to telomeric and rDNA silencing and genome stability. Deacetylation at H4K16 promotes a more compact chromatin fiber and is shared with SIRT2 at this residue in certain contexts. The relationship is directional and repressive: SIRT1-mediated deacetylation consolidates heterochromatin-like states. Defective H4K16 deacetylation is associated with the genomic instability seen when SIRT1 function is compromised.

nodes.label: SIRT1 deacetylation of p53
nodes.description: By deacetylating p53, SIRT1 lowers p53's transcriptional activation of BH3-only proteins and other apoptotic effectors, suppressing programmed cell death after oxidative or genotoxic stress. This creates a survival bias that helps cells tolerate damage but can also protect incipient cancer cells from elimination. The directionality is that SIRT1 activity on p53 is upstream of reduced apoptosis. A caveat is that chronic suppression of p53-dependent apoptosis is a double-edged sword: protective in normal tissue but potentially tumor-promoting.

nodes.label: HIC1
nodes.description: HIC1 (hypermethylated in cancer 1) is a tumor suppressor that binds the SIRT1 promoter via its POZ domain and directly represses SIRT1 transcription. Because p53 transactivates HIC1, a negative feedback loop exists: p53 induces HIC1, which then restrains SIRT1, preventing excessive p53 deacetylation and preserving p53 tumor-suppressive capacity. The directionality is HIC1 → SIRT1 repression, upstream of SIRT1's inhibition of p53. Disruption of this loop in cancer can unleash SIRT1 to silence p53.

nodes.label: SIRT1 promoter
nodes.description: HIC1 (hypermethylated in cancer 1) is a tumor suppressor that binds the SIRT1 promoter via its POZ domain and directly represses SIRT1 transcription. Because p53 transactivates HIC1, a negative feedback loop exists: p53 induces HIC1, which then restrains SIRT1, preventing excessive p53 deacetylation and preserving p53 tumor-suppressive capacity. The directionality is HIC1 → SIRT1 repression, upstream of SIRT1's inhibition of p53. Disruption of this loop in cancer can unleash SIRT1 to silence p53.

nodes.label: HIC1 transcription
nodes.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
nodes.description: p53 directly activates transcription of HIC1, a tumor suppressor that in turn represses the SIRT1 promoter, forming a negative feedback loop on SIRT1. This loop ensures that p53 activity is not indefinitely suppressed by SIRT1-mediated deacetylation. Directionally, p53 is the transcription factor and HIC1 the induced target gene. The biological significance is genome protection: by inducing HIC1, p53 prevents SIRT1 from over-deacetylating and silencing p53 itself.

nodes.label: Ku70
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates Ku70, the DNA-repair factor and regulatory subunit of the Ku complex that also binds and inhibits the pro-apoptotic protein Bax. Deacetylation of Ku70 increases its affinity for Bax, sequestering Bax away from mitochondria. The directionality is enzymatic: SIRT1 removes acetyl marks from Ku70 to modulate its protein-interaction state. This mechanism couples SIRT1's DNA-repair functions to a direct anti-apoptotic, cell-survival program.

nodes.label: Deacetylated Ku70
nodes.description: Once deacetylated by SIRT1, Ku70 binds the BH3 domain of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax and retains it in the cytosol, preventing Bax translocation to and permeabilization of mitochondria. This sequestration blocks the intrinsic apoptosis cascade downstream of many stress signals. The relationship is directional: deacetylated Ku70 is the binding partner that neutralizes Bax. The net effect is cytoprotection, though as with p53 suppression this can also shield damaged cells in oncogenic contexts.

nodes.label: Bax (pro-apoptotic)
nodes.description: Once deacetylated by SIRT1, Ku70 binds the BH3 domain of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax and retains it in the cytosol, preventing Bax translocation to and permeabilization of mitochondria. This sequestration blocks the intrinsic apoptosis cascade downstream of many stress signals. The relationship is directional: deacetylated Ku70 is the binding partner that neutralizes Bax. The net effect is cytoprotection, though as with p53 suppression this can also shield damaged cells in oncogenic contexts.

nodes.label: E2F1
nodes.description: The E2F1 transcription factor binds directly to the SIRT1 promoter and activates its transcription, particularly under proliferative or DNA-damage signals. This positions SIRT1 as a downstream effector of E2F1-driven programs that balance cell-cycle progression with survival. The directionality is E2F1 → SIRT1 gene activation. Notably, the relationship is reciprocal, because SIRT1 then feeds back to inhibit E2F1's apoptotic function.

nodes.label: FOXO3a
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO3a in multiple cell types, including neurons and fibroblasts, shifting its target-gene program toward stress resistance and away from apoptosis. Deacetylated FOXO3a induces antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and catalase and promotes autophagy while reducing death-gene expression. The directionality is SIRT1 → FOXO3a modification → altered transcription. This axis is a major mechanism by which SIRT1 confers longevity- and stress-resistance phenotypes.

nodes.label: FOXO4
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO4, which reverts FOXO4-mediated suppression and enhances cellular defenses against oxidative stress. Deacetylation of FOXO4 boosts expression of DNA-repair and antioxidant genes such as GADD45 while suppressing caspase activation. The relationship is directional: SIRT1 enzymatically licenses FOXO4 to drive protective transcription. This contributes to SIRT1's broad role in genomic maintenance and resilience to damage.

nodes.label: RelA/p65 (NF-κB subunit)
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates the RelA/p65 subunit of NF-κB, particularly at Lys310, reducing its ability to recruit the transcriptional machinery and activate pro-inflammatory genes. This post-translational modification dampens NF-κB target genes such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. The directionality is SIRT1 acting enzymatically on RelA to inhibit inflammatory transcription. Because NF-κB drives chronic inflammation implicated in aging and disease, SIRT1's action is a key anti-inflammatory node.

nodes.label: SIRT1 deacetylation of RelA/p65
nodes.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
nodes.description: Deacetylation of RelA/p65 by SIRT1 lowers NF-κB transactivation, thereby reducing expression of cytokines, chemokines, and adhesion molecules that propagate inflammation. This directly opposes the pro-inflammatory program and underlies many of SIRT1's protective effects in metabolic, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative contexts. The directionality is SIRT1 deacetylation → suppressed NF-κB signaling. A caveat is that excessive NF-κB suppression could impair host defense, so the effect is beneficial within physiological ranges.

nodes.label: NF-κB pro-inflammatory signalling
nodes.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
nodes.description: Deacetylation of RelA/p65 by SIRT1 lowers NF-κB transactivation, thereby reducing expression of cytokines, chemokines, and adhesion molecules that propagate inflammation. This directly opposes the pro-inflammatory program and underlies many of SIRT1's protective effects in metabolic, cardiovascular, and neurodegenerative contexts. The directionality is SIRT1 deacetylation → suppressed NF-κB signaling. A caveat is that excessive NF-κB suppression could impair host defense, so the effect is beneficial within physiological ranges.

nodes.label: SIRT1 and RelA/p65
nodes.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
nodes.description: Exposure to cigarette-smoke extract disrupts the SIRT1–RelA/p65 complex, diminishing deacetylation of RelA and leaving NF-κB in a more active, pro-inflammatory state. The consequence is heightened expression of inflammatory mediators in airway and other cells exposed to smoke. The directionality is that the environmental insult (smoke) reduces a protective protein–protein interaction, increasing inflammation. This provides a mechanistic link between smoking, impaired sirtuin function, and chronic inflammatory lung disease.

nodes.label: RNA Polymerase I transcription
nodes.description: SIRT7 activates RNA polymerase I-mediated transcription of ribosomal DNA, driving ribosome biogenesis and protein synthetic capacity in proliferating cells. It does so in part through deacetylation of histone H3K18 at rDNA and by stabilizing the Pol I transcriptional apparatus. The directionality is SIRT7 → enhanced rRNA production → increased ribosome output. Because uncontrolled ribosome biogenesis fuels tumor growth, this activity aligns with SIRT7's oncogenic associations.

nodes.label: RNA Polymerase I transcription (via TAFI68 deacetylation)
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates TAFI68, a subunit of the RNA polymerase I transcription factor complex, decreasing its DNA-binding activity and thereby repressing rRNA transcription. This contrasts with SIRT7, which activates Pol I, illustrating divergent sirtuin control of ribosome biogenesis. The directionality is SIRT1 → TAFI68 deacetylation → Pol I repression. By limiting ribosome production, SIRT1 can restrain growth and oppose the biosynthetic programs favored in cancer and hypertrophy.
nodes.norm_label: rna polymerase i transcription (via tafi68 deacetylation)

nodes.label: Glioma tumour formation
nodes.description: SIRT2 resides in a genomic region frequently deleted in human gliomas, and re-expression of SIRT2 markedly reduces colony formation by glioma cells, indicating tumor-suppressor function. Its activity deacetylates substrates such as α-tubulin and HNF4α that govern mitotic fidelity and metabolism. The directionality is that SIRT2 loss permits, and SIRT2 restoration suppresses, gliomagenesis. A caveat is that SIRT2 can act as either tumor suppressor or promoter depending on tissue and context.

nodes.label: SIRT2 expression
nodes.description: SIRT2 protein levels rise dramatically as cells enter mitosis and the enzyme is hyperphosphorylated at the G2/M boundary, timing its activity to chromosome condensation and division. This cell-cycle coupling links SIRT2 to proper mitotic progression and genomic stability. The directionality is that the G2/M transition drives SIRT2 upregulation and activation. Loss or dysregulation of this peak is associated with mitotic defects and, in some cancers, genomic instability.

nodes.label: Mitosis (G2/M phase)
nodes.description: SIRT2 protein levels rise dramatically as cells enter mitosis and the enzyme is hyperphosphorylated at the G2/M boundary, timing its activity to chromosome condensation and division. This cell-cycle coupling links SIRT2 to proper mitotic progression and genomic stability. The directionality is that the G2/M transition drives SIRT2 upregulation and activation. Loss or dysregulation of this peak is associated with mitotic defects and, in some cancers, genomic instability.

nodes.label: SIRT6 knockout mice
nodes.description: Mice lacking SIRT6 develop a striking premature-aging syndrome with reduced size, loss of subcutaneous fat, lymphopenia, colitis, and spinal curvature, dying early. The phenotype reflects defective base-excision repair, genomic instability, and metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation. The directionality is SIRT6 deficiency → multisystem premature aging. This makes SIRT6 one of the clearest single-gene links between sirtuins and mammalian longevity.

nodes.label: Premature aging phenotype
nodes.description: Mice lacking SIRT6 develop a striking premature-aging syndrome with reduced size, loss of subcutaneous fat, lymphopenia, colitis, and spinal curvature, dying early. The phenotype reflects defective base-excision repair, genomic instability, and metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation. The directionality is SIRT6 deficiency → multisystem premature aging. This makes SIRT6 one of the clearest single-gene links between sirtuins and mammalian longevity.

nodes.label: Tat (HIV-1 protein)
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates Lys50 of the HIV-1 transactivator Tat, a modification that increases Tat's affinity for the viral LTR and its ability to recruit the transcription machinery. This enzymatic action therefore activates, rather than suppresses, the viral protein. The directionality is SIRT1 → Tat activation → enhanced viral transcription. This reveals an unexpected pro-viral role for the otherwise cytoprotective SIRT1.

nodes.label: SIRT1 deacetylation of Tat
nodes.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
nodes.description: Because deacetylated Tat is a more potent transactivator, SIRT1-mediated deacetylation at Lys50 boosts HIV-1 transcription from the proviral LTR. The relationship is directional: SIRT1 acts on Tat to amplify viral gene expression. This positions host SIRT1 as a cofactor that HIV exploits, a caveat to the generally beneficial reputation of SIRT1 activation. Targeting this interaction is of interest for antiviral strategies.

nodes.label: HIV-1 viral transcription
nodes.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
nodes.description: Because deacetylated Tat is a more potent transactivator, SIRT1-mediated deacetylation at Lys50 boosts HIV-1 transcription from the proviral LTR. The relationship is directional: SIRT1 acts on Tat to amplify viral gene expression. This positions host SIRT1 as a cofactor that HIV exploits, a caveat to the generally beneficial reputation of SIRT1 activation. Targeting this interaction is of interest for antiviral strategies.

nodes.label: White adipose tissue
nodes.description: In white adipose tissue, SIRT1 promotes lipolysis and fat mobilization by repressing adipogenic transcription factors such as PPAR-γ and aP2 and by co-ordinating catabolic gene programs. This shifts storage tissue from lipid accumulation toward fatty-acid release for oxidation. The directionality is SIRT1 → repression of adipogenesis → enhanced fat mobilization. These actions contribute to the lean phenotype and metabolic health seen under caloric restriction.

nodes.label: PPAR-γ (adipogenesis)
nodes.description: SIRT1 represses PPAR-γ, the master regulator of adipogenesis, by deacetylating and interfering with its co-activator interactions, thereby inhibiting differentiation of preadipocytes into fat cells. Pharmacological SIRT1 activation or overexpression recapitulates this repression and blocks adipogenesis. The directionality is SIRT1 upstream of PPAR-γ suppression. This mechanism underlies SIRT1's anti-obesity and insulin-sensitizing effects.

nodes.label: UCP2 (Uncoupling Protein 2)
nodes.description: SIRT1 transcriptionally represses UCP2, a mitochondrial inner-membrane uncoupler that dissipates the proton gradient and reduces ATP yield. In SIRT1 knockout mice, UCP2 is upregulated, lowering ATP production in pancreatic β-cells. The directionality is SIRT1 → suppression of UCP2 expression. By keeping UCP2 low, SIRT1 preserves the mitochondrial membrane potential needed for efficient ATP generation and insulin secretion.

nodes.label: SIRT1 repression of UCP2
nodes.description: Repression of UCP2 by SIRT1 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP synthesis in pancreatic β-cells, which raises the ATP/ADP ratio and closes KATP channels to trigger insulin release. Mice overexpressing SIRT1 in β-cells show enhanced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. The directionality is SIRT1 → UCP2 downregulation → stronger insulin secretion. This links SIRT1 to improved glucose homeostasis and protection against diabetes.

nodes.label: Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion
nodes.description: Repression of UCP2 by SIRT1 preserves mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP synthesis in pancreatic β-cells, which raises the ATP/ADP ratio and closes KATP channels to trigger insulin release. Mice overexpressing SIRT1 in β-cells show enhanced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. The directionality is SIRT1 → UCP2 downregulation → stronger insulin secretion. This links SIRT1 to improved glucose homeostasis and protection against diabetes.

nodes.label: AceCS2 (mitochondrial acetyl-CoA synthetase)
nodes.description: SIRT3 deacetylates and activates acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 (AceCS2) in the mitochondrial matrix, enabling it to convert acetate into acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle and lipogenesis. Deacetylation relieves autoinhibition, increasing AceCS2 catalytic efficiency. The directionality is SIRT3 → AceCS2 activation → acetyl-CoA production. This allows mitochondria to use acetate as an alternative carbon source, contributing to metabolic flexibility during fasting.

nodes.label: AceCS1 (cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA synthetase)
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates and activates acetyl-CoA synthetase 1 (AceCS1) in the cytoplasm, analogous to SIRT3's activation of the mitochondrial AceCS2, permitting acetate utilization outside the mitochondrion. Activated AceCS1 supplies cytosolic acetyl-CoA for chromatin and lipid metabolism. The directionality is SIRT1 → AceCS1 activation. Together with SIRT3, this shows sirtuins broadly license acetate salvage across compartments.

nodes.label: Reactive oxygen species production
nodes.description: SIRT3 lowers mitochondrial ROS by deacetylating and activating antioxidant enzymes such as MnSOD and components of the electron-transport chain, while also reducing mitochondrial membrane potential in a manner that limits superoxide leak. Higher SIRT3 activity therefore shifts the mitochondrial redox balance toward less oxidative damage. The directionality is SIRT3 activity upstream of reduced ROS. This antioxidant function is a major basis for SIRT3's protective roles in heart, liver, and aging.

nodes.label: Cold exposure (brown adipose tissue)
nodes.description: Cold exposure induces SIRT3 in brown adipose tissue, where it promotes expression of mitochondrial genes and supports thermogenic programs. The induction enhances oxidative metabolism and uncoupled respiration needed for heat production. The directionality is cold stimulus → SIRT3 upregulation → thermogenic mitochondrial biogenesis. This ties SIRT3 to adaptive thermogenesis and the metabolic benefits of cold exposure.

nodes.label: GDH (Glutamate Dehydrogenase)
nodes.description: SIRT4 mono-ADP-ribosylates glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH), inhibiting its oxidative deamination of glutamate to α-ketoglutarate and thereby slowing anaplerotic carbon entry into the TCA cycle. This restrains amino-acid-derived ATP production and insulin secretion in β-cells. The directionality is SIRT4 enzymatic inhibition of GDH. SIRT4 thus acts as a mitochondrial brake on amino-acid catabolism, opposing anabolic fueling of secretion.

nodes.label: SIRT4 inhibition of GDH
nodes.description: By inhibiting GDH, SIRT4 blunts the ability of amino acids such as leucine to stimulate insulin release from pancreatic β-cells, because less α-ketoglutarate is generated to elevate ATP and trigger secretion. The relationship is directional: SIRT4-mediated GDH inhibition → reduced amino-acid-stimulated insulin secretion. This positions SIRT4 as a physiological negative regulator of nutrient-particular insulin release.

nodes.label: Amino-acid-stimulated insulin secretion
nodes.description: By inhibiting GDH, SIRT4 blunts the ability of amino acids such as leucine to stimulate insulin release from pancreatic β-cells, because less α-ketoglutarate is generated to elevate ATP and trigger secretion. The relationship is directional: SIRT4-mediated GDH inhibition → reduced amino-acid-stimulated insulin secretion. This positions SIRT4 as a physiological negative regulator of nutrient-particular insulin release.

nodes.label: β-amyloid toxicity
nodes.description: SIRT1 protects neurons from β-amyloid-induced toxicity, in part by inhibiting NF-κB signaling in microglia and reducing neuroinflammation, and by supporting neuronal stress-resistance pathways. This limits the inflammatory and oxidative damage that accompany amyloid pathology. The directionality is SIRT1 activity upstream of reduced neuronal injury. The effect dovetails with observations that caloric restriction, which raises SIRT1, protects against Alzheimer's-like neuropathology.

nodes.label: PGC-1α regulation
nodes.description: SIRT1 confers neuroprotection partly through deacetylation and activation of PGC-1α, which drives mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in neurons.
