links.context: Autophagy regulates Proteostasis by controlling the flux, activity, or abundance of the regulated process. Mechanistically, Autophagy acts as an upstream controller (enzymatic, transcriptional, or physical) that enforces balance in the target system. This is significant because proper regulation maintains homeostasis, and its failure contributes to neurodegeneration. A caveat is that regulation is context-dependent and often buffered by parallel systems, so disruption of one controller may be partially compensated.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuromelanin, aging, and neuronal vulnerability in Parkinson's disease.md
links.context: Autophagy and TFEB are reciprocally linked entities in the neuromelanin knowledge graph, reflecting their frequent co-occurrence and shared relevance to catecholamine biology or Parkinson's disease. Directionally, the graph relation is symmetric, although biologically Autophagy and TFEB may occupy distinct mechanistic roles. Their association is significant because both contribute to the chemical and pathological network that defines vulnerability of pigmented neurons. A caveat is that a bidirectional link denotes an association rather than a proven direct causal mechanism between the two entities.

Autophagy protects against Alpha-Synuclein Aggregation by neutralizing, scavenging, or removing the threatening species or condition. Mechanistically, Autophagy acts as a sink or reductant that limits oxidative, toxic, or aggregate burden within catecholaminergic neurons. This protective role is significant because it may explain why pigmented neurons survive despite high metabolic stress, at least below a pathogenic threshold. A caveat is that the protection is conditional; under overload, redox perturbation, or iron release the same entity can contribute to damage rather than prevention.

Autophagy suppresses the SASP by clearing damaged mitochondria and inflammasome components, restraining the innate immune activators that drive the secretome. Defective autophagy therefore permits accumulation of mitochondrial DAMPs and sustained inflammation. This positions autophagy as a brake on senescence-associated inflammation. Enhancing autophagy (e.g., with rapamycin) is a recognized senomorphic strategy.

Autophagy, particularly mitophagy, is impaired in senescent cells, permitting accumulation of ROS-emitting, damaged organelles that feed the SASP and mitochondrial dysfunction. This impairment is both a consequence and a driver of the senescent state, creating a feed-forward loop of damage and inflammation. Restoring autophagic flux can dampen the secretome. The relationship is well supported though not absolute across all senescence models.

Autophagy suppresses the inflammasome by clearing damaged mitochondria and inflammasome components (e.g., NLRP3), restraining activation and subsequent IL-1β release. In senescence, impaired autophagy permits inflammasome hyperactivation and sustained inflammation. This makes autophagy a negative regulator of the senescence-inflammatory circuit. Enhancing autophagic flux (e.g., with rapamycin) therefore dampens inflammasome-driven SASP.

NF-κB is the master transcription factor regulating SASP gene expression, controlling the bulk of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors in senescent cells. It is activated by p38 MAPK, GATA4, cGAS-STING, and IL-1R/MyD88 signaling and cooperates with C/EBPbeta at SASP enhancers. Inhibition of NF-κB robustly suppresses the SASP across models. Its regulatory role is central, though it operates with other axes (mTOR, AP-1) for full secretome output.

links.source_file: _document_ - Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Aging.md
links.context: NF-kB activation downstream of AGE-RAGE signaling drives transcription of a panel of pro-inflammatory genes, including the cytokine interleukin 6 (IL-6). IL-6 is a well-known inflammation promoter whose expression is increased in response to AGE accumulation in cells and tissues. Together with tumor necrosis factor alpha and adhesion molecules such as VCAM1, IL-6 production links persistent glycation stress to systemic inflammation. The NF-kB-driven induction of IL-6 illustrates how advanced glycation end products convert extracellular crosslinking chemistry into inflammatory signaling that contributes to chronic diseases of aging such as atherosclerosis and diabetes complications.

links.source_file: _document_ - Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Aging.md
links.context: NF-kB is the transcription factor that executes much of the inflammatory response initiated by AGE-RAGE interaction. After activation via MAPK and PI3K signaling, NF-kB translocates to the nucleus where it activates transcription of genes encoding cytokines, growth factors, and adhesion molecules, including tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), a well-known inflammation promoter. TNF-alpha is also a hallmark of the pro-inflammatory state seen in aging and chronic disease, and its upregulation by NF-kB in response to AGEs is one route through which glycation stress contributes to systemic inflammation and to the tissue injury observed in diabetic and age-related pathologies.

links.source_file: _document_ - Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Aging.md
links.context: NF-kB activation increases RAGE expression, creating a positive feedback cycle that enhances the production of inflammatory promoters. RAGE, the receptor for advanced glycation end products, is itself a transcriptional target of NF-kB, so the receptor-dependent signaling initiated by AGEs is amplified over time. This feed-forward loop means that chronic exposure to AGEs progressively strengthens inflammatory signaling, contributing to the accumulation of tissue damage. The NF-kB-RAGE positive feedback is regarded as an important mechanism explaining why AGE-driven pathology, such as vascular stiffening and diabetic complications, tends to worsen with continued glycoxidative burden.

NF-kappaB induces TNF-alpha along with over 500 other target genes, driving the pro-inflammatory cascade that amplifies oxidative and immune responses. This positions NF-kappaB upstream of a cytokine network central to inflammation. The directionality is transcription factor to cytokine output. A caveat is that TNF-alpha itself further activates NF-kappaB, so the relationship is reciprocally reinforcing rather than linear.

NF-kappaB antagonizes NRF2 through mutual competition, as the RelA subunit competes with NRF2 for the coactivators CBP and p300, limiting antioxidant gene transcription. This creates a molecular switch that favors inflammation over antioxidant defense. The directionality is transcriptional competition suppressing the antioxidant program. A caveat is that cross-talk is context-dependent and certain stimuli can co-activate both pathways transiently.

NF-kappaB upregulates an antioxidant gene program as a negative feedback that limits TNF-alpha-induced tissue damage, inducing enzymes such as MnSOD, ferritin, and heme oxygenase. This self-limiting loop tempers the oxidative consequences of inflammatory signaling. The directionality is NF-kappaB to adaptive antioxidant transcription. A caveat is that the same factor also drives pro-oxidant enzymes (NOX, iNOS), so the net redox outcome depends on stimulus and cell type.

NF-κB is activated by p38 MAPK, which was the first kinase shown to drive NF-κB-mediated SASP independently of the DDR. p38 MAPK integrates oxidative and stress signals to phosphorylate upstream kinases (e.g., TAK1) that liberate NF-κB. This provides a DDR-independent route to SASP activation. The p38-NF-κB axis is a conserved, druggable SASP regulatory module.

NF-κB is activated by GATA4, which promotes pro-inflammatory SASP via TRAF3IP2 (Act1) and by inhibiting autophagy that would otherwise limit damage signals. GATA4 accumulation in senescence makes it a specific upstream driver of NF-κB in the arrested state. This couples defective organelle turnover to inflammatory transcription. The GATA4-NF-κB link is a senescence-selective regulatory route.

NF-κB is inhibited by metformin in fibroblasts, macrophages, and senescent endothelial cells, contributing to its senomorphic effect. Metformin's AMPK activation indirectly suppresses NF-κB and mTOR, lowering SASP transcription. This anti-inflammatory action underlies many of metformin's age-related benefits. The inhibition is well documented though downstream of its primary metabolic targets.

NF-κB is inhibited by rapamycin, which interferes with the p38 MAPK-IL-1α-NF-κB cascade and suppresses mTOR-dependent SASP translation. This dual action reduces both SASP transcription and protein output. Rapamycin's blockade of NF-κB is a key component of its senomorphic profile. The inhibition is mechanistically well established.

NF-κB is inhibited by apigenin, which suppresses NF-κB-dependent SASP factors and the chemokine CXCL10. Apigenin additionally blocks the ASAP-to-SASP transition via ATM-HSPA8 and PRDX6 interactions. These actions reduce the inflammatory secretome in specific cancer and fibroblast models. The NF-κB inhibition supports apigenin's moderate-confidence senomorphic role.

NF-κB is inhibited by nutlin 3a indirectly: nutlin 3a stabilizes p53 (via MDM2 inhibition), and p53 restrains NF-κB-driven pro-inflammatory SASP. This leverages the tumor-suppressor rheostat to dampen inflammation. The effect is consistent with p53's SASP-restraining role. Mechanistically sound, though nutlin 3a is primarily a research compound.

NF-κB is inhibited by glucocorticoids, which block pro-inflammatory SASP by impairing IL-1α-mediated NF-κB activity. Glucocorticoids repress NF-κB transactivation via co-repressor recruitment, reducing SASP cytokine output. This explains their classic anti-inflammatory action in senescence contexts. The inhibition is well established pharmacologically, though chronic use carries significant side effects.

Active PI3K activates IRS1 indirectly via AKT, forming a positive feedback loop within the mTOR-PI3K signaling cascade. AKT also mediates the survival and cell cycle progression functions of mTORC2, the output node of the model. The levels of PI3K, the kinase upstream of the output mTORC2, are relevant to the mechanisms that induce hormesis, since the most important parameters in the principal component analysis of hormetic parameter sets correspond to the phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of PI3K.

Active PI3K (phosphoinositide 3-kinase) activates mTORC2 by phosphorylation in the mass-action model of the insulin signaling cascade. mTORC2 is the chosen output node of the pathway because it drives cell cycle progression and survival via AKT and regulates mitochondrial physiology, metabolism and integrity; mTORC2 activity increases with age and its elimination alleviates aging progression. Principal component analysis of hormetic parameter sets shows that the most important parameters correspond to the phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of PI3K, suggesting that PI3K levels are relevant to the mechanisms that induce the hormetic response of rapamycin.

Senomorphics suppress the harmful secretory and signaling activity of senescent cells, particularly the pro-inflammatory SASP, without inducing cell death. They act on upstream regulators such as mTOR, NF-κB, JAK-STAT3, p38 MAPK, and BRD4 to dampen factor production. This preserves the potentially beneficial arrest while neutralizing paracrine harm. Suppression of the SASP is the defining functional action of a senomorphic.

Senomorphics are complementary to senolytics: senomorphics dampen SASP and pro-inflammatory signaling without killing the cell, whereas senolytics eliminate the cell. This allows flexible intervention -- using senomorphics when preserving acute senescence is desirable (e.g., wound healing) and senolytics when clearance is preferred. The two strategies together span the senotherapeutic space. Their complementarity is a recurring theme in senescence therapeutics.

Senomorphics target mTOR to suppress the SASP, since mTOR promotes translation of SASP factors such as IL-1α and stabilizes SASP mRNAs. Inhibitors like rapamycin thereby reduce the secretome without reversing arrest. This mTOR-centered action also engages autophagy, limiting mitochondrial DAMPs. Targeting mTOR is a central, well-validated senomorphic mechanism.

Senomorphics target NF-κB, the master transcriptional regulator of the SASP, as a key mechanism to suppress the inflammatory secretome. NF-κB inhibitors (e.g., glucocorticoids, some natural compounds) blunt expression of the bulk of SASP cytokines and chemokines. Because NF-κB sits at the apex of SASP control, its inhibition is broadly effective. This makes NF-κB a prime senomorphic node.

Senomorphics target p38 MAPK, which activates NF-κB-mediated SASP independently of the DDR and stabilizes SASP transcripts. p38 MAPK inhibitors suppress the SASP from fibroblasts of older donors, supporting their senomorphic relevance. The kinase is a convergence point for oxidative and stress signals feeding the secretome. Inhibition is mechanistically well grounded though clinical senomorphic use is still investigational.

Senomorphics target the JAK-STAT3 axis, which promotes a pro-inflammatory SASP and contributes to age-related frailty via IL-6/STAT3 signaling. JAK1/2 inhibitors such as ruxolitinib reduce SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8, validating this as a senomorphic mechanism. The pathway also mediates the feed-forward inflammation of chronic senescence. Blocking it dampens both local and systemic senescence-associated inflammation.

Senomorphics target BRD4 using BET bromodomain inhibitors that block enhancer-driven SASP transcription. By displacing BRD4 from senescence-activated super-enhancers, these agents suppress expression of multiple SASP factors. This chromatin-reader approach is a mechanistically distinct senomorphic strategy. Efficacy is supported in cellular models, with clinical translation still emerging.

Senomorphics may target KDM4 histone demethylases, whose inhibition blocks SASP factor expression by preserving repressive H3K9me3/H3K36me3 at SASP loci. This is a candidate rather than established clinical strategy, as KDM4 inhibitors are still under characterization. The mechanistic logic is sound given KDM4's role in SASP licensing. Confidence is therefore moderate pending in vivo validation.

Fisetin exhibits both senolytic and senomorphic activities, suppressing the SASP at lower exposure while clearing cells at higher exposure. At senomorphic-relevant doses it reduces NF-κB/IL-6 signaling and SASP factor expression. This dual activity makes fisetin a versatile agent whose dominant effect depends on concentration and context. The senomorphic facet is supported by multiple studies though best characterized as secondary to its senolytic action.

The senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) is the major non-cell-autonomous output of senescent cells, comprising hundreds of secreted factors including cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and proteases. The SASP is not a passive byproduct but an active program orchestrated by transcription factors such as NF-κB, C/EBPbeta, and AP-1 and by innate immune sensors like cGAS-STING. It mediates paracrine senescence, immune recruitment, and systemic inflammation, making it central to both the beneficial (tumor-suppressive, wound-healing) and deleterious (inflammaging, fibrosis) effects of senescence. Directionally, the SASP is produced by and amplifies the senescence program in a feed-forward loop.
Senescence in adult tissues can be triggered by a persistent DNA damage response (DDR) induced by various internal and external factors.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of the dynamic epigenetic landscape in senescence_orchestrating SASP expression.md
links.context: Senescent cells display distinctive phenotypic changes encompassing chromatin remodeling, metabolic reprogramming, and establishment of SASP.

Cellular senescence is fundamentally defined as a state of stable, essentially irreversible cell-cycle arrest in which cells remain metabolically active but lose the capacity to proliferate, distinguishing it from quiescence and terminal differentiation. The arrest is actively enforced by tumor-suppressor networks -- the p53/p21 and p16/Rb axes -- that impose a durable G1-phase block and remain engaged even under strong mitogenic stimulation. Because the arrest is permanent, senescent cells can persist for the lifetime of the organism, accumulating in tissues with age. Importantly, senescence is not mere growth arrest but a comprehensive reprogramming entailing chromatin reorganization, metabolic shifts, and a distinctive secretory phenotype (SASP).

DNA damage, particularly persistent double-strand breaks, is a potent inducer of senescence through activation of the DNA damage response (DDR). The ATM/ATR kinases phosphorylate and stabilize the transcription factor p53, which transcribes p21CIP1 to inhibit cyclin-CDK complexes and enforce arrest. Damage-induced senescence acts as a barrier to malignant transformation by halting proliferation of genomically unstable cells. A caveat is that the same DDR can also drive a pro-inflammatory SASP, so DNA damage both suppresses and, chronically, may promote pathology.

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and other oxidative insults provoke a distinct form of stress-induced senescence, often in the absence of extensive DNA double-strand breaks. Mitochondrial dysfunction elevates intracellular ROS, which causes oxidative base damage, lipid peroxidation, and activation of stress kinases such as p38 MAPK that reinforce arrest and SASP. This pathway is particularly relevant to aging and to the turnover of tissue stem and progenitor cells exposed to chronic metabolic stress. A caveat is that the threshold and kinetics of oxidative-stress-induced senescence vary widely by cell type and insult intensity.

Progressive telomere shortening with each cell division eventually exposes chromosome ends that are recognized as DNA double-strand breaks, triggering replicative senescence at the Hayflick limit. Critically short or dysfunctional telomeres activate the ATM/p53 and ATR/p21 DDR cascades, halting proliferation to prevent chromosomal instability. This mechanism is the canonical explanation for the finite replicative capacity of primary human cells in culture. The directionality is one-way in normal cells, though telomerase reactivation can bypass the arrest -- a hallmark of cancer.

Activated oncogenes such as RAS, BRAF, and MYC drive hyperproliferation and replication stress, which in turn elicit oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) as an intrinsic tumor-suppressive failsafe. The unscheduled S-phase entry generates DNA replication stress and DNA damage that stabilize p53 and derepress the CDKN2A/p16INK4a locus, locking cells in arrest. OIS is observed in benign lesions such as melanocytic nevi and is a major barrier to tumor progression. The paradox is that OIS cells secrete a SASP that, while recruiting immune clearance, can also promote tumorigenesis in neighboring cells.

Senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHF) are DAPI-dense, punctate bodies of facultative heterochromatin assembled in senescent human cells to stably silence proliferation-promoting genes. They are deposited by the HIRA/ASF1a histone chaperone complex and macroH2A, marked by H3K9me3, and seeded through hypophosphorylated Rb recruitment of HDACs to E2F target loci. SAHF reinforce the arrested state by locking E2F-responsive S-phase genes into repressive chromatin. They are most prominent in oncogene-induced and replicative senescence of human fibroblasts and are a structural hallmark rather than a universal feature across all cell types.

The p53/p21 axis is a primary enforcement mechanism of senescence, especially in damage- and stress-induced forms. DNA damage stabilizes p53, which transcriptionally induces the CDK inhibitor p21CIP1; p21 inhibits cyclin E/A-CDK2, preventing phosphorylation of Rb and blocking S-phase entry. This pathway provides a rapid, p53-dose-dependent G1/S arrest that can be engaged acutely after genotoxic insult. A caveat is that the p53 pathway is frequently disabled in cancer, and p53 also restrains the SASP, so its loss reshapes rather than simply abolishes senescence.

The p16INK4a/Rb pathway enforces the long-term, irreversible phase of senescence independently of p53. p16 inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, keeping Rb hypophosphorylated and bound to E2F, thereby preventing expression of S-phase genes; this locks in a durable growth arrest. Unlike the p53/p21 arm, which can be transient, p16/Rb-mediated arrest is typically sustained for the life of the cell and is the stronger correlate of in vivo senescent burden with age. Its engagement is a key determinant of why senescence is considered irreversible rather than a quiescent state.

Both the p53/p21 and p16/Rb axes converge on suppression of the E2F family of transcription factors, which are master regulators of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase progression. Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F and, together with SAHF-mediated heterochromatinization, represses E2F target loci; p21 additionally blocks CDK-mediated release of this repression. Inhibition of E2F is therefore the final common effector of the senescent growth arrest. This directed, downstream suppression is a defining mechanistic feature shared across senescent cell types.

Senescent cells characteristically show reduced expression of lamin B1 (encoded by LMNB1), a structural component of the nuclear lamina. Lamin B1 loss detaches lamina-associated domains (LADs) from the nuclear periphery, spatially reorganizing chromatin and contributing to the altered gene expression and genomic instability of senescence. This marker is relatively conserved across cell types and tissues, making it a practical histological and molecular signature of senescent cells in vivo. A caveat is that lamin B1 loss can also occur in certain differentiation and disease states, so it is best used in combination with other markers.

The burden of senescent cells rises in multiple tissues with age, with some estimates suggesting an exponential increase, and this accumulation correlates strongly with age-related functional decline. Chronically accrued senescent cells and their SASP drive low-grade sterile inflammation (inflammaging) and tissue dysfunction across organs. The relationship is bidirectional in effect: aging promotes senescence (via telomere shortening, damage, and stem-cell exhaustion) while senescence accelerates aging phenotypes. This makes senescent-cell clearance a leading intervention strategy for alleviating age-related disease.

In established tumors and chronically, senescence can paradoxically promote cancer through its SASP, which is rich in growth factors, angiogenic cues, and EMT-inducing cytokines. The SASP can stimulate survival, therapy resistance, cancer stemness, and immune suppressive microenvironments that favor malignant progression. This duality -- tumor suppression acutely, tumor promotion chronically -- is a central theme of senescence biology. The strength of the promoting effect depends on context, SASP composition, and whether immune surveillance is intact.

Senescence is a direct therapeutic target of senolytics, agents that selectively eliminate senescent cells. Genetic or pharmacological clearance of p16-positive senescent cells in murine models delays age-related dysfunction, extends healthspan, and alleviates multiple pathologies. The strategy exploits the pro-survival SCAP network that senescent cells depend on, pushing them into apoptosis while sparing healthy cells. Clinical translation is ongoing, with the key caveat that intermittent, tissue-specific clearance is preferable to chronic ablation, which could impair beneficial acute-senescence functions.

Senescence is modulated by senomorphics, compounds that suppress the deleterious SASP without killing the senescent cell itself. By targeting upstream SASP regulators (mTOR, NF-κB, JAK-STAT3, p38 MAPK, BRD4), senomorphics dampen the paracrine and inflammatory consequences of senescence. This is conceptually complementary to senolytics, which remove the cell rather than its output. Senomorphics preserve potentially beneficial acute-senescence functions (e.g., wound healing, tumor suppression) while mitigating chronic harm.

Senescence is a major barrier to induced pluripotency, restricting the efficiency of cellular reprogramming by Yamanaka factors (OSKM). The p53/p21 axis in particular senses the oncogene-like OSKM program and triggers senescence or apoptosis, preventing widespread dedifferentiation. This refractoriness is exploited experimentally to select for cells that have bypassed senescence, but it also means aged or stressed donor cells reprogram poorly. Therapeutically, transient p53 inhibition or senolytic treatment can improve reprogramming yields, highlighting senescence as a gatekeeper of plasticity.

p53 is mutated in Cancer. p53 is the archetypal tumor-suppressor transcription factor that integrates stress signals into cell-cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The directionality runs from Cancer toward p53, so Cancer is the active agent and p53 the recipient of the effect. This altered abundance or activity is a recurring feature of malignancy that can serve as a diagnostic, prognostic, or predictive biomarker and sometimes as a therapeutic target.

p53 is inhibited by MDM2. p53 is the archetypal tumor-suppressor transcription factor that integrates stress signals into cell-cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis. MDM2 is the principal E3 ubiquitin ligase and transcriptional antagonist that keeps p53 quiescent in unstressed cells. The directionality runs from MDM2 toward p53, so MDM2 is the active agent and p53 the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

p53 is restored by Nutlins. p53 is the archetypal tumor-suppressor transcription factor that integrates stress signals into cell-cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis. Nutlins are cis-imidazoline small molecules that block the MDM2-p53 interface, stabilizing p53 to enforce arrest or apoptosis. The directionality runs from Nutlins toward p53, so Nutlins is the active agent and p53 the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

p53 induces Puma. p53 is the archetypal tumor-suppressor transcription factor that integrates stress signals into cell-cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis. Puma is a p53-inducible BH3-only protein that binds and neutralizes essentially all anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 relatives to license mitochondrial death. The relationship is directional, with p53 acting as the operative agent upon Puma rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

p53 induces Noxa. p53 is the archetypal tumor-suppressor transcription factor that integrates stress signals into cell-cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis. Noxa is a p53-inducible BH3-only protein with selective affinity for Mcl-1 and A1, sensitizing cells to mitochondrial apoptosis. The relationship is directional, with p53 acting as the operative agent upon Noxa rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

p53 regulates MOMP. p53 is the archetypal tumor-suppressor transcription factor that integrates stress signals into cell-cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis. Mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) is the committed, largely irreversible step of intrinsic apoptosis that releases intermembrane-space proteins. The relationship is directional, with p53 acting as the operative agent upon MOMP rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.
p53 activation during reprogramming leads to Senescence and Apoptosis, reducing reprogramming efficiency.

links.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
links.context: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which transcriptionally induces the CDK inhibitor p21CIP1; p21 binds and inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes (notably CDK2), enforcing a G1/S arrest. This p53 to p21 axis is a primary, rapid enforcement mechanism of senescence and quiescence. The induction is dose-dependent and reversible in the short term but locks arrest when sustained. It exemplifies tumor-suppressive cell-cycle control.

In most contexts p53 restrains the pro-inflammatory SASP, limiting cytokines and chemokines; loss of p53 dramatically amplifies SASP output. This restraint operates partly through suppression of NF-κB-driven inflammation. The directionality is suppressive, meaning intact p53 yields a more contained secretome. This nuance explains why p53 status strongly shapes senescence's net effects in tissues and tumors.

p53 regulates exosome production during senescence: p53 target genes including STEAP3 and VPS32 control the biogenesis and release of senescence-associated exosomes that can transmit signals to neighboring cells. This adds a vesicular communication route to p53's senescence functions. The relationship situates p53 within both arrest enforcement and paracrine signaling. Confidence is moderate as the exosomal regulatory network is still being mapped.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: p53 directly activates transcription of HIC1, a tumor suppressor that in turn represses the SIRT1 promoter, forming a negative feedback loop on SIRT1. This loop ensures that p53 activity is not indefinitely suppressed by SIRT1-mediated deacetylation. Directionally, p53 is the transcription factor and HIC1 the induced target gene. The biological significance is genome protection: by inducing HIC1, p53 prevents SIRT1 from over-deacetylating and silencing p53 itself.

Kynurenine and its derivatives activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), which promotes regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation while suppressing effector T and NK cells. This is a central effector arm of IDO1-mediated immunosuppression: IDO1 in antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells depletes local tryptophan and produces kynurenine, creating an immunosuppressive microenvironment that favors immune tolerance. This pathway underlies IDO1's physiological roles in maternal-fetal tolerance, regulation of inflammation and autoimmunity, antimicrobial defense, and tumor immune escape, where IDO1 is often upregulated in cancers and the tumor microenvironment.

Aspirin not only reduces inflammation, a hallmark of aging, it also reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease, thrombosis and cancer; low-dose aspirin prevents one-third of colorectal, gastric and esophageal cancers. Millions of people take aspirin daily to prevent cardiovascular disease and cancer, and it was calculated that the benefits of aspirin are greater than its risks despite side effects including life-threatening gastric bleeding. The author argues that the benefits of the anti-aging effects of rapamycin and everolimus may be even greater, and that aspirin can be combined with rapamycin in an anti-aging formulation.

Aspirin may increase cardiovascular disease risk specifically in individuals carrying the fast COMT (Val/Val, G/G) genotype, a pharmacogenetic interaction identified in prospective studies. The mechanism is thought to involve genotype-dependent differences in catecholamine and folate metabolism that alter aspirin's effects on vascular homeostasis. This contrasts sharply with slow COMT individuals, in whom aspirin is protective, underscoring the importance of COMT genotyping in cardiovascular prevention strategies.

Aspirin may increase cardiovascular disease risk in individuals with the fast COMT (G/G) genotype, reflecting a gene-drug interaction in which rapid COMT-mediated catecholamine clearance changes the vascular response to aspirin. Population studies have reported that the cardioprotective benefit of aspirin is absent or reversed in fast metabolizers. The directionality of this effect is genotype-specific, making COMT status a candidate biomarker for aspirin therapy personalization.

Aspirin is effective in preventing cardiovascular disease among individuals with the slow COMT (Met/Met, A/A) genotype, where its antiplatelet and anti-inflammatory actions translate into net cardiovascular protection. Slow COMT activity appears to create a metabolic milieu in which low-dose aspirin reduces thrombotic event risk. This protective association is the inverse of the effect seen in fast COMT individuals, highlighting a clear pharmacogenetic divergence.

Aspirin prevents cardiovascular disease specifically in the slow COMT (A/A) genotype, where the enzyme's reduced activity is associated with a favorable response to aspirin prophylaxis. Clinical and epidemiological evidence indicates that the cardiovascular benefit of aspirin is concentrated in this subgroup rather than the population at large. This genotype-dependent efficacy supports the use of COMT Val158Met status to guide aspirin-based prevention.

Cancer is characterized by Hallmarks of Cancer. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The Hallmarks of Cancer are the enabling biological capabilities acquired during tumorigenesis, including sustained proliferation, evasion of death, and metastasis. The directionality runs from Hallmarks of Cancer toward Cancer, so Hallmarks of Cancer is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Together these facts situate the relationship within the broader architecture of cancer biology, clarifying how the two entities connect as part of the hallmark or taxonomic framework.

Cancer evades Apoptosis. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, caspase-dependent form of cell death that dismantles cells without provoking inflammation. The relationship is directional, with Cancer acting as the operative agent upon Apoptosis rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer undergoes Metabolic Reprogramming. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Metabolic reprogramming is the rewiring of nutrient uptake and bioenergetics that supplies building blocks and redox balance to proliferating tumors. The relationship is directional, with Cancer acting as the operative agent upon Metabolic Reprogramming rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer induces Angiogenesis. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Angiogenesis is the sprouting of new vessels from preexisting vasculature that tumors must recruit to grow beyond a few millimeters and to metastasize. The relationship is directional, with Cancer acting as the operative agent upon Angiogenesis rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is a risk factor for Aging. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Aging is the foremost non-modifiable risk factor for cancer, reflecting accumulated mutations, epigenetic drift, and a senescence-shaped microenvironment. The directionality runs from Aging toward Cancer, so Aging is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Such relationships underscore how inherited or intrinsic factors shape cancer susceptibility and inform risk-stratified screening and prevention.

Cancer is driven by PI3K. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Phosphoinositide 3-kinase generates PIP3 at the membrane to recruit and activate Akt, a central node of growth and survival signaling. The directionality runs from PI3K toward Cancer, so PI3K is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by Akt. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Akt is a serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates a broad panel of substrates to promote growth, glycolysis, and suppression of apoptosis. The directionality runs from Akt toward Cancer, so Akt is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by mTOR. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. mTOR is a nutrient- and growth-factor-sensitive kinase that integrates PI3K/Akt inputs to control protein synthesis and cell growth. The directionality runs from mTOR toward Cancer, so mTOR is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by MAPK. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades relay extracellular signals to transcriptional programs governing proliferation and stress responses. The directionality runs from MAPK toward Cancer, so MAPK is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by ERK. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. ERK1/2 are the terminal effectors of the RAS-RAF-MEK cascade that phosphorylate nuclear and cytoplasmic targets to drive division. The directionality runs from ERK toward Cancer, so ERK is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by Wnt. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The directionality runs from Wnt toward Cancer, so Wnt is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

The directionality runs from JAK2 toward Cancer, so JAK2 is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by STAT3. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The directionality runs from STAT3 toward Cancer, so STAT3 is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. The directionality runs from NFκB toward Cancer, so NFκB is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by YAP1. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. YAP1 is the transcriptional co-activator of the Hippo pathway that, when nuclear, promotes proliferation and is inhibited by ivermectin in several cancers. The directionality runs from YAP1 toward Cancer, so YAP1 is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by EGFR. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose activating mutations and overexpression couple extracellular cues to proliferative and survival signaling. The directionality runs from EGFR toward Cancer, so EGFR is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is driven by HER2. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. HER2 (ERBB2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase that, when amplified, drives aggressive breast cancer and is the target of trastuzumab. The directionality runs from HER2 toward Cancer, so HER2 is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is suppressed by p53. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. p53 is the archetypal tumor-suppressor transcription factor that integrates stress signals into cell-cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis. The directionality runs from p53 toward Cancer, so p53 is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

Cancer is suppressed by BRCA. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressors that orchestrate homology-directed repair of DNA double-strand breaks and genome stability. The directionality runs from BRCA toward Cancer, so BRCA is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

Ki-67 is expressed in all active phases of the cell cycle and absent in quiescent cells, making it a robust immunohistochemical readout of proliferation. A high Ki-67 labeling index correlates with aggressive biology and, in some tumors, informs adjuvant therapy decisions. The relationship is directional as a biomarker: proliferation evidences the tumor's growth fraction rather than causing it. It is particularly integrated into grading of breast and neuroendocrine neoplasms.

Cancer evades Immune System. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The immune system surveys and eliminates nascent malignancies, a process tumors must subvert to establish and progress. The relationship is directional, with Cancer acting as the operative agent upon Immune System rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is treated by Cisplatin. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Cisplatin is a platinum compound that forms intra- and inter-strand DNA crosslinks, triggering damage responses that can culminate in senescence or death. The directionality runs from Cisplatin toward Cancer, so Cisplatin is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer is treated by docetaxel. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Docetaxel is a taxane that stabilizes microtubules, arresting mitosis and inducing cell death in a range of carcinomas. The directionality runs from docetaxel toward Cancer, so docetaxel is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer is treated by trastuzumab. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody against HER2 that inhibits signaling and recruits immune effector mechanisms in HER2-positive breast cancer. The directionality runs from trastuzumab toward Cancer, so trastuzumab is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer is treated by Ivermectin. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Ivermectin is an approved antiparasitic drug repurposed in oncology for its multi-kinase, anti-Wnt, and pro-death activities across cancers. The directionality runs from Ivermectin toward Cancer, so Ivermectin is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer is treated by Fenbendazole. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Fenbendazole is a benzimidazole anthelmintic under investigation for anticancer effects via microtubule interference, glycolysis suppression, and p53 activation. The directionality runs from Fenbendazole toward Cancer, so Fenbendazole is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer is treated by melittin. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Melittin is the principal peptide of honeybee venom that permeabilizes membranes and suppresses oncogenic receptors and checkpoints. The directionality runs from melittin toward Cancer, so melittin is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer is treated by Nutlins. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Nutlins are cis-imidazoline small molecules that block the MDM2-p53 interface, stabilizing p53 to enforce arrest or apoptosis. The directionality runs from Nutlins toward Cancer, so Nutlins is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer is treated by BH3 mimetics. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. BH3 mimetics are small molecules that occupy the hydrophobic groove of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 proteins, freeing Bax/Bak to kill tumor cells. The directionality runs from BH3 mimetics toward Cancer, so BH3 mimetics is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer is treated by BET inhibitors. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. BET inhibitors displace bromodomain proteins such as BRD4 from acetylated chromatin, silencing MYC and inflammatory transcription programs. The directionality runs from BET inhibitors toward Cancer, so BET inhibitors is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. Clinically, this positions the object as a therapeutic modality against the subject, though efficacy is shaped by biomarker selection and the eventual emergence of resistance.

Cancer overcomes Multidrug Resistance. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Multidrug resistance is the cross-resistance of tumors to structurally unrelated drugs, most classically mediated by ATP-dependent efflux pumps. The relationship is directional, with Cancer acting as the operative agent upon Multidrug Resistance rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer is linked to Oxidative Stress. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Oxidative stress arises from an imbalance of reactive oxygen species and inflicts DNA, protein, and lipid damage that can initiate and promote malignancy. The directionality runs from Oxidative Stress toward Cancer, so Oxidative Stress is the active agent and Cancer the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Cancer uses Integrins. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. Integrins are transmembrane receptors that connect the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton and intracellular survival kinases. The relationship is directional, with Cancer acting as the operative agent upon Integrins rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.
Epigenetic dysregulation underlies Cancer through silencing of tumor suppressors and global hypomethylation.

In established tumors, paracrine senescence from therapy-induced senescent (TIS) cells can promote cancer progression via a tumor-supportive SASP rich in growth factors, angiogenic cues, and EMT inducers. The spread of senescence-associated remodeling can enhance stemness, invasiveness, and therapy resistance in neighboring malignant cells. This duality mirrors senescence's overall Janus-faced relationship with cancer. The promoting effect depends on SASP composition and immune context, giving moderate confidence.

Cancer is suppressed by senescence surveillance, which clears oncogene-induced and damaged senescent cells in benign lesions before they can progress to malignancy. By eliminating arrested pre-malignant cells through NK, macrophage, and T-cell mechanisms, surveillance acts as a fail-safe tumor-suppression barrier. Loss of surveillance permits senescent-cell accumulation and tumor promotion. This positions immune clearance of senescence as a key anticancer defense.

Cancer is suppressed by senescence, which halts proliferation of damaged and oncogene-stressed cells, acting as an intrinsic barrier to malignant transformation. This tumor-suppressive role is evident in benign neoplasms and after cytotoxic therapy. By removing cells from the replicative pool and recruiting immune clearance, senescence constrains clonal expansion. The directionality is protective acutely, though chronic senescence can become tumor-promoting.

ATFS-1 (Activating Transcription Factor associated with Stress-1) is the transcription factor required for activation of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) in C. elegans. Uniquely, it possesses both a mitochondrial targeting sequence and a nuclear localization signal: in the absence of stress it is imported into mitochondria and rapidly degraded, whereas under mitochondrial dysfunction its import is impaired and it translocates to the nucleus to orchestrate a broad transcriptional response, including induction of mitochondrial chaperones. Nuclear ATFS-1 thereby couples mitochondrial status directly to nuclear gene expression.

In C. elegans, mitochondrial dysfunction caused by protein misfolding alters the subcellular localization of the transcription factor ATFS-1. In healthy mitochondria, ATFS-1 is imported into the organelle and degraded by the Lon protease. During stress, ATFS-1 instead traffics to the nucleus to drive transcription of genes involved in the coordinated UPRmt response. This import-versus-nuclear-translocation decision makes protein import a readout of mitochondrial health, a paradigm the review argues is extended in mammals by mechanisms involving DELE1 processing and PINK1 accumulation.

Activation of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) is an important determinant of lifespan in C. elegans. Knockdown of the mitochondrial ribosomal protein mrps-5 constitutively activates UPRmt and extends lifespan, and genetic inhibition of UPRmt abrogates this longevity benefit; restoration of NAD+ levels also extends longevity through a UPRmt-dependent pathway. Remarkably, tissue-specific knockdown of the cytochrome c oxidase component cco-1 in the brain activates UPRmt in distal tissues via mitokines and increases whole-organism lifespan, demonstrating cell-non-autonomous regulation of longevity.

The mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) is activated by the accumulation of misfolded proteins within the mitochondrial matrix, analogous to the classic ER stress response. Expression of a misfolding-prone mutant of the matrix protein ornithine transcarbamylase induces a nuclear transcriptional response that upregulates mitochondrial-specific chaperones. In C. elegans, activation of UPRmt requires the transcription factor ATFS-1, and matrix-derived peptides exported through the ABC transporter HAF-1 signal mitochondrial stress to the nucleus.

For a network to produce a biphasic dose-response curve, the probability is highly increased if one of the bivalent interactions of the inhibited target operates in the saturated enzymatic regime, i.e., a Michaelis-Menten interaction with high affinity towards its substrate whose reaction speed does not depend on substrate amount. Specifically, the Michaelis-Menten constant K21 of the backward interaction from Target to Input must be significantly low. Fixing K21 to a low value raises the percentage of hormetic parameter sets from about 6% to 80%, a roughly ten-fold increase in the probability of observing hormesis.
