In RAW264.7 macrophage-like cells stimulated with Porphyromonas gingivalis fimbriae, honokiol reduced COX-2 expression alongside inhibition of NF-kappaB activation, and it is generally more potent in this regard than the structurally related eugenol and bis-eugenol. By limiting COX-2-driven prostanoid production, honokiol dampens inflammation and inflammatory pain signaling, complementing its inhibition of TNF-alpha, nitric oxide, and NF-kappaB.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol inhibits neutrophil infiltration and reactive oxygen species production after cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, as measured by luminol-amplified chemiluminescence in neutrophils. By reducing the accumulation and oxidative burst of neutrophils at the site of ischemic injury, honokiol limits secondary tissue damage following stroke. This anti-inflammatory action is complemented by inhibition of glial NF-kappaB activation and cytokine production, together contributing to honokiol's ability to reduce infarct volume in focal cerebral ischemia-reperfusion models.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol suppresses NF-kappaB activation in multiple cell types, a key node in its anti-inflammatory activity. In LPS-stimulated macrophages honokiol inhibited NF-kappaB activation along with PKC-alpha membrane translocation and MAPK signaling, reducing TNF-alpha and nitric oxide production. It likewise suppressed glial NF-kappaB activation and cytokine production during cerebral ischemia-reperfusion and inhibited COX-2 expression in RAW264.7 macrophage-like cells. These convergent actions on the NF-kappaB pathway underlie honokiol's neuroprotective and analgesic anti-inflammatory effects.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol inhibits NMDA-evoked cationic influx, blocking excessive calcium entry that would otherwise drive excitotoxic neuronal injury and seizures. In rat cerebellar granule cells, honokiol inhibited repetitive firing by blocking glutamate-, NMDA-, and K+-evoked cation influx, and intraperitoneal honokiol (1 and 5 mg/kg) increased seizure thresholds in NMDA-infusion models, being more potent than magnolol. In ischemic conditions honokiol also disrupts PSD95-nNOS coupling at the NMDA receptor postsynaptic complex, preventing neurotoxic nitric oxide production downstream of NMDA receptor activation.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: In animal behavioral models, honokiol produces anxiolysis at doses as low as 0.2 mg/kg with fewer motor and cognitive side effects than the benzodiazepine diazepam. The anxiolytic effect of honokiol is blocked by flumazenil, bicuculline, CCK-4, and caffeine, whereas these agents differentially affect diazepam's anxiolysis (e.g., caffeine enhances diazepam's effect), suggesting honokiol may act through partly alternative pathways in addition to GABA-A potentiation. This favorable side-effect profile is a key rationale for developing honokiol as an anxiolytic.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol is a neuroprotective agent acting through a wide range of parallel mechanisms: preservation of Na+/K+-ATPase activity, phosphorylation of pro-survival factors such as Akt, preservation of mitochondrial function, positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors, and suppression of glucose intolerance, reactive oxygen species, and inflammatory damage. Preclinically it mitigates the effects of stroke and seizures and improves learning and memory in behavioral models. Its therapeutic potential spans anxiety, pain, cerebrovascular injury, epilepsy, and cognitive disorders including Alzheimer's disease.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol is a positive allosteric modulator of both synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors, a known target of benzodiazepines and other anxiolytics. It shows markedly higher efficacy at receptors containing the delta subunit (900-1100% response) compared with alpha-beta-gamma-only receptors (300-500%), and it allosterically increases the affinity of low-affinity sites, increasing [3H]muscimol binding about three-fold. This GABA-A modulation underpins honokiol's anxiolytic, hypnotic, and anticonvulsant properties and is the basis of its sleep-promoting effects via the benzodiazepine site.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol preserves mitochondrial function as part of its neuroprotective mechanism. In preclinical ischemia models, honokiol maintained enzymatic mitochondrial function alongside Na+/K+-ATPase activity, and it protects neurons by preventing glucose- and ROS-mediated damage while preserving mitochondrial integrity. Honokiol also reduces beta-amyloid-induced neuronal death through decreased ROS production, suppressed intracellular calcium elevation, and inhibition of caspase-3 activity. These effects collectively position mitochondrial preservation and reduced oxidative stress as core components of honokiol's cytoprotective profile.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol exerts neuroprotection in part by preserving the activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase, the membrane pump critical for maintaining neuronal resting potential and ion homeostasis. In mouse models of cerebral ischemia, honokiol treatment preserved Na+/K+-ATPase activity and enzymatic mitochondrial function, correlating with reduced neuronal damage. Together with phosphorylation of pro-survival factors, preservation of mitochondrial function, and GABA-A modulation, Na+/K+-ATPase preservation is one of at least five distinct parallel mechanisms through which honokiol protects neurons from ischemic and oxidative injury.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol promotes non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and shortens sleep latency. In mouse studies, honokiol at 10 and 20 mg/kg significantly decreased sleep latency and increased the amount of NREM sleep without affecting REM sleep or EEG power density, and it excited sleep-promoting neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area. These effects occur through the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor. The combined sleep-promoting and anxiolytic actions suggest a potential role for honokiol as an anesthetic adjunct.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol significantly decreased beta-amyloid (Abeta)-induced neuronal death in neuronal culture models of Alzheimer's disease. In screening nine compounds from Chinese herbs for anti-Alzheimer's activity, only honokiol and magnolol markedly reduced Abeta-induced cell death. The protective mechanism involves decreased ROS production, suppressed intracellular calcium elevation, and inhibition of caspase-3 activity. A honokiol-containing extract of Magnolia officinalis also prevented lipopolysaccharide-induced memory deficiency via antineuroinflammatory and antiamyloidogenic effects, supporting honokiol's therapeutic potential in Alzheimer's disease.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol protects the brain against ischemia-reperfusion injury. Intravenous honokiol given 15 minutes before or 60 minutes after middle cerebral artery occlusion dose-dependently reduced infarct volume by 20-70% without significant hemodynamic changes. Protective mechanisms include inhibition of neutrophil infiltration and ROS production, suppression of post-ischemic glucose intolerance, disruption of the PSD95-nNOS interaction at the NMDA receptor complex (preventing calcium-dependent neurotoxic nitric oxide production), and suppression of glial NF-kappaB activation and cytokine production.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol reduces cerebral infarction in rodent stroke models, including both pre-ischemic and post-ischemic administration paradigms. In MCA occlusion models, intravenous honokiol significantly reduced total infarct volume without creating significant hemodynamic changes. The neuroprotection is multifactorial, involving inhibition of neutrophil infiltration and reactive oxygen species production, suppression of post-ischemic glucose intolerance, disruption of PSD95-nNOS coupling to prevent neurotoxic nitric oxide generation, and inhibition of glial NF-kappaB activation and inflammatory cytokine production during ischemia-reperfusion.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol and its structural analog magnolol have been evaluated as potential therapies for epilepsy and related seizure disorders. Intraperitoneal injections of honokiol or magnolol (1 and 5 mg/kg) increased seizure threshold in mice challenged with intravenous NMDA, with honokiol appearing more potent than magnolol. Honokiol also ameliorated the behavioral and neurotoxic impairments induced by NMDA injection into the cerebral ventricular system, showing augmented neuroprotection compared with tea polyphenol or memantine alone, supporting a role for honokiol in seizure prevention.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol decreases formalin-induced c-Fos protein expression in the superficial (I-II) laminae of the L4-L5 lumbar dorsal horn in mice, a marker of spinal nociceptive neuron activation. Along with reducing formalin-induced paw-licking, this shows honokiol acts at the spinal level to dampen pain transmission during the inflammatory phase of the formalin model. Honokiol's ability to suppress dorsal-horn c-Fos parallels its blockade of NMDA-, glutamate-, substance P-, and PGE2-evoked nociception, supporting a spinal component to its analgesic activity.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol inhibits nitric oxide expression in LPS-stimulated macrophages, a key anti-inflammatory effect. Nitric oxide overproduction during inflammation drives vasodilation, tissue damage, and pain; honokiol suppresses its induction by blocking PKC-alpha membrane translocation, MAPK signaling, and NF-kappaB activation. In the setting of cerebral ischemia, honokiol additionally prevents neurotoxic nitric oxide production by disrupting the PSD95-nNOS coupling at the NMDA receptor complex, thereby limiting calcium-dependent nNOS activation and downstream nitrosative neuronal injury.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Honokiol reduces TNF-alpha secretion from LPS-stimulated mouse macrophages. Using lipopolysaccharide to induce inflammation, honokiol decreased tumor necrosis factor-alpha secretion, inhibited nitric oxide expression, blocked protein kinase C-alpha membrane translocation, and suppressed NF-kappaB activation in macrophages, with similar anti-inflammatory effects translated to human monocyte-derived dendritic cells. By dampening this central pro-inflammatory cytokine, honokiol mitigates the inflammatory cascade that drives neuroinflammation and inflammatory pain, making it a candidate adjunct for inflammatory conditions.

Honokiol, a biphenolic lignan from Magnolia, physically interacts with SIRT3, increasing its deacetylase activity and upregulating SIRT3 protein expression. The directionality is honokiol upstream of SIRT3 activation. This engagement yields downstream deacetylation of mitochondrial antioxidant and metabolic targets. Honokiol thereby mimics caloric-restriction benefits specifically within mitochondria.

Through SIRT3 activation, honokiol reverses pathological cardiac hypertrophy and protects against doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity in preclinical models. The directionality is honokiol → SIRT3 → antihypertrophic and antioxidant programs. By activating mitochondrial defenses, it counters the oxidative and energetic deficits of failing myocardium. This positions SIRT3 as a therapeutic node in heart failure.

Honokiol suppresses renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis by activating SIRT3, which inhibits the NF-κB/TGF-β1 pathway and limits fibrogenic signaling in kidney tubules. The directionality is honokiol → SIRT3 → antifibrotic transcription. This reduces collagen deposition and inflammatory infiltrate. It illustrates SIRT3's broad tissue-protective role beyond the heart.

Honokiol is highly lipophilic with very poor water solubility, so hot-water tea extraction is inefficient and ethanol tinctures or supercritical CO2 extracts are needed for therapeutic dosing. The directionality is physicochemical property upstream of formulation requirement. Its lipophilicity also aids cell and mitochondrial membrane penetration, supporting SIRT3 engagement. This is a practical caveat for honokiol use.

Akt phosphorylates TFEB at serine 467, a C-terminal residue within the regulatory cluster that contributes to cytoplasmic retention of the transcription factor downstream of insulin and growth-factor signaling. By adding to the phosphorylation state of TFEB, Akt reinforces the anabolic, autophagy-suppressed state promoted by PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling. This modification complements mTORC1-mediated marks and integrates proliferative cues with repression of degradative transcription. The Akt-TFEB link embeds TFEB within the canonical survival signaling network.

Akt activates mTORC1 by phosphorylating and inhibiting the TSC1/TSC2 complex (and PRAS40), thereby increasing Rheb-GTP and relieving the upstream brake on mTORC1. This places mTORC1 squarely downstream of the PI3K-Akt growth-factor signaling axis that promotes anabolism and suppresses autophagy. Akt-dependent mTORC1 activation is a hallmark of insulin/IGF-1 action and of many cancers with PI3K pathway mutations. The Akt-mTORC1 link is the principal route by which fed-state signals inhibit autophagic degradation.
AKT phosphorylates Caspase-9 at Ser196 (human specific), suppressing caspase activity in prostate and colon cancer cells.
AKT phosphorylates XIAP at Ser87, preventing ubiquitination and degradation, promoting tumor survival in ovarian cancer cells.

Caspase-3 is activated by Caspase-9. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. Caspase-9 is the mitochondrial initiator caspase activated by the apoptosome to launch the execution phase. The directionality runs from Caspase-9 toward Caspase-3, so Caspase-9 is the active agent and Caspase-3 the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Caspase-3 is activated by Caspase-8. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. Caspase-8 is the initiator caspase of the extrinsic pathway and also gates the intrinsic pathway through Bid cleavage. The directionality runs from Caspase-8 toward Caspase-3, so Caspase-8 is the active agent and Caspase-3 the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Caspase-3 cleaves PARP1. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. PARP1 is a DNA-damage-sensing poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase whose cleavage by caspase-3 inactivates repair and conserves energy for apoptosis. The relationship is directional, with Caspase-3 acting as the operative agent upon PARP1 rather than the reverse. The directness of this molecular event makes it a precise, often druggable point of control whose perturbation can decisively shift cell fate in cancer.

Caspase-3 cleaves Lamins. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. Lamins are the intermediate-filament proteins of the nuclear lamina whose cleavage by caspases drives nuclear collapse during apoptosis. The relationship is directional, with Caspase-3 acting as the operative agent upon Lamins rather than the reverse. The directness of this molecular event makes it a precise, often druggable point of control whose perturbation can decisively shift cell fate in cancer.

Caspase-3 cleaves ICAD. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. ICAD is the inhibitor of caspase-activated DNase that, upon caspase-3 cleavage, releases CAD to fragment nuclear DNA. The relationship is directional, with Caspase-3 acting as the operative agent upon ICAD rather than the reverse. The directness of this molecular event makes it a precise, often druggable point of control whose perturbation can decisively shift cell fate in cancer.

Caspase-3 is inhibited by XIAP. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. XIAP is the most potent mammalian IAP, directly inhibiting caspases-9, -3, and -7 and stabilized by survival kinases. The directionality runs from XIAP toward Caspase-3, so XIAP is the active agent and Caspase-3 the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

Caspase-3 is suppressed by p38 MAPK. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. p38 MAPK is a stress-activated kinase that can both promote and suppress apoptosis depending on context, including by phosphorylating caspases. The directionality runs from p38 MAPK toward Caspase-3, so p38 MAPK is the active agent and Caspase-3 the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

Caspase-3 is enhanced by PKCδ. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. PKCδ is a protein kinase C isoform that can both enhance caspase-3 activity and, in some contexts, promote apoptotic signaling. The directionality runs from PKCδ toward Caspase-3, so PKCδ is the active agent and Caspase-3 the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Caspase-3 is induced by melittin. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. Melittin is the principal peptide of honeybee venom that permeabilizes membranes and suppresses oncogenic receptors and checkpoints. The directionality runs from melittin toward Caspase-3, so melittin is the active agent and Caspase-3 the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Caspase-3 is induced by Ivermectin. Caspase-3 is the principal executioner caspase that cleaves hundreds of substrates to produce the apoptotic phenotype. Ivermectin is an approved antiparasitic drug repurposed in oncology for its multi-kinase, anti-Wnt, and pro-death activities across cancers. The directionality runs from Ivermectin toward Caspase-3, so Ivermectin is the active agent and Caspase-3 the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

Neutrophils are white blood cells that generate large quantities of reactive oxygen species, primarily superoxide anion and hydroxyl radicals, during the respiratory burst that accompanies infection and inflammation. This burst is the basis of their microbicidal activity but also mediates non-specific oxidation reactions, including the conversion of epinephrine to adrenochrome both intracellularly and extracellularly. Neutrophil-derived oxidants also include hydrogen peroxide and products of myeloperoxidase. In the lungs and other tissues flooded by neutrophils during conditions such as pneumonia, ARDS, COPD exacerbations, and acute lung injury, this ROS production makes epinephrine-to-adrenochrome oxidation a prominent local reaction.

Neutrophils are white blood cells that produce oxygen radicals when stimulated and that infiltrate the myocardium following infarction or inflammation. Their infiltration brings the oxidant-generating machinery of these cells directly into heart tissue, creating local conditions under which adrenaline can be oxidized through the adrenochrome pathway. This is significant because the resulting oxidation products, adrenochrome and adrenolutin, have been implicated in cardiotoxicity, including cell necrosis, arrhythmias, and coronary artery constriction. The presence of neutrophils in the damaged heart therefore provides a mechanistic link between inflammation, oxidative stress, and catecholamine oxidation, supporting the hypothesis that the adrenochrome pathway contributes to stress-induced heart disease and offering a rationale for measuring oxidase activity in serum after myocardial infarction.

Neutrophils are polymorphonuclear leukocytes whose respiratory burst generates large amounts of reactive oxygen species, including superoxide and hydroxyl radicals. Both stimulated neutrophils and cell-free granulocyte homogenates oxidize epinephrine to adrenochrome through a radical chain process, and medium released from activated cells can oxidize adrenaline extracellularly. This oxidation can account for more than 80% of adrenaline breakdown in certain inflammatory conditions, far outpacing the normal enzymatic routes such as catechol-O-methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase. Superoxide dismutase and catalase inhibit the reaction, confirming its dependence on reactive oxygen species. This mechanism provides a cellular basis for adrenochrome formation wherever neutrophils accumulate.

Adrenaline catabolism in the presence of stimulated neutrophils is driven largely by the ROS these cells release. Studies from the 1980s showed that this ROS-mediated oxidation is the major catabolic pathway for adrenaline in neutrophils, accounting for over 80% of oxidation at low micromolar adrenaline concentrations, compared with the usual COMT/MAO pathways. Stimulated neutrophils (e.g., with latex beads or chemotactic peptides such as fMLP) rapidly oxidize adrenaline to adrenochrome, and cell-free medium from activated neutrophils retains this oxidizing ability, indicating that released factors drive the conversion.

Activated neutrophils generate superoxide radicals and other reactive oxygen species through their NADPH oxidase system, with myeloperoxidase also contributing. These oxidants drive the conversion of adrenaline to adrenochrome, and superoxide-derived ROS account for much of the adrenaline oxidation in the presence of stimulated neutrophils, representing over 80% of oxidation at low micromolar concentrations. Superoxide anion is also produced by oxyhemoglobin autoxidation, and its oxidation of epinephrine is a non-enzymatic route to adrenochrome that operates at sites of inflammation and oxidative stress.

Neutrophils are a well-documented cellular site of adrenochrome formation in humans. During inflammatory responses, activated neutrophils undergo a respiratory burst releasing reactive oxygen species that oxidize epinephrine to adrenochrome, both inside the cell and in the surrounding medium. In studied conditions this neutrophil-driven route can account for the majority (over 80%) of adrenaline oxidation, exceeding the enzymatic pathways of catechol-O-methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase. This makes adrenochrome production a feature of neutrophil-mediated oxidative stress in inflamed or infected tissues such as the lungs, heart, and synovial fluid, rather than a routine process in healthy non-inflamed conditions.

Mitochondria communicate stress to the nucleus through retrograde signaling pathways. In yeast this involves the Rtg1/Rtg3 transcription factors, whose activation extends replicative lifespan; in mammals the retrograde response involves calcineurin-dependent NF-kappaB activation and may include the Retinoid X receptor alpha, PGC-1alpha, JNK, and ROS generation. Mitochondrial perturbations such as mtDNA deletion, respiratory chain inhibition, misfolded matrix proteins, or stalled ribosomes all elicit coordinated changes in nuclear gene expression that reconfigure metabolism and induce cytoprotective programs.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Drivers Stem Cell Aging Inflammaging Bautista 2026.md
links.context: Mitochondrial dysfunction is not merely a hallmark of aging but an upstream driver of stem cell exhaustion and inflammaging, the chronic low-grade inflammation characteristic of aging. Mitochondrial damage is decoded as inflammation through cytosolic mtDNA activating cGAS-STING and NF-κB pathways, while dysfunctional mitochondria persisting due to defective mitophagy remain metabolically active yet generate excessive ROS that sustains SASP signaling. Mitochondrial lipid peroxidation byproducts (4-HNE, oxidized cardiolipin) further stimulate inflammatory pathways via toll-like receptors and inflammasomes.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Fusion and Fission The fine-tune balance for cellular homeostasis.md
links.context: Mitochondria arose through the endosymbiosis of an alpha-proteobacterium with an ancestral eukaryotic cell, an event that occurred approximately two billion years ago. During evolution, most of the bacterial genes were transferred to the host nuclear genome, and mitochondria retained only a small genome encoding a handful of respiratory chain subunits, rRNAs, and tRNAs. This evolutionary origin explains mitochondria's double membrane structure, their own circular mitochondrial DNA, and the presence of a mitochondrial targeting sequence on most nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins that directs their import. The endosymbiotic origin also underlies the ability of mitochondria to fuse and divide like their bacterial ancestors.

Mitochondria act as platforms for orchestrating innate immune responses to external threats. The MAVS protein, an outer mitochondrial membrane adaptor, binds retinoic-acid-inducible gene I-like receptors (RLRs) that sense viral RNA, self-propagates in a prion-like fashion, and recruits TRAF2, TRAF6, and RIPK1 to activate antiviral signaling. Additionally, mitochondrial ROS prime the NLRP3 inflammasome, whose activation leads to caspase-1 activation and proteolytic cleavage of pro-interleukin-1beta, linking mitochondrial stress to the inflammatory response.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: In senescent cells the mitochondrial pyruvate-citrate-acetyl-CoA axis is upregulated, increasing the availability of acetyl-CoA to support histone acetylation at SASP gene loci. Although acetyl-CoA can be generated from alternative sources such as acetate, fatty acid oxidation and amino acid metabolism, in senescent cells mitochondria constitute a dominant source of acetyl-CoA for chromatin modification, creating a dependence on mitochondrial acetyl-CoA to sustain epigenetic activation of inflammatory gene programmes. Pathways controlling cytosolic acetyl-CoA production, including mitochondrial citrate export and its conversion by ATP-citrate lyase, are upregulated during senescence.

links.relation: is the primary endogenous source of
links.context: Mitochondria are the primary endogenous source of reactive oxygen species, because electron leakage at Complex I and Complex III generates superoxide as an intrinsic cost of aerobic respiration. This positions mitochondria at the center of cellular redox biology. The directionality is respiratory-chain leak to superoxide formation. A caveat is that other organelles and enzymes (NOX, XO, peroxisomes) also produce ROS, so mitochondria are the largest but not the only source.

Amyloid-beta binds redox-active metals (Cu2+ and Fe3+), forming complexes that generate superoxide and H2O2 via Fenton-like chemistry at the metal site. This positions Abeta as a localized source of ROS in the Alzheimer brain. The directionality is metal binding to radical generation. A caveat is that metal-free Abeta aggregation also drives pathology, so redox activity is one of several toxic functions.

Amyloid-beta catalyzes hydrogen peroxide formation because Cu2+-bound Abeta reduces oxygen to H2O2 via Fenton-like chemistry at the metal-binding site. This makes Abeta plaques local ROS generators in the Alzheimer brain. The directionality is metal-bound peptide to H2O2 production. A caveat is that Abeta also promotes ROS through microglial activation and mitochondrial dysfunction, so catalyzed H2O2 is one of several sources.

Amyloid-beta impairs mitochondrial Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) after accumulating in mitochondria, depressing respiration and increasing electron leak. This links protein misfolding to bioenergetic failure and ROS. The directionality is Abeta mitochondrial localization to respiratory inhibition. A caveat is that Complex IV inhibition can be both a cause and consequence of oxidative damage in a feed-forward loop.

Amyloid-beta induces lipid peroxidation through metal-catalyzed ROS and through direct interactions with membranes, generating MDA and 4-HNE. These aldehydes then further compromise synapses and proteins. The directionality is Abeta-driven oxidation to membrane damage. A caveat is that lipid peroxidation products also feed back to stabilize Abeta aggregation, creating a vicious cycle.

Atypical dose-response curves where a drug's effect does not follow a monotonic shape are referred to as hormetic or biphasic. This computational study shows that all hormetic networks share a similar core structure: an incoherent bivalent network motif centered on the target of the drug, in which the two interactions emanating from the target have net opposite (direct or indirect) effects over the downstream output. Around 18% of all three-node network topologies contain this motif, and topologies with an incoherent bivalent motif show a roughly five-fold increased probability of exhibiting hormesis compared with all topologies.

This study demonstrates that drug hormesis can be explained and predicted from network structure and should not be a cause for automatic rejection in the drug development pipeline. The two core ingredients are an incoherent bivalent network motif centered on the target of inhibition and an upstream (backward) interaction operating in the saturated enzymatic regime. Atypical dose-response curves are common among widely used drugs, including aspirin, heparin, progesterone, nicotinamide, metformin and curcumin, and understanding how the complex behavior arises allows definition of an optimal dose or strategy to benefit from the nonlinearity rather than discarding the drug.

The study screened 5346 possible three-node network topologies of a coarse-grained signaling cascade model using a high-throughput computational approach, with 5000 parameter sets and 30 inhibitor concentrations per topology. More than 500 topologies show clear non-monotonic dose-response curves, and hormesis is favored in networks with a high number of repressing interactions on average, with the highest fraction of hormetic parameter sets in a topology composed of four repressing interactions. The probability of hormesis increases as the network becomes more complex, indicating it depends on the density and complexity of the network.

The hormesis exhibited by rapamycin is proposed to arise from a network topology that resembles an incoherent bivalent motif centered in its target mTORC1. In this architecture mTORC1 has a dual role: it is the target of rapamycin inhibition and simultaneously feeds an indirect activating path (via IRS1/S6K negative feedback and PI3K) toward the output mTORC2, yielding two net-opposite influences over the output. This topology induces biphasic dose-responses with high probability, and the backward reaction of the motif has a low Michaelis-Menten constant, consistent with the general rules identified in the coarse-grained screening.

links.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
links.context: The ATM-TRAF6-TAK1 axis drives ASAP signaling: ATM activates TRAF6, which undergoes auto-ubiquitination and recruits TAK1 to propagate stress and inflammatory signals. TAK1 in turn activates p38 MAPK and NF-κB downstream, linking DNA damage sensing to SASP transcription. This axis is a conserved scaffold connecting genotoxic stress to senescence inflammation. It operates upstream of the established SASP regulatory network.

links.source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
links.context: p38 MAPK phosphorylates TFEB at serine 211, the same residue targeted by mTORC1, thereby promoting cytoplasmic retention under certain stress conditions. This convergence indicates that both growth-factor (mTORC1) and stress (p38) signaling can independently restrain TFEB nuclear entry. The p38-mediated phosphorylation underscores the role of stress-activated MAPK pathways in modulating degradative transcription. Context determines whether p38 signaling suppresses or, at other sites, activates TFEB.

links.source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
links.context: In contrast to its S211 effect, p38 MAPK phosphorylates TFEB at serine 401 in a manner that promotes nuclear translocation in specific cell types such as monocytes. This site-specific divergence illustrates that p38 can either retain or activate TFEB depending on cell context and the constellation of concurrent modifications. Such opposing outcomes highlight the combinatorial code by which multiple phosphorylations determine TFEB localization. The monocyte-specific response implicates TFEB in immune cell activation and inflammatory programs.

p38 MAPK activates NF-κB-mediated SASP independently of the DDR, having been the first kinase shown to drive this axis. It does so through TAK1 and downstream IKK activation that liberates NF-κB. This provides a stress-responsive, DDR-independent route to SASP transcription. The p38-NF-κB link is a conserved, druggable module in senescence.

p38 MAPK stabilizes SASP transcripts, particularly in the tumor microenvironment, by promoting mRNA stability and preventing decay of SASP mRNAs. Together with its activation of NF-κB, this sustains the secretome over time. p38 MAPK inhibition reduces SASP from aged fibroblasts, validating its stabilizing role. The stabilization complements transcriptional activation to maintain robust SASP output.

p38 MAPK is inhibited by SB203580, a classical pyridinyl imidazole inhibitor that suppresses p38alpha/beta and thereby reduces SASP from fibroblasts of older donors. By blocking p38, SB203580 lowers NF-κB activation and SASP transcript stabilization. This provides a tool compound validating p38 as a senomorphic target. The inhibition is specific and well characterized in cellular models.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: p38 MAPK phosphorylates caspase-3 at Ser150, suppressing its proteolytic activity; this inhibition is reversed by the phosphatase PP2A. The directionality is p38 upstream of caspase-3 inhibition. This provides a survival signal that tempers apoptosis under certain stresses. It shows stress kinases can directly restrain executioner caspases.

Human growth hormone (HGH) is widely used for rejuvenation and longevity, yet it actually accelerates aging and shortens lifespan. Growth hormone is a pro-aging hormone because it indirectly activates mTOR, and the hype around growth hormone is based on a single publication that misinterpreted its acute effects. Unlike HGH, the anti-aging effects of rapamycin are not based on a single paper or a wild guess but on the work of thousands of scientists studying mTOR and its inhibitors in diverse organisms from yeast to humans.

Growth hormone (GH) is a peptide hormone that impacts the immune system via its stimulatory effects on insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). Hematopoietic cells can produce GH that indirectly promotes immune reconstitution via IGF-1 production, and IGF-1 provides anti-apoptotic signals and promotes immune cell survival. IGF-1 may also act directly on thymic stromal cells as a component of the thymus microenvironment cross-talk network and stimulate IL-7 production, and intrathymic IL-7 in turn promotes and regulates T cell survival and function.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: FPRL1, a seven-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor, was the first humanin receptor to be described. Humanin acts as an agonist for FPRL1 by inducing Ca2+ mobilization and rapid activation of ERK1/2 signaling, a commonly induced downstream pathway of G-protein-coupled receptors. In neuroblasts, both the 42-aa form of beta-amyloid peptide and humanin activate FPRL1, but only Abeta42 is cytotoxic, and this cytotoxicity is reversed by humanin, suggesting that the neuroprotective effects of humanin might be accomplished by competitively binding to FPRL1, which may contribute to its cytoprotective aspects.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: The second reported humanin receptor is a trimeric complex consisting of the ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor (CNTFR), the cytokine receptor WSX-1, and the transmembrane glycoprotein gp130. Hashimoto et al showed that humanin induces STAT3 activation, which was required for its neuroprotective effects. In vitro pulldown assays showed humanin coprecipitates with CNTFR and WSX-1 but not IL-6 receptor alpha, and knockdown of CNTFR or WSX-1 abolishes humanin-dependent cytoprotection against AD-related insults. Humanin also promotes hetero-oligomerization of CNTFR, WSX-1, and gp130, which relays signals through JAK/STAT and ERK1/2 pathways.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Humanin was cloned by a third group as a binding partner of Bax, a central pro-apoptotic protein that translocates to the mitochondria to initiate a cell death signal. The humanin-Bax complex is retained in the cytoplasm and this interaction protects cells from apoptosis. Humanin also prevents Bax translocation and activation in response to staurosporine, preventing the subsequent release of cytochrome c into the cytoplasm, and binds to Bax-like BH3 proteins Bid and BimEL, inhibiting their pro-apoptotic activity. Endogenous humanin suppresses tBID- and BimEL-induced apoptosis in vitro.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: A second group cloned humanin using a yeast two-hybrid screen as a partner of IGFBP3, and demonstrated that humanin binds to IGFBP3 with high affinity and specificity. IGFBP3 regulates IGF bioactivity and also induces apoptosis and inhibits cell growth independently of IGFs, and humanin protects against IGFBP3-induced apoptosis. Humanin does not interfere with IGF-I/IGFBP-3 binding but appears to bind to the heparin-binding domain of IGFBP-3, and a single amino acid substitution of alanine for phenylalanine at position 6 (F6AHN) abrogates IGFBP-3 binding.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Humanin levels decline with age, suggesting that a relative deficiency of humanin may be involved in metabolic diseases during aging. In one study, older mice had significantly reduced levels of circulating humanin (2 versus 13 months old), and rats had decreased levels of hypothalamic and skeletal muscle humanin (3 versus 24 months old). Circulating humanin levels also gradually decline with age in humans (45-65 versus 66-80 versus 81-100 years old), and plasma humanin levels significantly decreased with age in healthy volunteers. This decline parallels the age-related increase in risk for diseases humanin protects against.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Peripheral intravenous and central intra-cerebro-ventricular infusion of humanin and its derivatives F6AHN, HNG, and HNGF6A significantly improve overall insulin sensitivity, mediated in part by hypothalamic STAT3 activation in rats. The enhanced insulin sensitivity was coupled with a significant reduction of hepatic glucose production together with increased peripheral glucose uptake, raising the rate of glucose infusion in euglycemic clamp studies. A single treatment with the highly-potent analog HNGF6A normalizes blood glucose levels in Zucker diabetic fatty rats, a model of type 2 diabetes.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Humanin is the first small peptide of a putative set of mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs), a novel concept that challenges the traditional view of mitochondria as passive end-function organelles. It was discovered in 2001 by screening a cDNA library from the surviving fraction of an Alzheimer's disease patient brain for clones protecting neuronal cells from cell death induced by APP mutants, and identified as a 75bp open reading frame yielding a 24 amino acid peptide encoded within the mitochondrial 16S rRNA. Humanin is a harbinger of additional MDPs, as numerous putative ORFs are dispersed throughout the mitochondrial genome.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Mitochondria communicate back to the cell through processes collectively referred to as retrograde signaling, and traditionally described means include Ca2+, cytochrome c, and ROS. Mitochondrial-derived peptides such as humanin are recently identified retrograde signals that are unique in that they are encoded within the mitochondrial genome sequences, unlike other retrograde molecules which are nuclear-encoded. Humanin functions as both an endocrine factor and an intracellular survival factor with several biological roles regulating cell survival and metabolism, and retrograde signaling is a biological process well conserved from simple yeast to humans.

Humanin is a peptide of approximately 24 amino acids believed to derive from a short, cryptic open reading frame within the mitochondrial 16S rRNA gene, and it was the first identified mammalian mitokine. Originally isolated as a protective factor against familial Alzheimer's disease, humanin circulates in plasma and exerts cytoprotective and metabolic effects in various experimental paradigms. It is considered the founding member of a class of mitochondrially-derived peptides (MDPs) causing systemic effects in mammals.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: The mitochondrial origin of humanin is supported by strong circumstantial evidence, though still debated. Northern blot analysis using the humanin ORF as a probe showed hybridization to total RNA from HeLa cells identical in size to mitochondrial 16S rRNA, whereas RNA from rho0 HeLa cells lacking mtDNA showed no significant hybridization. Formylated humanin has enhanced activity by increasing affinity to FPRL1, and N-terminal formylation is a hallmark of mitochondrially encoded proteins. However, NUMTs reflecting humanin sequences are found in chromosomes 1-13 with varying homology, so a NUMT-derived humanin has not been ruled out.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: The humanin peptide sequence has been proposed to contain a pseudo-signal peptide, and when transfected into neuronal cells humanin is detected in the culture medium, indicating a secretory capacity that is blocked by inhibition of ER-golgi transport processes. Humanin is secreted from cells and found in circulation (plasma) as well as bound to cellular membranes, and its actions are thought to be mediated by specific receptors. This endocrine mode of action distinguishes humanin from other stress-induced mitochondrial retrograde signals, which are cell-autonomous, and supports its role as a non-autonomous signaling factor.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Humanin modulates oxidative stress and apoptosis in the developing plaque to protect endothelial function and prevent atherosclerosis. Lerman and colleagues treated ApoE-deficient mice fed a high cholesterol diet with the humanin analogue HNGF6A for 16 weeks and showed a dramatic decrease of atherosclerotic plaque size, preserved endothelial function, and improved expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase in the aorta. Anti-oxidative stress, anti-apoptosis, and preservation of eNOS are mechanisms partially responsible for the protection against atherosclerosis by humanin.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Humanin's cytoprotective effects were first tested and confirmed in vitro against mutant forms of APP and presenilin 1 and 2 which cause familial AD. F11 neuronal cells were challenged by transfecting APP or PS1/2 cDNA or treating with Abeta1-43, and humanin effectively protected neuronal cells from these FAD-related toxicities as shown by trypan blue exclusion and WST-8 assays. Humanin also protects against Abeta25-35 cell death and behavioral deficits, scopolamine-induced memory loss, H2O2-induced cell death in cortical neurons, serum starvation-induced apoptosis, and CoCl2-induced apoptosis in retinal ganglion cells.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Humanin improves glucose tolerance and delays the onset of diabetes in NOD mice, a model of type 1 diabetes involving progressive accumulation of lymphocytes within the pancreatic islets of Langerhans. In NOD mouse pancreata, humanin treatment dramatically suppressed inflammation and lymphocyte infiltration. Furthermore, humanin decreases serum starvation- and cytokine-induced apoptosis in the pancreatic beta-cell line NIT-1, protecting against the IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, and IFN-gamma released by T cells and activated macrophages, in an ERK- and STAT3-dependent manner, suggesting it may be a therapeutic target for type 1 diabetes.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Humanin was originally discovered in 2001 by screening a cDNA library created from the surviving fraction of an Alzheimer's disease patient brain, using unbiased functional screening for clones that protect neuronal cells from cell death induced by amyloid precursor protein (APP) mutants associated with early-onset familial AD. The term humanin was coined by its discoverer, Professor Nishimoto, to denote the potential of this molecule to restore the humanity of patients with Alzheimer's disease. Humanin protects against Abeta25-35-induced cell death, behavioral deficits, and memory impairment in mice, and is protective in 3xTg-AD triple-transgenic AD mice, with cell surface receptor FPRL1 linked to AD-related cytoprotection.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Several laboratories have tested the protective effect of humanin on various types of stress or disease states, including myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury in mice and cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury in rats, as well as focal cerebral ischemia in mice as a stroke model. Humanin also protects against familial ALS in mice expressing mutant SOD1, dexamethasone-induced apoptosis in rat Leydig cells, and IGFBP-3-induced apoptosis in cerebral endothelial cells. Many of these stressors and models have oxidative stress as a common mechanistic denominator, suggesting a specific oxidative-insult-related cytoprotective role of humanin.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Humanin restores ATP levels in lymphocytes from MELAS patients, preventing them from falling into energy deficiency. MELAS is a mitochondrial disorder strongly associated with the A3243G mutant mitochondrial DNA, a location immediately downstream of the 16S rRNA locus, and MELAS patients have defective ATP synthesis which causes tissue damage especially in high-energy-demand tissues. Notably, humanin levels are considerably elevated in skeletal muscles of patients with MELAS and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, likely because the stress conferred by these pathological states induces elevated humanin levels.

links.source_file: _document_ - Humanin a harbinger of mitochondrial-derived peptides?.md
links.context: Mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs) are small peptides encoded within the mitochondrial genome in addition to the canonical 13 protein-coding mitochondrial genes. In theory, mtDNA could contain hundreds of short open reading frames that encode putative microproteins, and the mitochondrial transcriptome includes many discrete smaller mRNAs that do not map to traditional protein-encoding genes, particularly from the 16S rRNA region including the site of the humanin ORF. There is compelling evidence of biologically active peptides of 11-32 amino acids encoded by small open reading frames from polycistronic mRNA, supporting the concept of genes-within-genes in the compact mitochondrial genome.

Mitokines are soluble factors released by stressed mitochondria that communicate mitochondrial stress status to distal tissues, enabling cell-non-autonomous regulation of stress responses and lifespan. In C. elegans, knockdown of the cytochrome c oxidase component cco-1 in the brain activates the UPRmt response in the intestine and extends lifespan, implying that stressed mitochondria in the nervous system release signals that modulate stress defenses elsewhere in the soma. This allows mitochondria in one tissue to act as sensors of overall metabolic status for the entire organism.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Drivers Stem Cell Aging Inflammaging Bautista 2026.md
links.context: Somatic mtDNA mutations accumulate with age due to high replication frequency, proximity to mitochondrial ROS, and relatively inefficient DNA repair compared to nuclear DNA. This mutational burden can be framed both as a hallmark of aging (clonal mosaicism and rising heteroplasmy in aged tissues) and as a driver of stem cell aging by inducing respiratory insufficiency that feeds into inflammatory signaling and durable metabolic-epigenetic reprogramming. Compromised electron transport shifts availability of epigenetically active metabolites (alpha-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, acetyl-CoA) that gate chromatin-modifying enzymes, reshaping stem cell fate decisions.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: In senescence and ageing, mitochondrial dysfunction promotes the cytosolic release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which activates cGAS-STING signalling and drives inflammatory responses and the SASP. Cytosolic mtDNA levels were unchanged in senescent MRC5 and IMR90 fibroblasts following SLC25A1 inhibition, indicating that metabolic regulation of histone acetylation restrains SASP independently of mtDNA release. STING inhibition with SN011 suppresses SASP gene expression without affecting histone acetylation, showing that mtDNA-driven innate immune signalling and mitochondrial control of histone acetylation are independent but complementary inputs that converge to enable full SASP expression.

Mitochondrial DNA is particularly susceptible to oxidative DNA damage because it lies near the electron-transport chain, lacks protective histones, and has limited repair capacity relative to nuclear DNA. This makes mtDNA a sensitive early marker of mitochondrial oxidant stress. The directionality is proximity to ROS source to increased lesion frequency. A caveat is that mtDNA damage can also arise from replication errors and base-excision-repair intermediates, so ROS is a major but not exclusive cause.

IDO2, a less active paralog of IDO1, may compete for heme and act as a negative regulator in some settings. Both are heme-dependent dioxygenases functionally related to TDO (tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase, mainly hepatic). The existence of these compensatory pathways is a major challenge for IDO1-targeted therapy, as IDO2 and TDO can partially substitute for IDO1 in maintaining tryptophan catabolism and immunosuppression. This isospecificity issue, along with context-specific effects, has contributed to the mixed results of IDO1 inhibitor trials in immuno-oncology, where single-target blockade may be insufficient to relieve metabolic immunosuppression.

Interleukin 22, an IL-10 gene family member produced by T helper 17 cells and innate lymphoid cell subsets, signals through the IL-22 receptor on the surface of thymic epithelial cells and promotes the proliferation and survival of thymocytes. Dudakov et al. showed that IL-22 administration to wild-type mice after total body irradiation significantly increases thymic cellularity, including both developing thymocytes and TEC subsets, and that immune recovery in irradiated IL-22-deficient mice is impaired.

Thymic epithelial cells produce a number of colony stimulating factors and hematopoietic cytokines, including IL-1, IL-3, IL-6, IL-7, TGF-β, oncostatin M, and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF). Intrathymic and systemic production of these cytokines and growth factors regulates the complex process of thymopoiesis and is responsible for stromal cross-talk within the thymic microenvironment. IL-7 in particular is a crucial cytokine for thymocyte survival and T cell development, making the thymic cytokine milieu a candidate target for therapies aimed at reversing age-induced thymic involution. Loss of TEC-derived IL-7 production with age contributes to declining thymic output.

Thymic epithelial cells (TECs) in the cortex and medulla form a complex network that supports T cell differentiation, providing the essential microenvironment for productive thymopoiesis. The thymus consists of cells of stromal and hematopoietic origin, including TECs, mesenchymal cells (fibroblasts), endothelial cells and dendritic cells. Differentiating thymocytes migrate from the cortico-medullary junction through the cortex and back to the medulla, encountering functionally distinct microenvironments that regulate positive and negative selection.

Interleukin 7 is a 25 kDa glycoprotein produced by stromal cells in the thymus and bone marrow that promotes both survival and differentiation of immature triple-negative and mature single-positive thymocytes. IL-7 binds the IL-7 receptor expressed on lymphoid precursors (CD3-CD4-CD8-), double-positive CD4+CD8+ thymocytes, and single-positive CD4 or CD8 T cells. Schluns et al. demonstrated that IL-7 administration to non-lymphopenic mice expands naive and memory peripheral CD4 and CD8 T cells, and treatment with IL-7 restores thymopoiesis in IL-7-deficient mice. Recombinant human IL-7 (CYT 99 007) showed low toxicity and dose-dependent expansion of naive and memory T cells in patients.

In the periphery, IL-7 regulates T cell survival and function. IL-7 binds the IL-7 receptor expressed on many immune cells, including lymphoid precursors, double-positive thymocytes, and single-positive CD4 or CD8 T cells, promoting survival and differentiation of immature triple-negative and mature single-positive thymocytes. The IL-7 receptor is a target for therapeutic intervention, particularly for restoring T cells in subjects undergoing T cell-depleting regimens.

mTORC1, the complex formed when mTOR binds to raptor, activates the ribosomal protein S6 kinases S6K1/S6K2 (S6K1/2) by phosphorylation. Active S6K1/2 in turn inactivates IRS1 by phosphorylation, forming a negative feedback loop that regulates insulin signaling, and also deactivates mTORC2. In the mass-action model of the mTOR-PI3K pathway, the Michaelis-Menten constant for the activation of S6K1/2 by mTORC1 is significantly smaller on average than other pathway constants, correlating with the low backward-reaction constant that increases the rate of hormesis in rapamycin-treated networks.

links.source_file: _document_ - Rapamycin for longevity the pros, the cons, and future perspectives.md
links.context: mTORC1, the master kinase within the mTOR pathway, normally inhibits autophagy by phosphorylating components of the Unc-51-like autophagy-activating kinase 1 (ULK1) complex. When rapamycin inhibits mTORC1, this suppression is removed and autophagosome formation is initiated, activating the cellular recycling process that degrades protein aggregates and damaged organelles. This relief of autophagy inhibition is central to rapamycin's proposed geroprotective mechanism, maintaining proteostasis and reducing 'toxic burden' in post-mitotic cells, though the longevity claims derived from this pathway in online anti-aging contexts are not based in formal geroscience and lack precise biolo...

mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 211 in the presence of nutrients and growth factors, creating a binding site for 14-3-3 proteins. This phosphorylation event is the principal mechanism by which mTORC1 retains TFEB in the cytosol and prevents its nuclear translocation under fed conditions. S211 phosphorylation thus links nutrient abundance directly to repression of the lysosomal-autophagic transcriptional program. Relief of this phosphorylation during starvation is required for TFEB to enter the nucleus and activate clearance genes.

mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 122, an additional N-terminal regulatory site that contributes to cytoplasmic retention of the transcription factor under nutrient-rich conditions. Alongside S142 and S211, S122 forms part of the multi-site phosphorylation code through which mTORC1 enforces TFEB exclusion from the nucleus. Dephosphorylation of these sites by phosphatases such as PP2A is required for nuclear translocation. The multiplicity of mTORC1 sites provides tunable, robust control of lysosomal gene transcription.

mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 138, a residue also modified by GSK3β, and this phosphorylation promotes nuclear export of TFEB, complementing the cytosolic retention imposed at other sites. The accumulation of phosphates across the N-terminal regulatory region collectively suppresses TFEB transcriptional activity. Relief of S138 phosphorylation facilitates nuclear accumulation and activation of the autophagy-lysosomal program. This site therefore participates in the coordinated mTORC1 restraint of cellular clearance.

mTORC1 is recruited to the lysosomal surface, where it encounters its activator Rheb and receives upstream amino-acid and growth-factor inputs necessary for full activation. This spatial recruitment, mediated by Rag GTPases and the Ragulator scaffold, converts the lysosome into the signaling platform for mTORC1. Only when docked at the lysosome can mTORC1 efficiently phosphorylate its substrates, including TFEB and ULK1. Thus lysosomal localization is essential for mTORC1 function and for its inhibition of autophagy.

mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at both serine 142 and serine 211, two residues whose combined modification enforces 14-3-3 binding and robust cytosolic retention of the transcription factor. These sites act synergistically to prevent TFEB nuclear entry and thus block activation of the autophagy-lysosomal program under nutrient-replete conditions. Dephosphorylation of both marks is required for full TFEB activation during starvation. The dual-site control exemplifies the redundancy mTORC1 employs to firmly suppress degradative transcription.

mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) is composed of five core subunits: the catalytic kinase mTOR, the scaffold Raptor (which binds substrates and Rag GTPases), mLST8 (stabilizing the kinase domain), the inhibitory subunit PRAS40, and the negative regulator Deptor. This stoichiometric assembly defines mTORC1's substrate specificity and its sensitivity to upstream inputs such as amino acids and insulin. Raptor is essential for recruitment of mTORC1 to lysosomes and for phosphorylation of canonical substrates like S6K1 and 4E-BP1. The composition distinguishes mTORC1 from mTORC2, which shares mTOR, mLST8, and Deptor but includes Rictor instead of Raptor.

mTORC1 promotes cap-dependent protein synthesis by phosphorylating the eukaryotic initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1), releasing eIF4E to initiate translation, and by phosphorylating S6 kinase 1 (S6K1), which enhances ribosome biogenesis and translational capacity. These outputs prioritize anabolic processes when nutrients and growth factors are plentiful. The stimulation of protein synthesis is a major consumer of cellular energy and amino acids, balanced against the catabolic program of autophagy. Dysregulated mTORC1-driven translation contributes to hypertrophy and malignancy.

mTORC1 promotes lipid and cholesterol synthesis by activating the sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBP1) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ), transcription factors that drive expression of lipogenic and adipogenic enzymes. This anabolic output supports membrane biogenesis and energy storage during growth. The lipid-synthetic program is coordinated with mTORC1's stimulation of protein and nucleotide synthesis to build cellular mass. Its dysregulation contributes to hepatic steatosis and metabolic syndrome.

mTORC1 phosphorylates TFE3 at serine 321, an analog of the TFEB S211 site, thereby promoting cytosolic retention and inhibiting TFE3's transcriptional activity under nutrient-replete conditions. This parallel modification ensures that both MiT/TFE family master regulators are coordinately repressed by mTORC1. Upon starvation or mTORC1 inhibition, dephosphorylation permits TFE3 nuclear entry and activation of lysosomal genes. The conserved regulatory logic highlights the unified control of the degradative program.

Under nutrient-rich conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1 at Ser757, disrupting its interaction with AMPK and suppressing autophagy. The directionality is mTORC1 upstream of ULK1 inhibition. This couples nutrient abundance to autophagic restraint. Sirtuin/AMPK activation opposes mTORC1 to relicense ULK1.

IRS1 is the upstream insulin receptor substrate in the mTOR-PI3K signaling cascade: the IRS receptor upstream of the pathway is activated by binding reversibly to insulin, and active IRS1 promotes the activation of PI3K by phosphorylation. PI3K in turn activates mTORC2 by phosphorylation and activates IRS1 indirectly via AKT, forming a positive feedback loop. Active IRS1 is inactivated by phosphorylation by S6K1/2, closing a negative feedback arm. IRS1 therefore sits at the hub of the incoherent bivalent motif, and the backward reaction from the target toward IRS1 is central to the hormetic response.

Dietary isoleucine correlates with body mass index in humans, and increased circulating isoleucine is associated with increased mortality risk. In Western diet-fed mice, increasing dietary isoleucine promotes weight gain, fat accretion, glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance. In contrast, isoleucine restriction consistently improves metabolic health across dietary contexts and age groups, extends lifespan of both Drosophila and mice, reduces frailty and increases healthspan, rejuvenates aged mice at the molecular level, induces substantial epigenetic changes, and improves Alzheimer's disease outcomes in male mice. Isoleucine is described as an exceptionally powerful modifier of the hallmarks of protein restriction.

Keratinocyte growth factor (KGF, FGF7) signaling through FGFR2IIIb is critical for fetal thymus organogenesis and linked to proliferation and differentiation of fetal and postnatal thymic epithelial cells. KGF administration is well-documented to increase thymus size, TEC differentiation, and thymocyte production in aged animals. Min and colleagues showed that a single course of KGF treatment increases thymic cellularity in aged mice, maintained for two months, with restoration of cortical and medullary compartments, increased naive CD4 T cell output, and increased humoral responses to a T-dependent antigen.

The thymus is a vital organ for homeostatic maintenance of the peripheral immune system. Within its two compartments, the true thymic epithelial space (TES, comprising cortex and medulla) and the perivascular space (PVS), T cells develop, mature, and undergo induction of self-tolerance in a process called thymopoiesis. The cortex hosts early thymocyte development including T cell receptor gene rearrangement and positive selection, while the medulla carries out negative selection to remove autoreactive T cells. The perivascular space, composed of adipocytes, peripheral lymphocytes and stroma, is a non-thymopoietic component.

The thymus exhibits profound age-associated involution, a striking paradoxical feature of this critical lymphoid tissue. Thymic function begins to decrease from the first year of life; the lymphoid component of the thymic epithelial space involutes roughly 3% per year through middle age (35-45 years) and about 1% per year thereafter, while the perivascular space expands with adipocytes and peripheral lymphocytes. By age 70, the TES falls below 10% of total thymus tissue. Although thymic decline is of minimal consequence to healthy individuals, the reduced efficacy of the aging immune system has direct etiological links with opportunistic infections, autoimmunity, and cancer burden.

Kynurenine and its derivatives activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), promoting regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation and suppressing effector T/NK cells. This metabolite-driven AhR signaling is the second major mechanism of IDO1-mediated immunosuppression alongside local tryptophan depletion, and together they create an immunosuppressive microenvironment in tissues such as tumors, placenta and inflamed sites. The context-dependent nature of this pathway is notable: it is protective via tolerance induction in autoimmunity but potentially detrimental when overactive in metabolic inflammation, where elevated KP activity links to insulin resistance and chronic low-grade inflammation.

Downstream of IDO1, the kynurenine pathway (KP) leads to metabolites including kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine, quinolinic acid (a neurotoxin and NAD+ precursor), and ultimately NAD+. The KP accounts for about 95% of tryptophan degradation outside protein synthesis and serotonin production, making it the dominant route of tryptophan-to-NAD+ flux. Both type 1 and type 2 diabetes show disrupted NAD+ homeostasis, with the KP (via IDO1/TDO) being a major Trp-to-NAD+ route. This positions IDO1 at the intersection of metabolism, immunity and inflammation, integrating tryptophan availability with immune modulation and NAD+ biosynthesis.

The kynurenine pathway leads to metabolites including kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine, quinolinic acid (a neurotoxin and NAD+ precursor), and ultimately NAD+. Because the pathway accounts for approximately 95% of tryptophan degradation outside protein synthesis and serotonin production, its flux through IDO1 and TDO substantially shapes systemic NAD+ levels and neuroactive metabolite balance. KP dysregulation is implicated in neurodegeneration, depression, chronic inflammation, and infections (e.g., HIV modulates IDO1), in part because of the neuroactive and excitotoxic properties of kynurenine and quinolinic acid. This links IDO1 activity to both metabolic and neurological outcomes.

Leucine is a potent activator of the master nutrient sensor mTORC1 and stimulates skeletal muscle anabolism. Leucine signals to mTORC1 in specific neurons by binding to and activating a voltage-gated calcium channel (Cav3.1). In humans, leucine supplementation increases muscle protein synthesis but does not improve muscle function, and its effects on fat mass are mixed. Leucine's cardiovascular effects are divergent: some studies show supplementation accelerates atherosclerotic plaque progression in an mTORC1-dependent manner and its metabolite isovaleric acid accelerates atrial fibrillation, while others report improved vascular function. Notably, leucine supplementation does not extend mouse lifespan, suggesting changes in leucine are unlikely to be responsible for protein restriction benefits.

Luteinizing hormone releasing hormone (LHRH) analogues achieve pharmacological sex steroid ablation and are a clinically tolerable alternative to surgical castration. Agents such as Lupron (leuprolide) act on the pituitary gland, desensitizing LHRH receptors and thereby decreasing luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, leading to reduced estrogen and testosterone production. Human studies with LHRH analogues have resulted in increased thymic weight and reversal of age-related thymic structural defects.

Sex steroid ablation (SSA), accomplished surgically or with LHRH analogue administration, is a long-standing strategy for thymic rejuvenation. Mice castrated before puberty show delayed thymic atrophy; removal of sex steroids after puberty restores thymic architecture, increases thymic cellularity and enhances thymopoiesis in aged mice and humans. The number of early thymic progenitors, which decrease with age, is normalized after surgical castration. Thymic regeneration following castration is reversed in a dose-dependent manner by administration of testosterone or estrogen, indicating that sex steroids are primary drivers of thymic involution.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol A Review.md
links.context: Magnolol is the structural analog of honokiol, both being lipid-soluble polyphenolic lignans from Magnolia species. The two compounds show broadly overlapping pharmacology - both are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors, inhibit NMDA receptor signaling and NF-kappaB activation, protect neurons against beta-amyloid toxicity, and reduce inflammatory pain - but magnolol is generally slightly less potent or less selective, particularly for NMDA-driven responses where honokiol shows greater selectivity. The structural homology with the anesthetic propofol likely explains some shared pharmacologic actions.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
links.context: Mdivi-1 (mitochondrial division inhibitor 1), a quinazolinone derivative that specifically inhibits DRP1, attenuates cardiac dysfunction in diverse mouse cardiomyopathy models, likely by promoting mitochondrial elongation or reducing autophagy. It also attenuates neuronal cell death through mitochondrial elongation and inhibition of complex I activity and ROS generation in neurodegenerative disease models including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. However, treatment of myocardial infarction in pigs with Mdivi-1 did not reduce infarct size or preserve cardiac function, and Mdivi-1 has off-target effects such as cleaving L-OPA1 and altering OXPHOS complex protein expression.

Melatonin is described as a critical, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant whose endogenous production is maximized by ensuring complete darkness during sleep. Circadian alignment and sleep hygiene are presented as high-impact behaviors supporting the mitohormesis protocol, since deep sleep is when cellular repair and neural recovery occur. The document ties melatonin production to sleep quality, which in turn determines overnight HRV and recovery capacity, completing the loop between circadian biology, antioxidant defenses, and mitochondrial adaptation.

Melatonin is an alternative anti-inflammatory agent for slow COMT individuals because it is not a catechol and does not donate methyl groups nor inhibit COMT, so it leaves catecholamine metabolism undisturbed. Its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions operate through melatonin receptors and redox pathways. This makes it a safe option where methyl burden or COMT interaction is a concern.

Over 150 million people take metformin for adult-onset type II diabetes, and evidence supports mild inhibition of the mitochondrial electron transport chain as one key element of its beneficial actions, making it a clinically deployed example of mitohormesis. Metformin use correlates with a rise in circulating GDF15, a mitokine linked to the therapeutic weight loss seen in patients. Association studies suggest reduced incidence of age-related cancers and Alzheimer's disease, demonstrating the potential to exploit mitohormesis for therapeutic benefit in aging and age-related diseases.

Metformin extends lifespan not only in mice but also in worms, which do not suffer from human diseases, making it a conventional drug that can be viewed as somewhat anti-aging. It is indicated to treat type 2 diabetes as well as pre-diabetes, obesity, metabolic syndrome, cancer and polycystic ovary syndrome, and metformin may counteract rapamycin-induced hyperglycemia. The anti-aging formula can combine metformin, aspirin, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and PDE5 inhibitors, each of which prevents or treats more than one age-related disease.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
links.context: Metformin, a first-line treatment for diabetes, prevents the progression of heart failure and improves left ventricular function by activating AMPK and PGC-1alpha within the mitochondrial dynamics regulation pathway. It thereby modulates fusion/fission balance in the failing heart. Beyond metformin, other drugs such as melatonin and liraglutide reduce cardiac fibrosis, inflammatory responses and myocardial death by promoting mitophagy, while valsartan inhibits Parkin activity or mitophagy, alleviating left ventricular hypertrophy and increasing mitochondrial biogenesis in experimental hypertension.

Metformin is believed to exert its anti-diabetic effects through inhibition of complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, a mild perturbation of mitochondrial function that may generate a hormetic (mitohormetic) signal. In mice and lower organisms, metformin treatment induces increased oxidant defenses and extends lifespan, suggesting that gentle inhibition of mitochondrial function can trigger beneficial adaptive stress responses. This positions metformin as a potential prototype for drugs that exploit mitohormesis to treat age-related disease.

Metformin, a widely used antidiabetic drug and repurposable agent, reduces the SASP without causing substantial cytotoxicity to senescent cells, holding potential as a senomorphic agent. In this study, metformin-involving assays phenocopied those derived from apigenin: metformin lowered cancer cell malignancy by downregulating the activity of senescent stromal cell conditioned medium, indicating a common pattern shared by both agents. This supports the broader concept that pharmacologically targeting SASP development with senomorphic agents can deprive cancer cells of stroma-conferred gain-of-function phenotypes, specifically chemoresistance, and suggests strategies to improve the...

links.source_file: _document_ - Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Aging.md
links.context: Metformin has been shown to decrease circulating advanced glycation end products in patients with diabetes, as well as to decrease the activity of NF-kB. In a study of 22 women with polycystic ovary disease, six months of metformin therapy resulted in a reduction of serum AGEs. As a widely used anti-diabetic drug, metformin's ability to lower circulating AGEs offers an additional explanation for some of its beneficial metabolic and vascular effects beyond glycemic control. These observations position metformin among pharmacological agents studied as blockers of AGE formation or action.

links.source_file: _document_ - Autophagy takes it all – autophagy inducers target immune aging.md
links.context: Metformin, the first-line type 2 diabetes drug, activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) primarily by inhibiting mitochondrial respiratory complex I, which mildly elevates the cellular AMP/ATP ratio. Activated AMPK phosphorylates downstream targets that restore energy homeostasis, including TSC2 and Raptor, which in turn suppress mTORC1. This indirect, energy-stress-mediated activation distinguishes metformin from direct AMPK agonists and underlies many of its metabolic benefits. AMPK activation by metformin also accounts for its autophagy-inducing and potential anti-aging effects.

Metformin induces autophagy by activating AMPK and thereby inhibiting mTORC1, relieving the brake on the autophagic machinery. In primary CD4+ T cells isolated from older individuals, metformin treatment restored autophagic flux, suggesting a mechanism to counter age-associated immune dysfunction. The induction is consistent with the drug's broader metabolic and putative longevity effects mediated through energy-sensing pathways. By enhancing autophagic clearance, metformin may reduce senescence-associated inflammation and improve cellular resilience.

links.source_file: _document_ - Autophagy takes it all – autophagy inducers target immune aging.md
links.context: Metformin reverses the pro-inflammatory Th17 CD4+ T cell profile toward a more juvenile, balanced phenotype, an effect attributed to enhancement of autophagic flux within lymphocytes. By activating AMPK and inducing autophagy, metformin reduces the mitochondrial and metabolic perturbations that favor pathogenic Th17 differentiation. This phenotypic rebalancing may contribute to the drug's anti-inflammatory and immune-modulatory benefits beyond glycemic control. The observation links metformin's autophagy-inducing capacity to attenuation of age- and inflammation-associated T cell skewing.
Metformin and partial cellular reprogramming have shown measurable clock reversal in some studies.

Metformin is classified as a senomorphic agent that inhibits NF-κB signaling and activates AMPK, thereby suppressing the pro-inflammatory SASP.
