links.context: High efficiency of vitamin B3 (niacin or nicotinamide) in preventing lung tissue damage was confirmed in several animal models with bleomycin- and LPS-induced lung injury, and considering this strong lung-protective effect, vitamin B3 has been proposed as an early treatment-supporting agent against COVID-19, which otherwise causes a maladaptive hyperinflammatory response with a cytokine storm in lung tissue. Nicotinamide riboside (NR), as a vitamin B3 derivative, is therefore considered a potential therapeutic or supporting agent to reduce hyperinflammation and regenerate damaged lung tissue during SARS-CoV-2 infection, where excess leucocyte infiltration causes extensive tissue damage

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: Adenosine kinase (ADK) acts as an NRH kinase in a recently discovered novel biosynthetic route of NAD+ from NRH (the reduced form of nicotinamide riboside) through the NMNH intermediate, providing a NMRK-independent pathway for the NRH-induced NAD+ increase. NRH is more stable than nicotinamide riboside (NR), which degrades to nicotinamide in the blood, and NRH increases NAD+ in both cultured cells (5-10-fold above the baseline) and mice, in a more potent and faster manner than NR. Endogenous NRH was detected in the liver of mouse models, establishing NRH as a valid natural precursor of NAD+.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: Nicotinic acid (NA, niacin) is implicated with flushing at doses higher than 50 mg/day, and several preclinical studies have confirmed that both NA and nicotinamide (NAM) can cause painful flushing sensations at therapeutic doses or other toxic effects. NA shows lowering effects on blood lipid levels and is used to treat dyslipidemia, but this flushing side effect limits its tolerability. In contrast, nicotinamide riboside (NR) elevates NAD+ levels without activating GPR109A, the receptor that mediates nicotinic acid-induced flushing, and was confirmed across a number of studies as well-tolerated up to 2 g of a daily dose, with no flushing or severe side effects.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: Nicotinic acid (NA, niacin) shows lowering effects on blood lipid levels, and it is used to treat dyslipidemia, although it is implicated with flushing at doses higher than 50 mg/day. In contrast, nicotinamide (NAM) does not affect lipid blood levels, yet it can exhibit sirtuin-inhibiting effects at higher doses, while nicotinamide riboside (NR) does not cause flushing because it does not activate GPR109A. The distinct physiological responses of the NAD+ precursors NA, NAM, and NR, despite all three raising NAD+ and NADP+ levels, are important for selecting the appropriate precursor for specific therapeutic indications.

links.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
links.context: Pomegranate is cited as one of the primary and richest dietary sources of urolithin A. Pomegranate peel and seeds contain abundant polyphenolic compounds, including ellagitannins that are metabolized by the gut microbiota into urolithin A. Consequently, consuming pomegranate supplies an abundance of precursor molecules for intestinal microbial metabolism, facilitating the generation of urolithin A, and pomegranate consumption is a standard dietary route to increase systemic urolithin A exposure alongside other sources such as walnut, almond, strawberry, and blueberry.

links.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
links.context: Urolithin A and its metabolites can be excreted from the body through the kidneys and intestines. Renal function can influence the rate of urolithin A elimination, since a portion of the compound and its conjugated forms is cleared in the urine, while additional urolithin A is further metabolized into other compounds within the intestines before being eliminated through feces. Renal function, intestinal permeability, and individual characteristics are therefore among the physiological factors that shape the bioavailability, metabolism, and distribution of urolithin A.

links.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
links.context: Rifampicin is a hepatic enzyme inducer that can increase the activity of certain metabolic enzymes in the liver, potentially accelerating the metabolism of urolithin A and reducing its half-life in the body. This illustrates the broader principle that drugs interacting with cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver can competitively inhibit or induce these enzymes, thereby disrupting the metabolism and clearance of urolithin A and altering its systemic exposure. Common antibiotics, antifungal drugs, and anticancer drugs have been reported to interact with CYP450 enzymes in this way.

links.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
links.context: PPARγ is a transcription factor involved in adipocyte differentiation, glucose metabolism, and cholesterol metabolism, among other processes. Urolithin A increases PPARγ expression and the transcription of its downstream target genes, thereby promoting fatty acid oxidation, improving insulin sensitivity, and reducing cholesterol synthesis and absorption. PPARγ signaling thus contributes to the metabolic regulatory effects attributed to urolithin A, complementing its activation of the AMPK pathway in supporting muscle energy metabolism.

links.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
links.context: Urolithin A activates AMPK through a cascade involving the activation of SIRT3 and subsequently LKB1, with LKB1 acting as the upstream kinase that directly activates AMPK. LKB1 is a master upstream kinase for the AMPK family, and its activation links mitochondrial deacetylase activity to cellular energy sensing. AMPK activation in turn promotes fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and improved muscle energy supply and metabolism, supporting the ergogenic and metabolic effects reported for urolithin A.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: LKB1 requires binding to STRAD and MO25 to exit the nucleus and gain full kinase activity; without this scaffold it remains inactive. The directionality is STRAD/MO25 upstream of LKB1 activation. SIRT1/AMPK deacetylate/phosphorylate LKB1 to modulate its localization. This gating is essential for LKB1's role as the master AMPK kinase.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: LKB1 is the primary upstream kinase phosphorylating AMPK at Thr172 in the activation loop, increasing AMPK activity over a hundred-fold. The directionality is LKB1 upstream of AMPK activation. This couples energy sensing to metabolic reprogramming. Sirtuins feed into this node via LKB1 deacetylation and AMPK-dependent NAD+ elevation.

links.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
links.context: The FoxO (forkhead box O) family is a group of transcription factors involved in regulating the synthesis and degradation of muscle proteins. Under catabolic conditions, nuclear FoxO drives expression of atrophy-related genes and activates specific protein degradation pathways that break down muscle proteins. Urolithin A suppresses FoxO activation, primarily by inhibiting its nuclear activity and reducing its regulation of these degradation pathways, thereby attenuating muscle protein degradation and helping to preserve muscle mass.

Ubiquitin-Proteasome System and Lewy Bodies are reciprocally linked entities in the neuromelanin knowledge graph, reflecting their frequent co-occurrence and shared relevance to catecholamine biology or Parkinson's disease. Directionally, the graph relation is symmetric, although biologically Ubiquitin-Proteasome System and Lewy Bodies may occupy distinct mechanistic roles. Their association is significant because both contribute to the chemical and pathological network that defines vulnerability of pigmented neurons. A caveat is that a bidirectional link denotes an association rather than a proven direct causal mechanism between the two entities.

Ubiquitin-Proteasome System regulates Proteostasis by controlling the flux, activity, or abundance of the regulated process. Mechanistically, Ubiquitin-Proteasome System acts as an upstream controller (enzymatic, transcriptional, or physical) that enforces balance in the target system. This is significant because proper regulation maintains homeostasis, and its failure contributes to neurodegeneration. A caveat is that regulation is context-dependent and often buffered by parallel systems, so disruption of one controller may be partially compensated.

Persulfates are employed as the oxidizing agent to convert adrenaline (epinephrine) into adrenochrome. The use of persulfates is advantageous because it precludes the effluent disposal problems associated with potassium ferricyanide and is significantly cheaper, although persulfate oxidation alone is slow and requires catalysts such as water-soluble bismuth salts. Suitable persulfates include potassium persulfate, sodium persulfate, and ammonium persulfate, with the sodium and ammonium salts preferred for their good solubility in water.

Water-soluble salts of bismuth, such as bismuth nitrate, bismuth oxynitrate, bismuth oxycarbonate, and bismuth citrate, accelerate the persulfate oxidation of adrenaline into adrenochrome, producing high-quality adrenochrome in high yields in a short period of time (about 30 to 45 minutes). Bismuth salts are used in amounts of 0.001 to 0.01 mole per mole of adrenaline; amounts below this do not significantly increase the reaction rate, while amounts above 0.01 mole may cause excessive oxidation and decompose the adrenochrome into tar-like by-products.

Adrenochrome has been commercially prepared by oxidizing adrenaline or its salts with potassium ferricyanide in an aqueous medium. This process is uneconomical because of the large quantities of potassium ferricyanide needed, the ensuing effluent disposal problems, and variability in product quality. The patent presents a bismuth-catalyzed persulfate process as a superior alternative that precludes these problems and yields less-colored carbazochrome and adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine products.

Adrenochrome is very unstable due to its ortho-quinoid structure and is therefore usually stabilized by conventional derivatization with hydrazines, e.g., aminoguanidine, semicarbazide, phenylhydrazine, o-nitrophenylhydrazine, p-nitrophenylhydrazine, and 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine. These hydrazine derivatives serve both for the stabilization of adrenochrome and for the preparation of useful medicines such as hemostatics. The stabilization treatment is generally conducted for 30 minutes to 3 hours at a temperature of 0 to 15 degrees C.

Semicarbazide reacts with adrenochrome to form adrenochrome monosemicarbazone (carbazochrome), a hemostatic agent. In the patented process, semicarbazide hydrochloride is added to the adrenochrome solution at below 10 degrees C in the presence of a potassium acetate buffer, with the stabilization carried out at pH 5 to 7. The reaction yields about 40.0 g of crude powder that is purified by dissolving in dilute sodium hydroxide, active carbon treatment, and precipitation at pH 5.5, and the purified product shows an ultraviolet absorption maximum at 354 nm and characteristic infrared absorptions matching those of an authentic sample.

The aqueous reaction medium for adrenochrome synthesis is maintained at a pH from 4 to 8, preferably with a buffer such as sodium hydrogencarbonate, sodium dihydrogenphosphate, disodium hydrogenphosphate, potassium acetate, or sodium acetate, with sodium hydrogencarbonate being preferred. The buffer is generally used in an amount of 4 to 7 moles, preferably 5 to 6 moles, per mole of adrenaline. Maintaining this pH range supports the persulfate oxidation of adrenaline catalyzed by water-soluble bismuth salts.

Ammonium persulfate is one of the suitable persulfate oxidizing agents for converting adrenaline into adrenochrome, together with potassium persulfate and sodium persulfate. Sodium and ammonium persulfates are preferred over potassium persulfate for their good solubility in water. In the examples, ammonium persulfate (about 0.42 mole) is used with a sodium hydrogencarbonate buffer and a bismuth salt catalyst at 0 to 5 degrees C to produce adrenochrome in maximum yield within about 30 to 45 minutes.

Yoshinori Ohsumi was awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his pioneering work using yeast genetics to identify the core autophagy-related (ATG) genes that govern the process. Through systematic mutagenesis screens, he uncovered the molecular machinery responsible for autophagosome formation, including the ubiquitin-like conjugation systems that build the phagophore membrane. His discoveries established autophagy as a genetically tractable and evolutionarily conserved degradation pathway, providing the conceptual framework for all subsequent mammalian autophagy research. The recognition underscored the fundamental importance of autophagy in cellular homeostasis, development, and human disease.

The ULK1 complex, composed of ULK1 or ULK2 kinase together with Atg13, FIP200, and Atg101, acts as the primary initiator of autophagosome formation downstream of nutrient sensing. Under starvation, AMPK directly activates ULK1 while mTORC1 is withdrawn, allowing the complex to phosphorylate targets and recruit the downstream PI3K III/Beclin 1 nucleation machinery. ULK1 kinase activity is essential for the localized recruitment of ATG proteins to the phagophore assembly site and for the earliest steps of membrane expansion. Thus the ULK1 complex serves as the integration point that converts nutrient and energy signals into the physical initiation of autophagosome biogenesis.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: ULK1 functions within a stable initiation complex containing ATG13, FIP200 (RB1CC1), and ATG101, which nucleates autophagosome formation in response to nutrient status. The directionality is the complex upstream of autophagy initiation. SIRT1 deacetylates and activates ULK1 within this complex. This positions sirtuins at the top of the autophagic machinery.

The class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K III) complex, centered on Vps34 and including Beclin 1, Atg14, Vps15, and Ambra-1, generates phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) at membranes to drive autophagosome nucleation. PI3P recruits effector proteins carrying PI3P-binding domains that organize the expanding phagophore and tether downstream ATG conjugation systems. Beclin 1 is a tumor suppressor whose activity is modulated by interacting partners and by anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins that restrain autophagy under fed conditions. This nucleation complex functions immediately downstream of the ULK1 initiator and is a critical control node for the magnitude of autophagic responses.

Intermittent fasting lowers circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), a potent mitogenic and pro-survival hormone whose signaling converges on the PI3K-Akt-mTOR axis to inhibit autophagy. In a breast cancer model, a 48-hour fasting period reduced IGF-1 levels by approximately 70%, dampening pro-tumorigenic IGF-1 receptor signaling. The resulting reduction in mTORC1 activity contributes to the fasting-induced activation of autophagy and the enhanced stress resistance of normal tissues. Lower IGF-1 during fasting is therefore a key endocrine mechanism linking IF to both tumor suppression and longevity.

Intermittent fasting induces autophagy as an early cellular adaptation to the periodic nutrient and energy deficit it imposes. In vitro, fasting-mimetic conditions activate the autophagic machinery and concurrently downregulate the ectonucleotidase CD73, altering extracellular adenosine metabolism. The induction is largely mediated through AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition as nutrient and insulin signals fall during the fasting window. This autophagic engagement is thought to underlie many of the cytoprotective and anti-aging effects attributed to IF regimens.

Beclin 1 is a core autophagy protein and a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor whose monoallelic deletion is frequently observed in human ovarian, breast, and prostate cancers. Loss of one BECN1 allele reduces autophagic flux, increasing susceptibility to oxidative damage, genomic instability, and inflammation that favor tumor initiation. Mechanistically, Beclin 1 functions as the scaffold of the PI3K III nucleation complex, and its interaction with Bcl-2 family members further couples autophagy to apoptotic regulation. Its frequent deletion in epithelial cancers established autophagy as a genuine tumor-suppression pathway.

Oncogenic RAS signaling drives a metabolic reprogramming in which transformed cells upregulate basal autophagy to supply the amino acids, lipids, and nucleotides needed for sustained proliferation. Mutant RAS activates both mTOR and, via nutrient and energy stress feedback, the autophagic machinery, allowing tumor cells to survive in nutrient-poor microenvironments. Pharmacologic or genetic blockade of autophagy selectively impairs the viability of RAS-driven tumors, highlighting autophagy as a dependency in these cancers. This dependency has motivated clinical efforts to combine RAS pathway-targeted or standard therapies with autophagy inhibition.

links.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
links.context: Constitutive oncogenic RAS signaling pushes cells into hyper-replication, where DNA replication forks are initiated at excessive frequency and become stalled or collapsed. This generates single-stranded DNA gaps and replication stress that activate checkpoint kinases. The relationship is a central mechanism linking oncogene activation to senescence-inducing damage. It is well established in OIS biology.

Dietary restriction (DR) and its variants are among the most potent physiological activators of autophagy, engaging the pathway in most cultured cells and across many organs in vivo. By lowering circulating nutrients and insulin while raising AMP/ATP ratios, DR relieves mTORC1 inhibition and activates AMPK, thereby de-repressing the ULK1 complex and TFEB-dependent lysosomal programs. In model organisms such as C. elegans, DR induces autophagy through coordinated transcriptional changes mediated by orthologs like HLH-30/TFEB. The health- and lifespan-extending effects of DR are widely attributed in substantial part to this induction of adaptive autophagy.

Caloric restriction mimetics are pharmacological agents that reproduce the metabolic and autophagic benefits of caloric restriction without sustained food reduction. Representatives such as 2-deoxyglucose, metformin, and spermidine activate AMPK and/or inhibit mTORC1, recapitulating the low-energy signaling state that drives autophagy. By mimicking nutrient scarcity at the signaling level, these compounds induce lysosomal and autophagic gene programs similar to those engaged during DR. They are attractive translationally because they avoid the practical and compliance limitations of long-term dietary restriction in humans.

Cisplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapeutic whose efficacy is augmented when combined with intermittent fasting in both cellular and animal models. Fasting generates a differential stress resistance in which normal cells enter a protective, autophagy-dependent quiescent state while many tumor cells remain vulnerable to platinum-DNA adduct formation. The improved therapeutic window reduces chemotherapy-associated toxicity while slowing tumor growth, suggesting a combinatorial strategy. These findings support IF as an adjunct to sensitize tumors and protect host tissue during cisplatin-based regimens.
Cisplatin induces premature senescence via DNA intrastrand cross-links. Mechanism involves p53-p21 pathway activation and ROS-dependent signaling.

Autophagic flux—the complete rate of cargo delivery to and degradation within lysosomes—declines progressively with age in many tissues. This decline stems from impaired initiation, reduced lysosomal proteolytic capacity, and accumulated lipofuscin that compromises lysosomal function, producing a state of proteostatic insufficiency. The resulting accumulation of damaged organelles and protein aggregates contributes centrally to the aging phenotype and to age-related diseases such as neurodegeneration and sarcopenia. Restoration of autophagic flux is therefore a major hypothesized mechanism through which longevity interventions exert their benefits.

Autophagy-inducing interventions have been shown to rejuvenate features of adaptive immune aging, a process characterized by thymic involution, reduced naïve T cell output, and diminished responses to vaccination and infection. By clearing damaged mitochondria and improving proteostasis in lymphocytes, autophagy inducers restore hematopoietic stem cell function and enhance memory CD8+ T cell generation. Pharmacological or dietary activation of autophagy counteracts the functional defects that accumulate in immune cells with age. These effects position autophagy enhancement as a plausible strategy to mitigate immunosenescence.

Autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin, spermidine, metformin) suppress the SASP by clearing damaged organelles and limiting inflammasome activation, thereby reducing the inflammatory secretome. By restoring quality-control pathways, they counteract senescence-associated mitochondrial and innate-immune dysfunction. This makes autophagy induction a central, translatable senomorphic strategy. The suppression is mechanistically coherent and supported across multiple inducers.

Spermidine enhances autophagy through multiple complementary mechanisms, prominently including induction of histone H3 deacetylation that relaxes chromatin at autophagy gene loci and promotes their transcription. It additionally supports autophagy via hypusination-dependent translation of TFEB and direct effects on the autophagic machinery. These actions produce a safe, sustained upregulation of autophagic flux associated with lifespan extension in model organisms. Spermidine is therefore a leading natural caloric-restriction mimetic for promoting healthy aging.

links.source_file: _document_ - The autophagy enhancer spermidine reverses arterial aging.md
links.context: Spermidine supplementation rejuvenates age-impaired B cell responses by inducing autophagy in memory T and B lymphocytes, restoring their functional competence. The polyamine's ability to clear damaged organelles and enhance proteostasis in these cells counteracts the decline in vaccine responsiveness seen with immune aging. By supporting lymphoid cell fitness, spermidine addresses a key component of immunosenescence through an autophagy-dependent mechanism. These effects complement its broader rejuvenation of adaptive immunity.
Spermidine drives eIF5A hypusination, which promotes TFEB translation, leading to autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis.

links.source_file: _document_ - The autophagy enhancer spermidine reverses arterial aging.md
links.context: Spermidine promotes TFEB translation through hypusination of eIF5A, a modification essential for efficient translation of mRNAs containing polyproline tracts such as that of TFEB. By facilitating the synthesis of TFEB protein, spermidine expands the pool of the master regulator available for nuclear activation. This translational enhancement complements spermidine's other autophagy-inducing mechanisms, including histone deacetylation. The eIF5A-TFEB link provides a molecular explanation for spermidine's potent, safe induction of the lysosomal-autophagy network.

Spermidine reverses features of arterial aging, including large elastic artery stiffening, and restores nitric-oxide-mediated endothelial function in aged vessels. These vascular benefits are linked to spermidine-induced autophagy, which clears damaged mitochondria and reduces vascular oxidative stress and inflammation. By improving endothelial-dependent vasodilation, spermidine counteracts the stiffening that drives systolic hypertension and cardiovascular risk with age. The findings support spermidine as a candidate intervention for vascular rejuvenation.

links.source_file: _document_ - The autophagy enhancer spermidine reverses arterial aging.md
links.context: Spermidine supplementation reduces oxidative stress in arterial and other tissues by enhancing autophagic and mitochondrial quality control, limiting the accumulation of reactive oxygen species-generating damaged organelles. The polyamine also exerts direct antioxidant effects and supports redox homeostasis through improved proteostasis. Reduced oxidative damage is a key mediator of spermidine's cardiovascular and cognitive protective effects. This antioxidant action is tightly coupled to its autophagy-inducing capacity.
Spermidine induces autophagy without caloric deficit by directly inhibiting histone acetyltransferase p300, causing global deacetylation and upregulation of Atg gene transcription.

The senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) is the ensemble of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and matrix-remodeling enzymes secreted by senescent cells. Accumulation of senescent cells with age creates a chronic, low-grade inflammatory milieu that drives inflammaging—the sterile inflammation implicated in nearly all age-related diseases. SASP factors recruit immune cells, promote fibrosis, and induce paracrine senescence in neighboring cells, establishing feed-forward tissue deterioration. Targeting senescent cells or their SASP is a major therapeutic avenue to reduce inflammaging.

Once TFEB is phosphorylated at serine 211 by mTORC1, 14-3-3 proteins bind the phosphorylated motif and mask the transcription factor's nuclear localization signal. This cytosolic sequestration prevents TFEB from accessing CLEAR elements in the nucleus, thereby suppressing expression of lysosomal and autophagic genes. The 14-3-3 interaction thereby converts a single phosphorylation event into a durable spatial exclusion of TFEB. Disruption of this complex is a key step in starvation- and drug-induced TFEB activation.

TRPML1 (mucolipin-1) is a lysosomal cation channel that releases Ca2+ from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol in response to stimuli such as PI(3,5)P2 or lumenal cues. The resulting local calcium signal activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates TFEB and promotes its nuclear translocation. Through this mechanism, TRPML1 functionally links lysosomal ion homeostasis to the transcriptional activation of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Loss of TRPML1 underlies the lysosomal storage disorder mucolipidosis type IV.

TRPML1 is the principal lysosomal Ca2+ release channel, activated by PI(3,5)P2 and other cues to efflux Ca2+ from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol. The released Ca2+ activates calcineurin, driving TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and thereby coupling ion flux to transcriptional activation of lysosomal biogenesis. TRPML1 also participates in lysosomal trafficking and autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Loss of TRPML1 causes mucolipidosis type IV, a lysosomal storage disorder, confirming its essential role in degradative homeostasis.

Cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (CDK4/6), central drivers of G1 cell-cycle progression, phosphorylate TFEB at serine 142 and promote its nuclear export through a CRM1-dependent mechanism. This action sequesters TFEB in the cytoplasm during phases of active proliferation, when degradative programs are downregulated. Conversely, pharmacological CDK4/6 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear retention and enhances lysosome biogenesis and autophagy. The CDK4/6-TFEB link couples cell-cycle state to the metabolic and degradative status of the cell.

CDK4/6 phosphorylate TFEB at serine 142, driving CRM1-dependent nuclear export and cytoplasmic sequestration during cell-cycle progression. This modification aligns TFEB repression with the biosynthetic demands of dividing cells, when autophagy is downregulated. Pharmacologic CDK4/6 inhibitors relieve this constraint, permitting TFEB nuclear accumulation and enhancing lysosome biogenesis and autophagic flux. The axis thereby couples cell-cycle machinery to the metabolic state of the cell.

MAP4K3 phosphorylates TFEB at serine 3, an N-terminal modification that primes TFEB for subsequent phosphorylation at S211 by mTORC1. This hierarchical phosphorylation reveals that TFEB regulation involves ordered, multi-site modification in which upstream kinases license downstream ones. By enabling the mTORC1 repressive mark, MAP4K3 integrates amino-acid and growth-factor inputs into TFEB control. The finding adds a further layer of complexity to the kinase network governing lysosomal gene transcription.

Tankyrase 1 (TNKS1) poly-ADP-ribosylates (PARsylates) TFEB, a modification that promotes its nuclear translocation and activation of target genes. PARsylation addsADP-ribose polymers that alter TFEB interactions and trafficking, providing a non-phosphorylation route to TFEB activation. This modification broadens the enzymatic toolkit—alongside kinases, phosphatases, acetylases, and ubiquitin ligases—that regulates the autophagy-lysosomal master switch. The TNKS1-TFEB relationship suggests potential crosstalk with Wnt/β-catenin and other PARsylation-dependent pathways.

The oncogenic transcription factor MYC competes with TFEB for binding to CLEAR elements in the promoters of lysosomal and autophagy genes. By occupying these sites, MYC represses the TFEB-driven transcriptional program while simultaneously driving its own proliferative gene network. This competitive binding creates a molecular antagonism between growth-promoting and degradative transcriptional programs. The interplay explains how MYC-high tumors suppress autophagy-lysosomal capacity even as they increase metabolic demand.

MYC antagonizes TFEB and TFE3 transcriptional activities at lysosomal gene promoters, thereby repressing lysosome biogenesis in proliferating cells. Through direct competition for CLEAR elements and broader chromatin effects, MYC suppresses the degradative capacity that would otherwise constrain growth. This repression aligns cellular resources toward biosynthesis rather than turnover during oncogenic drive. The MYC-lysosome antagonism is a key axis by which cancer cells reshape their degradative landscape.

METTL3, the catalytic subunit of the m6A methyltransferase complex, methylates TFEB mRNA at N6-methyladenosine residues, a mark that targets the transcript for destabilization and degradation. By reducing TFEB mRNA stability, METTL3 negatively regulates TFEB protein abundance and consequently the autophagy-lysosomal program. This epitranscriptomic control links RNA methylation to degradative pathway output. The finding situates TFEB within the expanding regulatory influence of m6A modification on stress-response genes.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of the dynamic epigenetic landscape in senescence_orchestrating SASP expression.md
links.context: METTL3-METTL14 complex catalyzes N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation in mammalian nuclear RNAs.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of the dynamic epigenetic landscape in senescence_orchestrating SASP expression.md
links.context: Genome-wide redistribution of METTL3-METTL14 in senescent cells promotes SASP expression through chromatin looping.

Programmed cell death protein 4 (PDCD4) suppresses TFEB translation by binding eukaryotic initiation factor 4A (eIF4A) and inhibiting the RNA helicase activity required for ribosome scanning of the TFEB mRNA. This translational blockade limits TFEB protein synthesis independently of its transcriptional or degradative regulation. PDCD4 thereby acts as a brake on the autophagy-lysosomal program at the level of protein synthesis. Its own downregulation in cancer may contribute to the elevated TFEB activity observed in some malignancies.

Eltrombopag (EO), a small-molecule thrombopoietin receptor agonist, was identified as the first direct inhibitor of TFEB, disrupting TFEB-DNA interactions at CLEAR elements. By preventing TFEB from binding its target promoters, EO blocks transcriptional activation of the autophagy-lysosomal network. This tool compound has enabled dissection of TFEB-dependent versus independent autophagy and has therapeutic implications where TFEB hyperactivation is pathogenic. Its discovery established pharmacological feasibility of directly targeting the MiT/TFE family.

The lysosome is the cell's terminal degradation center, containing acidic hydrolases that break down proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy. Beyond catabolism, lysosomes serve as signaling hubs that integrate nutrient and growth-factor inputs, most notably by hosting the activation of mTORC1 at their surface. This duality—as both waste-disposal organelle and metabolic command post—places lysosomes at the center of cellular homeostasis, development, and aging. Lysosomal dysfunction underlies a broad spectrum of storage and degenerative diseases.

Lysosome biogenesis is regulated by CDK4/6 such that inhibition of these kinases leads to nuclear retention of TFEB and enhanced expression of lysosomal genes. During active proliferation, CDK4/6-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB restrains lysosomal expansion; when CDK4/6 is blocked, the degradative network is unleashed. This regulation connects cell-cycle control to organelle homeostasis and may contribute to the metabolic effects of CDK4/6 inhibitors used in cancer therapy. It reveals lysosomal biogenesis as a cell-cycle-responsive process.

The lysosome serves as the physical platform for mTORC1 activation, hosting the recruitment of mTORC1 via Rag GTPases and Ragulator and its encounter with the activator Rheb at the lysosomal surface. Amino-acid sensing, growth-factor inputs, and calcium signals all converge at this organelle to determine mTORC1 activity. By colocalizing mTORC1 with its upstream regulators, the lysosome functionally couples nutrient detection to the control of autophagy and anabolism. This spatial organization is essential for the rapid, reversible regulation of the pathway.

TFE3, the closely related MiT/TFE family member, also binds CLEAR elements and induces lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy in response to nutrient deprivation and stress. Like TFEB, TFE3 is repressed by mTORC1 through phosphorylation and released upon starvation, calcineurin activation, or ER stress. The overlapping but non-identical target sets of TFEB and TFE3 provide redundancy and specificity in the lysosomal program. TFE3's distinct regulation, including PERK-dependent activation, broadens the stress-responsive control of degradation.

TFE3 is, together with TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, binding CLEAR elements to induce expression of lysosomal and autophagic genes. Its activation occurs via mTORC1 inhibition, calcineurin signaling, and ER-stress-dependent PERK activation, providing partially distinct triggers from TFEB. TFE3 overexpression similarly expands lysosomal capacity and promotes autophagic flux. The overlapping master-regulator roles of TFE3 and TFEB ensure robustness in the control of cellular degradation.

TFE3 is activated in response to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress through a pathway that is mTORC1-independent but requires the ER stress sensor PERK. Under unfolded protein accumulation, PERK signaling promotes TFE3 nuclear translocation, engaging lysosomal and autophagic genes to alleviate proteotoxic burden. This distinct trigger allows TFE3 to contribute to the integrated stress response without relying on nutrient sensing. The mechanism expands the repertoire of stressors that can recruit the MiT/TFE degradative program.

TFE3 is recurrently involved in Xp11.2 translocation renal cell carcinomas, in which it fuses with partner genes such as ASPSCR1, PRCC, or SFPQ, creating chimeric transcription factors that drive tumorigenesis. These gene fusions define a distinct subset of RCC, often arising in children and young adults, with characteristic clear-cell or papillary features. The fusion proteins typically retain the TFE3 DNA-binding domain and are constitutively active, deregulating MiT/TFE target genes. Detection of TFE3 rearrangement is important for correct diagnosis and classification of these tumors.

The Ragulator is a multiprotein scaffold anchored at the lysosomal membrane that interacts with Rag GTPases to recruit mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface in response to amino acids. By tethering the Rag-mTORC1 complex at the lysosome, Ragulator enables amino-acid sensing to converge with Rheb-mediated activation. Loss of Ragulator disrupts nutrient-dependent mTORC1 signaling and de-represses autophagy. The complex is therefore the lynchpin coupling lysosomal amino-acid detection to mTORC1 and autophagy control.

PIKfyve is a phosphoinositide kinase that converts phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) into phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate (PI(3,5)P2) on endolysosomal membranes. PI(3,5)P2 serves as a crucial lipid messenger that regulates membrane trafficking, vacuole homeostasis, and the activity of the lysosomal channel TRPML1. By generating PI(3,5)P2, PIKfyve controls lysosomal morphology and the calcium release that activates calcineurin-TFEB signaling. Its inhibition causes massive lysosomal vacuolation, underscoring its centrality to lysosomal function.

Autophagic lysosome reformation (ALR) is the process by which spent autolysosomes tubulate and bud off new lysosomes to restore the lysosomal pool after autophagy. ALR requires the coordinated actions of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2), clathrin, and adaptor proteins AP2 and AP4 to drive membrane scission and vesicle formation. This reformation step is essential to prevent lysosomal depletion during sustained autophagy. Defects in ALR cause accumulation of enlarged autolysosomes and impaired degradative capacity.

ZKSCAN3 is a zinc-finger transcription factor that represses the expression of lysosomal and autophagy genes, acting in opposition to TFEB/TFE3. Under basal conditions it limits autophagic and lysosomal capacity, and its inhibition or loss enhances cellular clearance. ZKSCAN3 thereby functions as a transcriptional brake on the degradative network, complementary to the post-translational repression by mTORC1. Targeting ZKSCAN3 has been proposed as a strategy to boost autophagy in disease.

SLC-36.1 (a solute carrier) forms a complex with the PPK-3/PIKfyve kinase module to regulate phagocytic lysosome reformation (PLR), the process by which phagolysosomes regenerate new lysosomes after phagocytosis. By influencing PI(3,5)P2 generation and membrane dynamics, this complex ensures restoration of the lysosomal pool following immune or clearance challenges. Defects in PLR impair the ability of phagocytes to sustain repeated rounds of degradation. The pathway connects solute transport and phosphoinositide metabolism to innate immune function.

The TSC1-TSC2 tumor-suppressor complex acts as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for the small G protein Rheb, converting active GTP-bound Rheb to its inactive GDP-bound form. Because only GTP-Rheb directly activates mTORC1, TSC1/TSC2 functions as a critical upstream brake on mTORC1 in response to energy, oxygen, and growth-factor signals. Loss-of-function mutations in TSC1 or TSC2 cause tuberous sclerosis complex, characterized by constitutive mTORC1 activation, hamartoma formation, and autophagy suppression. The complex is therefore a major gatekeeper of mTORC1 and cellular growth.

Rheb (Ras homolog enriched in brain) is a small GTPase that directly binds and activates mTORC1 when in its GTP-bound state, provided mTORC1 is localized at the lysosomal surface. Rheb's activity is held in check by the TSC1/TSC2 GAP complex, making it the immediate effector that relays growth and nutrient signals to mTORC1. GTP-Rheb relieves the autoinhibitory conformation of mTORC1, enabling substrate phosphorylation. As the proximal activator, Rheb sits at the convergence point of multiple upstream inhibitory pathways.

Rag GTPases (RagA/B and RagC/D) function as heterodimers that bind the mTORC1 subunit Raptor and promote relocalization of mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface, where activator Rheb resides. Amino-acid sufficiency favors the active Rag conformation, positioning mTORC1 for activation; amino-acid starvation inactivates Rags and disperses mTORC1, de-repressing autophagy. The Rags therefore act as amino-acid sensors that bridge nutrient availability to mTORC1 spatial activation. Their regulation by the Ragulator and GAPs (e.g., GATOR complexes) is central to nutrient signaling.

REDD1 (regulated in development and DNA damage responses 1) inhibits mTORC1 specifically under hypoxia by binding and releasing TSC2 from inhibitory 14-3-3 association, thereby activating the TSC GAP complex. This allows Rheb to be converted to its inactive GDP form and mTORC1 to be suppressed, conserving energy when oxygen is limiting. REDD1 thus provides a hypoxia-responsive brake that engages autophagy and limits anabolic consumption. Its induction is transcriptionally controlled by HIF-1α, integrating oxygen sensing with mTORC1 regulation.

PRAS40 is an mTORC1-associated protein that acts as a negative regulator by competing for substrate binding and limiting mTORC1 kinase activity, particularly when the complex is in a low-activity state. Growth-factor signaling through Akt phosphorylates PRAS40, releasing its inhibition and permitting mTORC1 activation. Thus PRAS40 provides a built-in brake that is relieved by anabolic signals. Its dynamic association fine-tunes mTORC1 output in response to the cellular environment.

Deptor is an endogenous inhibitor that binds both mTORC1 and mTORC2, suppressing the catalytic activity of each complex. By dampening both arms of mTOR signaling, Deptor broadly restrains anabolic growth, survival, and autophagy suppression. Its expression is itself feedback-regulated by mTORC1/mTORC2 activity, forming part of a homeostatic loop. Reduced Deptor levels in certain cancers correlate with hyperactive mTOR signaling, highlighting its tumor-suppressive potential.

In C. elegans, the MAX-like transcription factor MXL-3 represses transcription of lysosomal lipase genes (lipl-1, lipl-2, lipl-3, lipl-5) when food is abundant, limiting lipid mobilization. This repression maintains lipid storage under fed conditions and is relieved during fasting, allowing lipolysis. MXL-3 thus acts as a nutritional gatekeeper of lysosomal lipid catabolism, analogous to MYC's repression of lysosomal programs in mammals. Its activity positions lipid degradation within the broader nutrient-responsive regulatory network.

During fasting, MXL-3::GFP signal disappears from intestinal nuclei within about two hours, indicating that the repressor exits the nucleus and ceases to suppress its target genes. This delocalization is a rapid, nutrient-responsive event that permits de-repression of lysosomal lipase and autophagy genes. The nuclear export of MXL-3 complements the concurrent nuclear accumulation of HLH-30, creating a switch from storage to mobilization. The observation provides direct in vivo evidence for dynamic regulation of the lipid-degradation program.

MXL-3 promotes aging under abundant food conditions; worms lacking mxl-3 are long-lived, indicating that its repressive activity on lysosomal and lipolytic genes accelerates age-related decline. By maintaining a storage-oriented, low-autophagy state when nutrients are plentiful, MXL-3 limits the clearance and metabolic flexibility that promote longevity. This pro-aging effect is consistent with the broader principle that reduced nutrient signaling extends lifespan. The phenotype positions MXL-3 as a negative regulator of the pro-longevity degradative program.

HLH-30, the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian TFEB, induces expression of the lysosomal lipase genes (lipl-1, lipl-2, lipl-3, lipl-5) in response to fasting, promoting mobilization of stored lipids. This transcriptional activation mirrors TFEB's induction of lipolytic and autophagic programs in mammals during nutrient scarcity. The HLH-30–lipase axis provides a molecular explanation for fasting-induced lipophagy and lifespan extension in worms. It demonstrates deep conservation of the MiT/TFE nutrient-response program.

HLH-30 translocates to and accumulates in intestinal nuclei of fasted C. elegans, where it activates the lysosomal, autophagic, and lipolytic transcriptional programs. This nuclear enrichment mirrors the starvation-induced nuclear entry of mammalian TFEB/TFE3 and is essential for the organism's adaptive response to food deprivation. The translocation is opposed by insulin/IGF and CeTOR signaling that retain HLH-30 cytoplasmically when food is available. Its nuclear localization thus serves as a key determinant of fasting-induced longevity.

HLH-30 prevents aging and extends lifespan in C. elegans; hlh-30 mutants are short-lived, and loss of hlh-30 suppresses the longevity conferred by mxl-3 deletion. By driving autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lipid mobilization, HLH-30 preserves proteostasis and metabolic homeostasis that decline with age. Its activity embodies the conserved mechanism by which enhanced clearance promotes longevity across species. The epistasis with mxl-3 places HLH-30 downstream as the effector of the pro-longevity program.

HLH-30 is required for survival during prolonged starvation; hlh-30 mutant animals die prematurely under nutrient-deprived conditions due to their inability to mount sufficient autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lipid mobilization. By activating the clearance and energy-mobilization programs, HLH-30 enables worms to withstand food absence. This essential role mirrors the dependence of mammalian cells on TFEB for stress resilience. The phenotype establishes HLH-30 as a critical effector of adaptive starvation responses.

HLH-30 regulates longevity in C. elegans, as its overexpression extends lifespan while loss of hlh-30 shortens it and suppresses the longevity of other mutants. By inducing autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lipid mobilization, HLH-30 preserves proteostasis and metabolic homeostasis that decline with age. Its activity integrates insulin, mTOR, and dietary signals into a pro-longevity transcriptional program. The worm findings provide a conserved model for how TFEB orthologs promote healthspan in higher organisms.

LIPL-1 is a lysosomal lipase in C. elegans that co-localizes with the lysosomal marker PGP-2, confirming its residence within the lysosomal lumen where it hydrolyzes stored triglycerides. Its expression is induced by HLH-30 during fasting, supporting lipophagy-mediated lipid mobilization. LIPL-1 is part of a family of lysosomal lipases (lipl-1 through lipl-5) that together govern organismal lipid turnover. Loss or reduction of these lipases impairs the ability to survive nutrient scarcity.

LIPL-3 is a lysosomal lipase in C. elegans that, like LIPL-1, co-localizes with the lysosomal marker PGP-2 and contributes to intralysosomal lipid hydrolysis. It is transcriptionally induced by HLH-30 under fasting conditions, enabling the breakdown of lipid droplets delivered via lipophagy. Together with other lipl family members, LIPL-3 is required for efficient energy mobilization during starvation. Its lysosomal localization anchors it within the autophagy-lysosomal degradative system.

The mammalian transcription factor MAX, a partner of MYC, is the functional homolog of C. elegans MXL-3, as expression of mouse MAX in worms rescued the mxl-3 mutant phenotype. This conservation indicates that the MYC/MAX network's repression of lysosomal and metabolic genes is an ancient feature retained from nematodes to mammals. The rescue experiment directly demonstrates mechanistic equivalence between the worm repressor and its mammalian counterpart. It strengthens the translational relevance of MXL-3 studies to human lipid and lysosomal regulation.

Lipophagy—the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets—is conserved across metazoans, as shown by the fact that inactivation of the autophagy genes lgg-1 and lgg-2 in C. elegans leads to increased fat accumulation. By delivering lipid droplets to lysosomes for lipase-mediated hydrolysis, lipophagy mobilizes stored energy during fasting. The conservation from worms to mammals indicates an ancient and essential role for autophagy in lipid homeostasis. Defective lipophagy contributes to hepatic steatosis and metabolic disease in higher organisms.

DAF-2, the C. elegans insulin/IGF-1 receptor ortholog, partially regulates MXL-3 expression such that impaired insulin signaling leads to modest repression of mxl-3 transcription. This places MXL-3 downstream of the insulin-signaling axis that broadly controls metabolism and longevity in worms. The partial effect indicates that additional nutrient and developmental inputs also govern mxl-3, consistent with its role as a multifactorial repressor. The linkage reinforces the canonical insulin→autophagy/lipid regulatory cascade.

CeTOR, the C. elegans ortholog of mTOR, controls HLH-30 at the transcriptional level; inactivation of CeTOR induces hlh-30 expression, increasing the abundance of the master degradative transcription factor. This upstream control parallels mammalian mTORC1's post-translational repression of TFEB, adding a transcriptional layer in worms. By inducing HLH-30, CeTOR inhibition engages the full lysosomal-autophagic and lipolytic program. The relationship confirms mTOR as an evolutionarily conserved suppressor of the TFEB/HLH-30 axis.

The peroxisome biogenesis network receives material from autophagy when damaged peroxisomes are engulfed and fragmented, generating precursors that can be reassembled into functional peroxisomes. This autophagic-lysosomal processing of peroxisomal components allows recycling of membrane and matrix constituents to support new organelle formation. The relationship couples selective peroxisome degradation (pexophagy) to organelle turnover and renewal. It highlights autophagy's role not only in disposal but also in enabling peroxisome homeostasis.

PERO1 functions as a sensor of oleic acid accumulation on damaged peroxisomes, triggering autophagic removal of these defective organelles. By detecting lipid imbalance indicative of peroxisomal dysfunction, PERO1 initiates quality-control degradation that prevents the propagation of impaired organelles. This lipid-sensing mechanism links metabolic state to organelle surveillance. The pathway exemplifies how selective autophagy integrates metabolic cues to maintain peroxisome integrity.

Selective autophagy targets damaged peroxisomes for degradation through a process termed pexophagy, in which ubiquitin tagging of peroxisomal proteins and recruitment of ESCRT (endosomal sorting complex required for transport) machinery mark the organelle for autophagic engulfment. This cargo-specific pathway contrasts with bulk autophagy by requiring receptor proteins that bridge the peroxisome to the autophagosomal membrane. Pexophagy protects cells from the oxidative and metabolic damage caused by defective peroxisomes. Its failure leads to accumulation of aberrant organelles and disease.

PEX1 is an ATPase essential for peroxisome membrane assembly and matrix protein import, operating as part of the peroxisomal AAA (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities) machinery. Loss of PEX1 causes a complete lack of functional peroxisomes, as import and biogenesis cannot proceed. This essential role makes PEX1 mutations among the most common causes of peroxisome biogenesis disorders. The gene thus sits at the foundation of peroxisome formation and metabolic competence.

Mutations in ABCD1, encoding a peroxisomal ATP-binding cassette transporter for very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD). Impaired ABCD1 disrupts VLCFA import into peroxisomes for beta-oxidation, leading to toxic accumulation of VLCFAs in adrenal cortex and central nervous system white matter. The resulting demyelination and adrenal insufficiency define the clinical syndrome. The disorder illustrates how peroxisomal transport defects produce severe neurodegeneration and underscores the importance of peroxisomal lipid homeostasis.

Zellweger syndrome, the most severe form of the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, is caused by mutations in PEX genes required for peroxisome assembly and matrix protein import. Affected individuals lack functional peroxisomes, leading to accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, bile acid intermediates, and pipecolic acid, with profound neurologic, hepatic, and skeletal abnormalities. The spectrum's severity correlates with the degree of residual peroxisomal function. These disorders highlight the non-redundant essentiality of peroxisomes in human development.

Lysosomal Biogenesis and TFEB are reciprocally linked entities in the neuromelanin knowledge graph, reflecting their frequent co-occurrence and shared relevance to catecholamine biology or Parkinson's disease. Directionally, the graph relation is symmetric, although biologically Lysosomal Biogenesis and TFEB may occupy distinct mechanistic roles. Their association is significant because both contribute to the chemical and pathological network that defines vulnerability of pigmented neurons. A caveat is that a bidirectional link denotes an association rather than a proven direct causal mechanism between the two entities.

links.context: SIRT2, a cytosolic NAD+-dependent deacetylase, deacetylates ATG4B in response to starvation, modulating the activity of this cysteine protease that processes and delipidates the autophagosome marker LC3/GABARAP. Deacetylation of ATG4B influences the dynamics of LC3 conjugation and autophagosome maturation, fine-tuning autophagic flux. Because SIRT2 activity rises when NAD+ is elevated during CR and exercise, this modification links energy status to autophagosome biogenesis. The SIRT2-ATG4B axis adds an acetylation layer to core autophagy machinery regulation.

SIRT2 is the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin and is most abundant in the cytosol, where it deacetylates α-tubulin and a range of metabolic and regulatory proteins. Its localization is cell-cycle regulated, with SIRT2 accumulating and being hyperphosphorylated as cells transit the G2/M boundary. The cytoplasmic residence underpins its roles in microtubule dynamics, mitosis, and cytoplasmic autophagy regulation rather than direct chromatin modification. Note that SIRT2 can also shuttle to the nucleus under certain stress conditions, so localization is not absolute.

SIRT2 resides in a genomic region frequently deleted in human gliomas, and re-expression of SIRT2 markedly reduces colony formation by glioma cells, indicating tumor-suppressor function. Its activity deacetylates substrates such as α-tubulin and HNF4α that govern mitotic fidelity and metabolism. The directionality is that SIRT2 loss permits, and SIRT2 restoration suppresses, gliomagenesis. A caveat is that SIRT2 can act as either tumor suppressor or promoter depending on tissue and context.

SIRT2 deacetylates Lys16 on histone H4, a modification linked to chromatin condensation during the G2/M transition of mitosis. Removing H4K16ac promotes a more compact mitotic chromatin state compatible with chromosome segregation. The directionality is enzymatic: SIRT2 directly deacetylates H4K16 to remodel chromatin at division. This activity complements SIRT2's role in microtubule and cell-cycle regulation.

SIRT2 interacts with HOXA10, a conserved homeobox transcription factor critical for embryonic cell-type determination and adult tissue homeostasis. The interaction suggests SIRT2 influences HOXA10-dependent transcriptional programs, though the precise deacetylation outcome is less characterized. The directionality is SIRT2 engaging HOXA10 as a partner/substrate. This connection links SIRT2 to developmental regulation and possibly to differentiation defects in disease.

SIRT2 is expressed in oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, the myelin-forming glia of CNS and PNS respectively, where it deacetylates α-tubulin and regulates microtubule stability. Its presence in myelinating cells ties SIRT2 to axonal support and myelin integrity. The directionality is SIRT2 acting within glia to control cytoskeletal dynamics. Dysregulation is implicated in demyelinating and neurodegenerative conditions.

SIRT2 deacetylates the p65 subunit of NF-κB, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and ameliorating arthritis severity in models. The directionality is SIRT2 enzymatic inhibition of NF-κB. This reveals an anti-inflammatory role for SIRT2 in myeloid and joint cells. It adds SIRT2 to the set of sirtuins that restrain NF-κB-driven inflammation.

SIRT2 prevents liver steatosis and lipid metabolic disorders by deacetylating hepatocyte nuclear factor 4α (HNF4α), a master regulator of hepatic lipid and drug-metabolizing genes. The directionality is SIRT2 enzymatic activation of HNF4α. This maintains lipid homeostasis and protects against fatty liver. It adds a hepatic metabolic function to SIRT2's repertoire.

SIRT2 expression is decreased in cervical cancer tissue versus adjacent normal tissue, and higher SIRT2 predicts favorable survival, indicating it suppresses cervical cancer progression. The directionality is SIRT2 loss associated with, and putatively enabling, tumor advancement. Its deacetylase actions on metabolic and mitotic substrates likely enforce differentiation and genome stability. This adds to the context-dependent tumor-suppressor face of SIRT2.

SIRT2 binds and deacetylates the nuclear factor of activated T-cell c2 (NFATc2) transcription factor, regulating its transcriptional activity in immune and cardiovascular contexts. The directionality is SIRT2 enzymatic tuning of NFATc2. Because NFATc2 drives interleukin and hypertrophic gene programs, its deacetylation influences inflammation and cardiac remodeling. It links SIRT2 to calcineurin/NFAT signaling.

Genetic knockdown and chemical inhibition of SIRT2 attenuate TGF-β1-induced fibroblast activation and MDM2 expression, reducing fibrogenic responses. The directionality is SIRT2 inhibition → less TGF-β1 fibroblast activation. This is unusual because it implies SIRT2 can promote, rather than suppress, fibrosis in this context. It underscores the context-dependence of sirtuin-fibrosis relationships.

Cytoplasmic SIRT2 directly binds to the 3'-UTR of TFEB mRNA and facilitates its stability, promoting lysosomal biogenesis and autophagosome-lysosome fusion. [HYPOTHESIS: novel finding from triple database]

SIRT2 deacetylates BRCA1 and promotes its localization to DNA-damage foci; SIRT2 knockdown impairs homologous recombination repair. The directionality is SIRT2 enzymatic licensing of BRCA1 for repair. This links cytoplasmic/nuclear SIRT2 to genome stability. It reveals a tumor-suppressive function of SIRT2 through DNA-repair fidelity.

SIRT2 is the first identified tubulin deacetylase, with α-tubulin as its most characterized substrate; deacetylation regulates microtubule stability and dynamics. The directionality is SIRT2 enzymatic tuning of α-tubulin acetylation. Reduced α-tubulin acetylation is linked to neurodegeneration, explaining why SIRT2 inhibitors protect neurons. It is the mechanistic basis for SIRT2's mitotic and axonal roles.

SIRT2 deacetylates FOXO1 in the cytoplasm, regulating its transcriptional and pro-autophagic activity in a manner distinct from nuclear SIRT1. The directionality is SIRT2 enzymatic tuning of FOXO1. This influences metabolic and stress responses in the cytosolic compartment. It shows overlapping yet compartment-specific sirtuin control of FOXO factors.

SIRT2 deacetylates FOXO3a, regulating its transcriptional activity in the cytoplasm and contributing to stress-resistance and autophagic programs. The directionality is SIRT2 enzymatic modification of FOXO3a. This complements SIRT1/SIRT3 actions on the same factor. It broadens the sirtuin–FOXO regulatory network.

links.context: The small-molecule ATG4B inhibitor S130 blocks the cysteine protease required for LC3 processing and autophagosome maturation; when combined with caloric restriction, this inhibition shifts the balance toward apoptotic death in colorectal cancer cells. By preventing autophagic protection of tumor cells while CR imposes metabolic stress, S130 sensitizes malignancy to cell death. The synergy illustrates a therapeutic strategy of pairing CR or CR-mimetics with targeted autophagy inhibition in cancer. The approach exploits the reliance of some tumors on basal autophagy for survival.

Insulin signaling inhibits autophagy by activating the PI3K-Akt axis, which in turn activates mTORC1 and promotes phosphorylation of ULK1 and TFEB that suppress autophagic initiation and lysosomal gene expression. Through this cascade, the fed-state hormone maintains an anabolic, autophagy-off condition in peripheral tissues. The relief of insulin signaling during fasting or caloric restriction is therefore prerequisite for autophagic induction. This relationship is a primary reason why nutrient excess and insulin resistance are associated with impaired autophagy and metabolic disease.

Akt phosphorylates and inhibits the FOXO1/FOXO3 transcription factors, which normally promote autophagy and stress-resistance gene expression, thereby indirectly suppressing autophagy downstream of insulin/PI3K signaling. The reciprocal interaction reflects the broader antagonism between growth-factor-driven anabolism (via Akt-mTOR) and the autophagy-promoting FOXO program. When Akt is inactive during fasting, FOXO factors are de-repressed and contribute to autophagic and longevity pathways. This axis embeds autophagy control within the insulin-signaling network that also regulates mTORC1.

Ketogenic diets, characterized by high fat and very low carbohydrate intake, activate autophagy by lowering insulin and glucose while elevating ketone bodies and AMPK activity. The metabolic shift toward fatty-acid oxidation and mild energy stress mimics aspects of caloric restriction, engaging the autophagic machinery. This activation contributes to the reported healing and neuroprotective effects of ketogenic regimens in epilepsy, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disease. The diet thus provides a non-fasting nutritional strategy to recruit autophagic clearance.

links.context: The acetyltransferase p300 acetylates ATG4B, an modification that inhibits its proteolytic activity required for LC3 lipidation and autophagosome formation, thereby restraining autophagy under normal conditions. This acetylation-dependent repression adds a transcriptional coactivator-derived control layer to core autophagy machinery beyond the well-studied phosphorylation circuits. Relief of p300-mediated acetylation during stress can de-repress ATG4B and facilitate autophagic flux. The finding situates autophagy regulation within the broader acetylome governed by p300/CBP.

Metabolic Reprogramming is a hallmark of Hallmarks of Cancer. Metabolic reprogramming is the rewiring of nutrient uptake and bioenergetics that supplies building blocks and redox balance to proliferating tumors. The Hallmarks of Cancer are the enabling biological capabilities acquired during tumorigenesis, including sustained proliferation, evasion of death, and metastasis. The directionality runs from Hallmarks of Cancer toward Metabolic Reprogramming, so Hallmarks of Cancer is the active agent and Metabolic Reprogramming the recipient of the effect. Together these facts situate the relationship within the broader architecture of cancer biology, clarifying how the two entities connect as part of the hallmark or taxonomic framework.

Metabolic Reprogramming includes Warburg Effect. Metabolic reprogramming is the rewiring of nutrient uptake and bioenergetics that supplies building blocks and redox balance to proliferating tumors. The Warburg effect is the preference of many cancer cells for aerobic glycolysis with lactate fermentation even in the presence of oxygen, supporting anabolic growth. The relationship is directional, with Metabolic Reprogramming acting as the operative agent upon Warburg Effect rather than the reverse. Together these facts situate the relationship within the broader architecture of cancer biology, clarifying how the two entities connect as part of the hallmark or taxonomic framework.

Metabolic Reprogramming relates to GLUT1 through the relation involves. Metabolic reprogramming is the rewiring of nutrient uptake and bioenergetics that supplies building blocks and redox balance to proliferating tumors. GLUT1 is a high-capacity glucose transporter markedly upregulated on the tumor-cell surface to feed the glycolytic phenotype. The interaction is specific and directional within the cancer context. Understanding this link contributes to the broader map of tumor biology and potential intervention points.

Metabolic Reprogramming relates to Hexokinase 2 through the relation involves. Metabolic reprogramming is the rewiring of nutrient uptake and bioenergetics that supplies building blocks and redox balance to proliferating tumors. Hexokinase 2 is the glycolytic first-step enzyme most strongly induced in cancer, where it often tethers to mitochondria to couple glycolysis to survival. The interaction is specific and directional within the cancer context. Understanding this link contributes to the broader map of tumor biology and potential intervention points.

Metabolic Reprogramming relates to Pyruvate Kinase M2 through the relation involves. Metabolic reprogramming is the rewiring of nutrient uptake and bioenergetics that supplies building blocks and redox balance to proliferating tumors. Pyruvate kinase M2 is the embryonic/warburg isoform that diverts glycolytic flux toward biosynthetic precursors rather than efficient ATP production. The interaction is specific and directional within the cancer context. Understanding this link contributes to the broader map of tumor biology and potential intervention points.

Metabolic Reprogramming is inhibited by Fenbendazole. Metabolic reprogramming is the rewiring of nutrient uptake and bioenergetics that supplies building blocks and redox balance to proliferating tumors. Fenbendazole is a benzimidazole anthelmintic under investigation for anticancer effects via microtubule interference, glycolysis suppression, and p53 activation. The directionality runs from Fenbendazole toward Metabolic Reprogramming, so Fenbendazole is the active agent and Metabolic Reprogramming the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.
ERK phosphorylates BIM at Ser55/Ser65/Ser100, causing inactivation under the control of cytokine IL3.

YAP1 promotes Cancer. YAP1 is the transcriptional co-activator of the Hippo pathway that, when nuclear, promotes proliferation and is inhibited by ivermectin in several cancers. Cancer is a family of diseases driven by the stepwise acquisition of mutations and epimutations that confer proliferative autonomy, survival, and dissemination. The relationship is directional, with YAP1 acting as the operative agent upon Cancer rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

YAP1 is inhibited by Ivermectin. YAP1 is the transcriptional co-activator of the Hippo pathway that, when nuclear, promotes proliferation and is inhibited by ivermectin in several cancers. Ivermectin is an approved antiparasitic drug repurposed in oncology for its multi-kinase, anti-Wnt, and pro-death activities across cancers. The directionality runs from Ivermectin toward YAP1, so Ivermectin is the active agent and YAP1 the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

BRCA repairs DNA Damage. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressors that orchestrate homology-directed repair of DNA double-strand breaks and genome stability. DNA damage, particularly unrepaired double-strand breaks, is both a driver of mutagenesis and a trigger of p53-dependent tumor suppression. The relationship is directional, with BRCA acting as the operative agent upon DNA Damage rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

BRCA predisposes to Breast Cancer. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressors that orchestrate homology-directed repair of DNA double-strand breaks and genome stability. Breast cancer is a heterogeneous malignancy in which molecular subtypes (luminal, HER2-enriched, basal/triple-negative) dictate targeted therapy choice. The relationship is directional, with BRCA acting as the operative agent upon Breast Cancer rather than the reverse. Such relationships underscore how inherited or intrinsic factors shape cancer susceptibility and inform risk-stratified screening and prevention.

BRCA predisposes to ovarian cancer. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressors that orchestrate homology-directed repair of DNA double-strand breaks and genome stability. High-grade serous ovarian cancer is characterized by frequent BRCA1/2 dysfunction and exquisite sensitivity to platinum and PARP inhibition. ABT-263 inhibits Bcl-2. ABT-263 (navitoclax) is the orally bioavailable successor to ABT-737 whose Bcl-xL inhibition causes on-target thrombocytopenia. Bcl-2 is the founding anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family member that preserves mitochondrial outer-membrane integrity and was the first apoptosis regulator linked to cancer. The relationship is directional, with ABT-263 acting as the operative agent upon Bcl-2 rather than the reverse. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

ABT-263 causes Thrombocytopenia. ABT-263 (navitoclax) is the orally bioavailable successor to ABT-737 whose Bcl-xL inhibition causes on-target thrombocytopenia. Thrombocytopenia is an abnormally low platelet count that, when caused by Bcl-xL inhibition, reflects the dependence of platelets on that survival protein. The relationship is directional, with ABT-263 acting as the operative agent upon Thrombocytopenia rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

ABT-263 (navitoclax) is the orally bioavailable successor developed to overcome the poor solubility of the earlier pan-BH3 mimetic ABT-737. Both agents inhibit Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, and Bcl-w, but ABT-263 enabled clinical translation. The relationship is directional in drug-development lineage rather than biological mechanism. Its Bcl-xL inhibition still causes on-target thrombocytopenia, limiting the achievable dose.
